Run the damping test at those frequencies (start damping around 0.1-0.2)
Save to firmware, e.g. Klipper SET_INPUT_SHAPER or Marlin M593, and to the printer profile
Repeat yearly or after moving the printer or changing belts, motors or frame
facts: Built-in accelerometer calibration is usually more accurate and faster
RepRapFirmware can only set one frequency for both axes
Default shaper types: Klipper MZV, Marlin ZV, RRF 3.4+ MZV

entries.title: Max volumetric speed (max flowrate) test
entries.summary: The max flowrate test prints a tower whose volumetric flow increases with height. Find where the surface starts to fail (gaps, roughness, or a change from glossy to matte) and measure that height. Max flow = start + height x step. The result is a best case without retractions, so set the filament's max volumetric speed 10-20% lower. Printing near the limit weakens layers and risks clogs.
steps: Set the nozzle temperature first; a hotter nozzle allows more flow
Open Calibration > Max flowrate; defaults are 5 to 20 mm3/s in 0.5 steps
Print and measure the height just below the first defects
Compute start + height x step, e.g. 5 + 19 x 0.5 = 14.5 mm3/s
Or read the flow at that height in the Preview with the Flow color scheme
Save 80-90% of the result as max volumetric speed in the filament profile

settings.advice: Enter 10-20% below the measured failure point.

sources.title: OrcaSlicer wiki - Max Volumetric Speed calibration
Ellis' Print Tuning Guide - Determining max volumetric flow rate

entries.title: Pressure advance line method
entries.summary: The line method prints single lines that switch between slow and fast sections, each at a different PA value. Choose the line with the most even width through the speed changes. It is the fastest test but depends heavily on first-layer quality, so use bed mesh leveling and a good Z offset before running it.
steps: Make sure bed leveling or mesh is active and the first layer is good
Run the PA line test for direct drive or Bowden
Pick the line with no thickening or thinning at speed transitions
Save the value, e.g. 0.016, as pressure advance in the filament profile

settings.advice: Enter the PA of the most uniform line.

entries.title: Pressure advance pattern method (chevrons)
entries.summary: The pattern method, adapted from Andrew Ellis' generator, prints rows of nested chevrons, each at a different PA value labeled with numbers. Pick the row whose corner tips are sharpest with no bulge (PA too low) and no gap or thinning (PA too high). It is quick, readable and can batch several tests on one plate, which is also how adaptive PA data is gathered.
steps: Open the PA pattern test, set start, end and step (e.g. 0.001 steps for fine tuning)
Optionally add several speed/acceleration combinations for batch tests
Print; move the small prism handle to place the pattern on the plate
Choose the row with the sharpest corners and even lines
Save the value in the filament profile

settings.advice: Use the best row; if two rows look equally good, either is fine.

facts: The pattern uses only default and first-layer line widths, and first-layer and outer-wall speeds
The pattern is added as custom G-code per layer, so its fill cannot be changed in infill settings
Test parameters such as flow and acceleration are printed on the sample in newer versions

entries.title: Pressure advance tower method
entries.summary: The PA tower raises pressure advance by one step per millimeter of height. It takes longer but does not depend on first-layer quality. Look at the corners and seams, find the height with the sharpest corners without bulges or gaps, and compute PA = start + step x height. Choose the direct-drive or Bowden version of the test. When in doubt between heights, prefer the lower value.
steps: Select printer, filament and process; choose direct drive or Bowden version
Run the PA tower from the Calibration menu and print it
Ignore the corner where the layer change happens; judge the other corners
Measure the height with the best corners using calipers
Compute start + step x height, e.g. 0 + 0.002 x 8 = 0.016
Save it as pressure advance in the filament profile

settings.advice: Enter the computed value; slightly lower if unsure.
Enable so the value is sent with the filament.

facts: Marlin needs Linear Advance (M900) enabled in firmware
Klipper's own tuning tower uses factor 0.005 per mm for direct drive and 0.020 for long Bowden
On belt printers only the tower method is available

entries.title: OrcaSlicer calibration order: which test to run first
entries.summary: Run filament calibrations in order, because each builds on the last: temperature, max volumetric speed, pressure advance, flow ratio, then retraction. Repeat these for each new filament. Advanced tests (cornering, input shaping, VFA, adaptive PA, tolerance) tune the printer and only need repeating after hardware changes; do tolerance last. Start a new project afterwards to leave calibration mode.
steps: Confirm extruder E-steps or rotation distance in firmware (usually correct from the factory)
Temperature tower: pick the nozzle temperature
Max volumetric speed: set the flow limit 10-20% below the failure point
Pressure advance: tower, pattern or line method
Flow ratio: YOLO or 2-pass; rerun PA if flow changed a lot
Retraction test, only if stringing remains
Optional: cornering, input shaping, VFA, adaptive PA, then tolerance last
Save results to the filament or printer profile and create a new project
facts: Orca runs PA before flow ratio because PA is more often wrong and a tuned PA makes the flow test easier to read
Printers with built-in accelerometer input shaping should use that instead of the manual test

entries.title: Retraction test tower
entries.summary: The retraction test prints a tower whose retraction length increases with height. Find the lowest section with clean, string-free travel and look up its value at that height (search the Calib_Retraction_tower comment in the G-code preview). Use the shortest length that is clean. Defaults (0-2 mm, 0.1 mm steps) suit direct drive; Bowden users can try 1-6 mm in 0.2 mm steps. If strings remain at the top, dry the filament and check the nozzle.
steps: Calibrate pressure advance and flow ratio first, since both change nozzle pressure
Open Calibration > Retraction test; set start, end and step
Print with your usual Z-hop and high fan for these small towers
Find the lowest clean section and measure its height
Read the retraction length at that height from the Calib_Retraction_tower comment
Save it as retraction length (or as a filament override)

settings.advice: Shortest length that gives a clean section.
About 30-40 mm/s; rerun the test if you change it a lot.

facts: For low-ooze filaments like PLA or ABS the tower may be clean from the start; 0.2-0.4 mm is then enough
Use the calibration comment, not the ; retract line, because the latter omits retract-before-wipe amounts
Ellis notes very wet filament can make stringing nearly unfixable by retraction alone

entries.title: Temperature tower calibration and how to read it
entries.summary: The temperature tower prints stacked blocks at different nozzle temperatures. Pick the block with the best balance of low stringing, good bridges and overhangs, clean surface and strong layers (try snapping blocks apart). If several look good, use the middle, or the upper end if you print fast. Enter it as the filament's nozzle temperature. Too cold gives under-extrusion and weak layers; too hot gives stringing, sagging and degradation.
steps: Select printer, filament and process, then Calibration > Temperature
Set the temperature range around the manufacturer's recommended range
Slice and print; auto-scale adapts the tower to your nozzle size
Inspect each block for stringing, bridges, overhang sag and surface finish
Test layer strength by trying to break blocks
Save the chosen value as nozzle temperature in the filament profile

settings.advice: Set to the best block; use the hotter end of the good range for high-speed printing.
Usually the same or up to 5 C hotter than the chosen temperature.

sources.title: Bambu Lab forum - PLA matte layer adhesion (temperature tower to judge strength)

entries.title: Tolerance test for holes and fit
entries.summary: The Orca tolerance test is a handy model: a base with six hexagonal holes at clearances of 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4 mm plus a hex tester (or use a 6 mm Allen key). Measure the holes and tester with calipers and see which clearance fits. Adjust XY hole and contour compensation, and filament shrinkage if the whole part is scaled, then reprint until fits are right. Do this last, after all other calibration.
steps: In Prepare, right-click the plate > Add Handy Model > Orca Tolerance Test
Print with your normal profile and filament
Check which hole the tester or 6 mm Allen key fits; measure with calipers
Adjust XY hole compensation (holes) and XY contour compensation (outside size)
Reprint to confirm

settings.advice: Increase if holes are tight; change in small steps.
Use negative values if outer sizes are too big.
Correct uniform scaling errors from material shrinkage.
Enable to improve outer dimensional accuracy.

entries.title: VFA speed test for vertical fine artifacts
entries.summary: Vertical fine artifacts are small regular ripples on walls, often from stepper motor resonance at certain speeds. The VFA test prints a tower with angled walls at increasing speeds. Look for speed bands where the surface gets rougher or smoother, then set resonance avoidance to skip the bad band, or choose outer wall speeds outside it. Run it after input shaping.
steps: Set a speed range covering all outer wall speeds you use (e.g. 20-200 mm/s) and a step (e.g. 10 mm/s)
Print the tower; check whether filament max volumetric speed capped the top speed
Mark the heights where ripples appear and convert them to speeds
Enter that band in resonance avoidance, or pick an outer wall speed outside it

settings.advice: Enable and enter the band found in the test.
Lower edge of the artifact band.
Upper edge of the artifact band.
Choose a speed outside the artifact band.

facts: Jerk/junction deviation and mechanical issues such as belts and pulleys also contribute to VFA
Don't slow down outer walls helps avoid layer-cooling slowdowns pushing walls into a VFA speed band

entries.title: Snapmaker Artisan 3D printing specifications
entries.summary: With the dual extrusion module the Artisan prints 350 x 400 x 400 mm using both nozzles, 375 mm wide with only the left nozzle and 400 mm with only the right. Nozzles reach 300 C; recommended print speed is up to 180 mm/s. The dual textured PEI bed has a 260 x 260 mm inner zone to 110 C, with the outer zone limited to 80 C. Only the right hotend lifts on its own; the left moves with the module.
facts: Work area: 350 x 400 x 400 mm dual nozzle; 375 mm wide left nozzle only; 400 x 400 x 400 mm right nozzle only
Standard 0.4 mm brass nozzle; 0.2, 0.6, 0.8 mm and hardened steel optional
Max nozzle temperature 300 C; max recommended speed 180 mm/s
Bed inner zone 260 x 260 mm up to 110 C; outer zone up to 80 C
Supported: PLA, ABS, ASA, PETG, TPU of 90 Shore A or harder, breakaway PLA, PVA, HIPS, nylon, CF/GF nylon
Hardened steel nozzle required for nylon and reinforced nylon
TMC2209 drivers, 40 mm lead X/Y and 8 mm lead Z linear modules, repeatability +/-0.05 mm
Only the right hotend raises and lowers independently (forum answer confirmed by support)

sources.title: Snapmaker Artisan left nozzle doesn't lift up (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Artisan auto-calibration drives the nozzle into the bed
entries.summary: Artisan owners have had calibration drive the head down until it scraped the bed. One case was a loose jumper on the Z limit switch being hit by the cable track; reseating it per the wiki limit-switch guide fixed homing. Others recovered with a factory reset or M502/M500. After calibration several users still add about +0.1 to +0.4 mm Z offset on the touchscreen.
symptoms: Nozzle scrapes or presses into the bed during calibration
Manual calibration page stays blank until auto calibration succeeds
causes: Z limit switch not triggering (loose jumper or connector)
Corrupted calibration data
Filament drag lifting the right hotend during the calibration print
steps: Home the machine and watch whether Z stops at the limit switch
Open the linear module and check the limit-switch jumper and cable, per the wiki guide
Try a factory reset from Maintenance, or send M502 then M500
Protect the bed with paper while testing
After a successful calibration, fine-tune Z offset on the touchscreen in 0.05-0.1 mm steps

settings.advice: A slightly thicker first layer tolerates a few hundredths of a mm of offset error.

sources.title: Artisan autocalibration failing and bed scarping (Snapmaker forum)
Snapmaker Artisan left nozzle doesn't lift up (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Idle nozzle oozing onto prints with the Artisan dual extrusion module
entries.summary: In dual prints the idle nozzle on the Artisan can drip onto the part. A forum moderator used about 15 mm tool-change retraction at 1500 mm/min (25 mm/s) with an ooze shield and prime tower. Some users saw less ooze after removing the nozzle silicone covers; another thread reports raising rather than lowering temperature helped, without a clear explanation. Check the idle temperature your slicer sets is actually reaching the printer.
steps: Enable a prime tower, and an ooze shield (draft shield) if drips persist
Set tool-change retraction around 15 mm at about 25 mm/s and tune from there
Use ooze prevention with a lower idle temperature, and confirm on the controller that it applies
Try printing without the silicone nozzle covers if drool remains

settings.advice: About 15 mm at 25 mm/s worked for one experienced user on the dual module.
Keep on so each nozzle is primed and wiped after a switch.
An enabled shield around the part catches drips from the idle nozzle.
Drops the idle nozzle temperature between uses; verify the printer honours it.

entries.title: Heat creep clogs on long dual prints and idle temperature on the Artisan
entries.summary: Users report dual-module nozzles clogging 30 minutes to 2 hours into long prints, even with the enclosure door open. One Artisan owner found slicers' idle temperature did not take effect, so both nozzles sat above 200 C; setting the idle nozzle to 50 C manually reduced heat creep. Other remedies: the official ventilated front door, heat-break thermal paste, dry filament and calibrated e-steps.
symptoms: Extrusion stops on one nozzle after a while
Filament pulled out shows a swollen end
causes: Idle nozzle kept at print temperature for long periods
Weak heat-sink cooling of the original module door
Many retraction cycles on dual prints
steps: Watch the controller during a dual print to see the idle nozzle's real temperature
If it stays near print temperature, lower it manually or enable ooze prevention
Fit the replacement-kit front cover
Dry filament and calibrate e-steps before tuning retraction

settings.advice: A low idle value reduces heat creep in the waiting nozzle; check the printer applies it.
Use a large negative delta so the idle nozzle cools meaningfully.

sources.title: I give up on Dual Extrusion thanks to heat creep (Snapmaker forum)
Dual Extrusion Head: Heat creep discussion thread (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Artisan XY offset calibration will not save Y or results look far off
entries.summary: One Artisan owner could save X but not Y during XY offset calibration, with test lines far apart. Support said the module's stored default offsets had changed and had them restore defaults with M2000 F5 X26 Y0 Z-1.5, entered in the Luban Workspace console, then save with M500. Recalibration then worked with both values at centre. Another user fixed the same symptom by swapping hotends.
steps: Check both hotends are fully seated and the nozzles sit level
Try swapping the left and right hotends and recalibrating
If it still fails, contact support with exported logs
If support confirms changed defaults, connect Luban, open the Workspace console and send M2000 F5 X26 Y0 Z-1.5
Send M500 to store the values, then rerun XY offset calibration

sources.title: Initial setup: X Offset Calibration says it saved, but save Y Offset screen just loops (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Snapmaker dual extrusion module clogging, popping levers and false runouts: the replacement kit
entries.summary: The same dual extrusion module is used on the Artisan and Snapmaker 2.0. Snapmaker linked its clogging to poor heat-sink cooling and its failures to feeder levers popping open and a filament sensor lever wearing into false runouts. The 2023 replacement kit has a better-ventilated front cover, silicone buckle wedges, a new sensor part and 0.5 mm bed shims for the Artisan platform. Snapmaker advises fitting it only if you have these symptoms.
symptoms: Nozzle stops extruding 30 minutes to 2 hours into dual prints
Feeder levers pop open
Filament runout alarms with filament present
Leveling misses points on some Artisan platforms
causes: Insufficient heat sink airflow through the original metal front door
Buckle loosening on the feeder levers
Wear on the runout sensor trigger lever
Incomplete platform contact during leveling on some Artisans
steps: Fit the redesigned front cover (or print Snapmaker's published front-cover STL in PLA, flat)
Install the silicone buckle wedges to stop levers popping
Replace the filament runout sensor part if false alarms continue
On Artisan, add the 0.5 mm silicone bed shims if leveling contact is incomplete
Follow the Snapmaker wiki guides for each part
facts: Support suggested M412 S0 (disable runout detection) as a temporary workaround for false runouts to one user
Users who fitted the new door and wedges report long two-filament prints without heat creep

sources.title: Front Cover STL file & Replacement Kit Update (Dual Extrusion Module) (Snapmaker forum)
Dual extruder clogging and new Replacement Kit (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: 'Extruder is continuously pulled up' error on the Artisan / 2.0 dual extrusion module
entries.summary: The dual module's right hotend is on a spring, so filament drag can lift it and trigger 'extruder is continuously pulled up', pausing the print. Users trace it to feed resistance: spools not rolling freely, heavy or cardboard spools, long PTFE runs from dry boxes and tangles. Fixes were free-turning spools, short feed paths, the buckle wedges, and reseating the hotend. A warped part hitting the nozzle can also trigger it.
symptoms: Print pauses with extruder continuously pulled up
Error clears when you pull some slack by hand
causes: High pulling force from the spool or feed tube
Cardboard spools or spools rubbing on rollers
Long PTFE tubes from external dry boxes
Filament tangled on the spool
Hotend not fully snapped in
Warped print surface pushing the nozzle up
steps: Check how hard it is to pull filament by hand at the toolhead
Mount spools so they turn freely, for example hung on a rod or standing on bearings
Shorten PTFE tubes or place dry boxes close to the toolhead
Check the spool for crossed windings
Unclip and re-snap the hotend
Fit the silicone buckle wedges from the replacement kit

sources.title: Extruder is continuously pulled up (Snapmaker forum)
Help - The Extruder is continuously pulled up and printing is paused? (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: J1 'Calibration Failed' during XY offset or bed calibration
entries.summary: J1 calibration detects nozzle contact electrically through the hotend, so a loose heat-sink fan screw (part of that path) or a wire pinched during hotend service makes calibration fail. Another cause is a Y belt that jumped a tooth in shipping, leaving the X axis out of square so the head misses its targets. Support also showed users how to exit the setup wizard to fix this.
symptoms: Calibration Failed near the datum point
Head misses the left contact point
Stalling sound on the Y axis
causes: Loose heat sink fan screw breaking the contact path
Pinched fan or sensor wire after hotend disassembly
Dirty nozzle
Y belt skipped teeth, X axis not perpendicular
steps: Clean both nozzle tips
Check the hotend heat-sink fan screws are tight and no wire is pinched
With motors off, check whether the X rail is square to the Y rails
If not square, realign following support's belt and coupling guidance
For the right extruder, set height with its adjustment wheel rather than bed knobs
Re-run calibration after every firmware update

sources.title: J1s First Use - Calibration Failure, possibly need to factory reset? (Snapmaker forum)
Copy and Mirror not available on dual extruder models (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Snapmaker J1/J1s hotend clogging, clicking extruders and the newer press-fit hotend
entries.summary: Clogging was the J1's most reported fault. Snapmaker's analysis blamed retraction set too high, false 'failed to load filament' alarms, misaligned or loose extruder gears, wet or silk filament, and factory defects (metal debris in nozzles, badly cut internal PTFE, thermal paste leaks). It released an all-metal hardened press-fit hotend that reached 20 mm3/s in Snapmaker's test versus 16 mm3/s for the original, but its nozzle is not swappable. Some owners instead fitted a Bondtech copperhead heat break.
symptoms: Extruder clicking and skips
Repeated failed-to-load or clog warnings
Under-extrusion mid-print
causes: Excessive retraction distance pulling soft plastic into the heat break
Loose drive gear set screw or misaligned gears
Moist or silk filament
Factory defects in early hotends
Short melt zone of the original hotend
steps: Lower retraction distance; one user also cut retraction speed from 40 to 25 mm/s and stopped load errors
Check the extruder drive-gear grub screw is tight and gears line up
Dry filament and avoid problem silk spools
Raise temperature or slow down for high-flow prints
Feed filament with less friction (top-down feed or a PTFE guide)
Replace a hotend with internal defects; consider the newer all-metal hotend

settings.advice: Keep low on the J1; Snapmaker named over-long retraction as a common clog cause.
Slower retraction (about 25 mm/s) helped one user stop filament-load errors.
Stay near 16 mm3/s on the original hotend; the newer hotend handled about 20 mm3/s in Snapmaker tests.

sources.title: J1/J1s Clogging Issues and New Hotend Kit Update (Snapmaker forum)
Findings and solution for the Snapmaker J1 clogging problem (Snapmaker forum)
Things to do first with a new J1 (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: J1 says copy or mirror mode is disabled for dual-extrusion models
entries.summary: Copy and mirror are chosen on the J1 touchscreen at print time, and only work on G-code that references a single extruder. Any trace of the second extruder (enabled in Cura, a prime tower, support, brim or skirt on it) makes the J1 refuse with 'copy or mirror mode is disabled for dual-extrusion models'. Both heads use the main extruder's settings, so two materials with different temperatures cannot run in copy mode.
symptoms: Touchscreen message that copy/mirror is disabled for dual-extrusion models
Copy mode starts but the left head prints in the wrong place
causes: Second extruder enabled or referenced in the slicer
Model placed outside the copy/mirror area
Firmware updated without re-running calibration
steps: Slice with only extruder 1 (left) assigned to everything; disable extruder 2
Turn off the prime tower and make sure skirt, brim and supports use extruder 1
Keep the model within the reduced copy (160 mm) or mirror (150 mm) width
Choose Copy or Mirror on the touchscreen when starting the print
Load the same material in both heads; the second head follows the first head's settings
Re-run all calibrations after a major firmware update

settings.advice: Disable when slicing for copy or mirror mode so no second-extruder moves remain.

sources.title: Copy and Mirror not available on dual extruder models (Snapmaker forum)
2 different materials in copy/mirror mode possible? (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: J1 firmware notes: direct Snapmaker Orca upload, M600 and Z-offset steps
entries.summary: J1 firmware V2.8.0 (beta from late 2025, released 2026) lets Snapmaker Orca send jobs over Wi-Fi without Luban using the OctoPrint protocol at the printer's IP plus port 8080. Known issues: jobs fail if Luban and Orca upload together, and uploads can stall at 0% until reboot. Earlier releases added M600 pause (2.4.7), homing stall detection (2.4.7), glass thickness (2.5.9) and 0.01 mm Z-offset steps (2.7.1).
steps: Update the J1 to V2.8.0 via USB (Settings > Firmware Update > Local Update) or Wi-Fi
In Snapmaker Orca add the printer with the printer IP followed by :8080
Do not send jobs from Luban and Orca at the same time
If an upload hangs at 0%, restart the printer and send logs to support

sources.title: Snapmaker J1/J1s Firmware Updates and Downloads (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: J1 hotend swaps, mirrored left/right heads and clearing a clog
entries.summary: J1 hotends come off with two screws and are auto-identified by a PCB, but left and right are mirrored and cannot be swapped between sides. Both sides share identical heat sinks, heater blocks, heat breaks, fans and nozzles. Nozzles are standard MK7/MK8, though a manually swapped nozzle is not detected. Most clogs clear without parts: open the latch, heat to about 250 C and push filament with the H2.0 key.
steps: Open the latch on the printhead front to release gear tension and see the filament
For a hotend clog, heat to about 250 C and push filament through with the H2.0 hex key
Remove debris from the extruder gears with tweezers if the clog is above the hotend
To replace a hotend, loosen its two screws and fit the correct side part
After manually changing a nozzle size, set the diameter yourself since detection reads the hotend PCB

entries.title: J1 knocking noise, layer shifts and Z banding from dry linear bearings
entries.summary: Early J1s often shipped with almost dry linear rails and Z bearings, causing knocking noises, layer shifts and Z-banding. Users recommend an NLGI class 1 or 2 grease made for linear bearings. Grease on the rod or rail surface barely enters sealed bearings, so users inject it with a fine syringe. Newer carriages with green sides are the improved version; a hot X motor was also suspected in one noise case.
symptoms: Rhythmic beating or knocking during fast moves
Layer shifts after hours of printing
Regular marks on walls (Z-binding)
Clicking when the bed moves
causes: Insufficient factory grease in linear guides and Z bearings
Damaged balls in a carriage that ran dry
High motor temperature near a bearing
steps: Use a grease rated for linear bearings, NLGI 1 or 2
For Z bearings, use a 3 ml luer-lock syringe with a straight 25G tip slid along the rod past the seal
Inject from top and bottom at several points, then run the axis slowly to spread it
Repeat greasing a few times until clicking stops
Follow the wiki axis lubrication guide for rails and carriages
Replace carriages or bearings that stay rough after greasing

sources.title: Snapmaker J1 Linear Bearings Z-Binding Issues (Snapmaker forum)
Things to do first with a new J1 (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Why the J1 still uses a prime tower despite its nozzle wipers
entries.summary: Snapmaker explained that a prime tower may be skippable on IDEX at low temperature and speed (about 195 C PLA at 40-60 mm/s). At its 200 mm/s-plus speeds the J1 needs PLA above about 210 C, so the idle nozzle oozes despite the silicone pad, and a tower is recommended for clean two-colour prints. Each J1 head can use a different nozzle size in one print.

settings.advice: Keep on for fast dual-colour J1 prints; consider off only for slow, low-temperature prints.
Lowering the idle head's temperature reduces drips between swaps.
Sets how far the idle head drops below print temperature when ooze prevention is on.

entries.title: Snapmaker J1/J1s IDEX specifications and print-mode build volumes
entries.summary: The J1s is an IDEX printer with two independent toolheads on a shared X axis. Default and backup modes use 300 x 200 x 200 mm; copy mode shrinks width to 160 mm and mirror mode to 150 mm. Rated 350 mm/s and 10,000 mm/s2, hotends to 300 C, bed to 100 C, on a PEI/glass hybrid plate. XY offsets are measured by electrical contact; Snapmaker chose glass because it judged mesh compensation impractical on IDEX.
facts: Default and Backup modes: 300 x 200 x 200 mm
Copy mode: 160 x 200 x 200 mm; Mirror mode: 150 x 200 x 200 mm
Max speed 350 mm/s, max acceleration 10,000 mm/s2
Hotend max 300 C; heated bed max 100 C
Paired hotends offered in 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 mm, plus 0.4 mm hardened steel for PA, PA-GF and PA-CF
Layer height 0.05-0.3 mm with a 0.4 mm nozzle
Calibration uses electrical conduction for hands-free XY offset; built-in nozzle wipers; vibration compensation

sources.title: Snapmaker J1s High Speed IDEX 3D Printer - MatterHackers

entries.title: J1 crash protection during calibration and the glass plate
entries.summary: The J1's TMC2209 drivers use StallGuard to stop the bed rising when the nozzle fails to register contact during calibration, preventing a crash into the bed. Snapmaker found the extra weight of the glass plate made detection unreliable on some drivers; firmware V2.2.10 fixed that and added stall protection for Z homing. Keep firmware current and follow the prompt to remove the glass plate before calibrating.
steps: Update firmware past V2.2.10
Remove the glass build plate when the calibration screen tells you to
Stop the machine if the bed keeps rising after the nozzle touches

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 printhead gouging the build plate on first print
entries.summary: Bed gouging was a top early 2.0 complaint. Snapmaker named proximity sensor height, print sheet thickness and firmware as causes, with a guide to lower the sensor to about 1 mm above the nozzle tip after updating firmware and Luban. A user found another cause: socket-head instead of flat-head M4 x 10 screws on the heated bed (22 needed) leave the surface uneven.
symptoms: Nozzle digs into the build sheet during the first layer
First layer looks very flat and thin with no filament visible
causes: Proximity sensor mounted too high relative to the nozzle
Outdated firmware
Socket-head screws used where flat-head screws belong on the heated bed
steps: Update controller firmware and Luban first
Check all 22 bed screws are the flat-head M4 x 10 type
Power off, mount the module so you can reach the sensor screws, lower the nozzle to touch the bed
Set the sensor about 1 mm above the nozzle using a card as a gauge, then remount the module
Re-run auto leveling with a 5 x 5 grid and check the first layer closely

sources.title: Snapmaker official response to print head gouging? (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Getting a good first layer on the Snapmaker 2.0: mesh size and manual tweaks
entries.summary: The 2.0 probes a 3 x 3 grid by default and interpolates a 7 x 7 mesh, which may not match a warped bed. Owners prefer 5 x 5 or larger grids and check points hot with a paper card, then nudge points that are off. M420 V prints the mesh; its top row is the front of the bed. Re-level after module changes or when first layers change, not every print.
steps: Choose a 4 x 4 or 5 x 5 grid for auto leveling
Level with the bed hot at printing temperature
Connect Luban and send M420 V to read the mesh
Use a check-level G-code or a first-layer test across the bed to find high and low spots
Adjust individual points, or re-probe, until a full-bed first layer is even

entries.title: Calibrating extruder e-steps on the Snapmaker 2.0 printing modules
entries.summary: Forum members call e-step calibration a must on Snapmaker 2.0 printing modules. Send M83 and G1 E100 F50 from the Luban console, measure what was actually used, compute new steps as old E x 100 / (100 - remaining), then set with M92 and store with M500. It works the same on the dual extrusion module. Re-check after firmware updates; v1.12.0 reset the value for some users.
steps: Preheat the nozzle to printing temperature and load filament
Mark the filament 100 mm (or 110-120 mm) above the extruder inlet
Connect Luban (USB, or Wi-Fi on newer Luban) and open the console
Send M83 for relative mode, then G1 E100 F50
Measure the remaining distance R to the mark
Send M503 and read the E value on the M92 line
New steps S = E x 100 / (100 - R); for example 212.21 with R = 11 gives 238.44
Send M92 E<S> then M500, power-cycle, and confirm with M503
Repeat the 100 mm test until within about 1 mm
facts: Use a decimal point, not a comma, when entering values
One dual-module owner corrected 5.25 mm under-extrusion to an E value of 704.19
Without M83 the test gives wrong results

sources.title: Summary: Extruder calibration a must (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 layer heights in multiples of 0.04 mm
entries.summary: On Snapmaker Z modules with an 8 mm lead screw and 1.8 degree steppers, one full motor step moves Z by 0.04 mm. A long-standing forum recommendation, which Snapmaker said improved quality and adopted in Luban 3.x presets, is layer heights that are multiples of 0.04 mm between 0.08 and 0.28 mm.

settings.advice: Choose 0.08, 0.12, 0.16, 0.20, 0.24 or 0.28 mm on 8 mm-lead Z modules to land on full motor steps.
Also a multiple of 0.04 mm, such as 0.24 or 0.28 mm.

facts: 8 mm lead / 200 full steps per revolution = 0.04 mm per full step

sources.title: Recommended Layer Heights: Multiples of 0.04mm (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 A vs T/F models: build volumes, temperatures and linear modules
entries.summary: Snapmaker 2.0 models move on lead-screw linear modules. A review gives 230 x 250 x 235 mm (A250T) and 320 x 350 x 330 mm (A350T), 275 C nozzle, and bed limits of 100 C on the A250T versus 80 C on the A350T. Original A models used 8 mm lead modules; T and F models use 20 mm lead XY modules with TMC2209 drivers, which are quieter and faster. Practical print speeds are modest, about 60 mm/s by that review.
facts: A250T build volume 230 x 250 x 235 mm; A350T 320 x 350 x 330 mm
Max nozzle temperature 275 C
Max bed temperature 100 C (A250T) and 80 C (A350T); the review found the A350T bed slow to heat
Original A models: 8 mm lead XY modules; T/F and upgraded modules: 20 mm lead XY (engraved, quieter)
Bed attaches with 22 screws, so swapping work platforms takes time without the Quick Swap Kit
Leveling uses a proximity sensor and works only with the magnetic heated bed

sources.title: Vibration Compensation Beta Firmware for 2.0 Series (Snapmaker forum)
Vibration Compensation Firmware Open Beta for 2.0 Series (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 problems after fitting the Quick Swap Kit or Bracing Kit
entries.summary: The Quick Swap Kit fits A250/A350 and their T/F versions (not the A150) and needs recalibration on first use. Users' calibration and leveling problems after fitting the Quick Swap or Bracing Kit often came from the kit status set on the touchscreen not matching the hardware. One F250 lost its mesh at every reboot because the bracing kit was marked installed when it was not. Usable work area also shrinks with these kits.
symptoms: Leveling data lost after every restart
Head drags or scars the bed after installing a kit
Wrong start position or reduced printable area
causes: Kit installed/not-installed status set incorrectly in touchscreen settings or Luban
Old calibration data after changing the mechanics
steps: In the touchscreen settings, set Quick Swap and Bracing Kit status to exactly what is installed
Match the same options in Luban or your slicer's printer profile
Update firmware, power-cycle and run a full bed calibration
Reduce the slicer bed size to the smaller work area with the kits
If Z remains wrong, note manual settings and try a factory reset

sources.title: The long-awaited quick swap kit for Snapmaker 2.0 250/350 machines (Snapmaker forum)
A350 Won't level correctly after installing bracing kit (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Retraction on Snapmaker 2.0 single and dual extrusion modules
entries.summary: An experienced user says Luban's single extruder default of about 5 mm at 60 mm/s is too much for a direct drive and causes clogs and stringing. That user settled on 1 mm at 10 mm/s for PLA and 2 mm at 50 mm/s for PETG. Luban's dual-module PLA profile uses 1 mm at 35 mm/s normally and 16 mm at 25 mm/s on nozzle switch. Users suspect frequent dual-print retractions grind filament, so calibrate e-steps first, then tune with retraction towers.
steps: Calibrate e-steps first so retraction distances are accurate
Print a retraction tower varying only distance, then one varying only speed
Keep normal retraction short (about 1-2 mm) on direct drive modules
On the dual module, tune switch retraction separately from normal retraction
Limit retractions on short travels to reduce filament grinding

settings.advice: About 1-2 mm on the direct-drive 2.0 modules; 5 mm is reported to cause clogs.
Users found slower values (10-35 mm/s) cleaner than 60 mm/s for PLA.
Luban's dual-module PLA default is 16 mm at 25 mm/s; tune per filament.
Skip retraction on short moves to cut grinding on dual prints.

sources.title: Dual Extrusion Head: Heat creep discussion thread (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Printing TPU on the Snapmaker 2.0 single extrusion module
entries.summary: Owners printing TPU on the 2.0 single extrusion module report that it buckles or coils inside the head when pushed too fast. Working settings shared were 220-235 C, about 15-20 mm/s with no retraction, and infill no faster than walls (Luban's auto infill speed was too fast for one user). One user raised the first-layer Z by about 0.05 mm compared with PLA.
steps: Turn retraction off or nearly off
Print at about 15-20 mm/s, including infill
Use 220-235 C depending on the filament
Raise the first-layer gap slightly compared with PLA
If it jams, open the extruder and look for coiled filament at the gear

settings.advice: Set to 0 or close to it for TPU on the 2.0 module.
Match wall speed (about 15-20 mm/s); fast infill caused jams.
220-235 C; users saw big differences between 210 and 220 C.

sources.title: Printing TPU with A250 (or any SM 2.0) (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 vibration-compensation beta firmware: speeds, limits and Orca upload
entries.summary: Snapmaker offers a separate beta 2.0 firmware with vibration compensation. On 20 mm lead XY modules (F, AT and upgraded A) it raised recommended speed from 100 to 125 mm/s and acceleration from 1000 to 3500 mm/s2, cutting a test Benchy from 1 h 15 min to 33 min. 8 mm lead machines should stay under 60 mm/s with it. Beta v2.4.0 adds direct Snapmaker Orca upload at the printer IP plus :8080; merging into main firmware is on hold.

settings.advice: Up to about 3500 mm/s2 on 20-lead machines with this firmware; keep low on 8-lead modules.

facts: Recommended with 20-lead XY: max print speed 125 mm/s, acceleration 3500 mm/s2
8-lead XY with this firmware: stay under about 60 mm/s or steps may be lost
Known issues listed: X axis can appear tilted on some large models, occasional layer shifts, slight noise while the bed heats
v2.4.0 beta: Snapmaker Orca connects via OctoPrint protocol at <printer IP>:8080; Luban and Orca uploads at the same time fail
Vibration compensation source code was published in the Snapmaker2-Controller GitHub repo in January 2025

sources.title: Vibration Compensation Beta Firmware for 2.0 Series (Snapmaker forum)
Vibration Compensation Firmware Open Beta for 2.0 Series (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: U1 0.2 mm hotend nozzle slides down during filament loading
entries.summary: One user's freshly installed 0.2 mm hotend pushed its nozzle 1.5 mm down during the first load, scraping the cleaning area and bed, while the printer still reported a 0.4 mm nozzle. A second 0.2 mm hotend worked; forum members believed the faulty ones were non-genuine. Set the nozzle size on the printer and in the slicer, and use genuine hotends.
steps: Set the new nozzle diameter on the touchscreen and confirm Fluidd shows the right size
Select the matching 0.2 mm printer profile in Snapmaker Orca
Watch the first load; stop if the nozzle moves relative to the heater block
Replace a hotend whose nozzle shifts; prefer genuine Snapmaker parts (they carry a logo on the side)

settings.advice: Must match the installed hotend, otherwise flow and pressure targets are set for the wrong nozzle.

sources.title: 0.2mm hotend slips down by 1.5mm during loading (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Printing MakerWorld/Bambu 3MF files on the U1 without importing the wrong printer settings
entries.summary: Opening a Bambu 3MF as a project can carry over the original printer, its G-code and single-nozzle flushing settings, which led to errors and failed prints for U1 users. Use Import (Ctrl+I) to bring in geometry and colour painting, then pick U1 profiles; or set load behaviour to always ask and choose geometry only. Community converters exist, though one strips custom painted supports.
steps: Use Import 3MF/STL (Ctrl+I) instead of Open Project for files made for other printers
Or set Preferences > Load behaviour to Always ask and choose Import geometry only
Select the U1 printer, process and filament profiles and map colours to toolheads
Check the Multimaterial settings: a U1 profile should not contain flushing volumes
If you opened the project anyway, inspect settings and switch every profile back to U1 before slicing

settings.advice: Should not be in use on a U1; values here usually mean a single-nozzle printer's project settings were loaded.

sources.title: Easy way to print Makerworld colored files on Snapmaker U1 (Snapmaker forum)
U1 how to minimize prime tower in Orca? (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: U1 bed edges and corners run cooler than the set temperature
entries.summary: The U1 bed has a single sensor in the middle, so the screen shows the centre temperature. Snapmaker staff said corners are usually 5-12 C cooler, more in a cold room. One owner measured 72-74 C mid-bed and low 60s at the corners with 80 C set and had large parts lift at the edges. Snapmaker's FAQ calls heating generally uniform, so expect differences across the plate.
symptoms: Corners of large parts lift while the centre sticks
Poor adhesion only near the plate edges, often front left
causes: Single central sensor and heat loss at the edges
Low room temperature or no top cover
steps: Place warping-prone parts toward the centre and away from the edges
Let the bed soak for several minutes before printing
Raise the plate temperature 5-10 C for parts reaching the edges
Add a brim and enclose the printer for PETG, ASA and other warping materials

settings.advice: Add 5-10 C for large parts that reach the edges of the textured PEI plate.
Use a wider brim on large parts with sharp corners near the plate edge.

facts: Bed heater 1000 W with one temperature sensor (Snapmaker FAQ)
Staff estimate: corners 5-12 C below the centre

sources.title: U1 FAQ - Official Info Summary (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: How often to run U1 heated bed leveling
entries.summary: The pre-print Heated Bed Leveling option is remembered once you untick it. A Snapmaker forum moderator runs it about every two weeks to a month. A beta tester adds a fresh mesh when changing material and bed temperature, swapping plates, after big room temperature changes, after moving the printer or mechanical work, and when printing high-temperature materials like ASA. Some users mesh every time they reseat the plate.
steps: Tick Heated Bed Leveling in Print Preferences when the plate, material or environment changes
Otherwise leave it off and re-mesh every few weeks
Always re-mesh after a firmware update that asks for it or after moving the printer

entries.title: Re-tensioning U1 XY belts and checking the result
entries.summary: The U1 has spring-loaded belt tensioners. Snapmaker's method: loosen the two tensioner screws with a 2.0 hex key (do not remove them), move the printhead to all four corners, tighten and run vibration compensation again. Users repeat this two or three times when they have parking errors or layer shifts. To verify without a gauge, check the input-shaper graphs in Fluidd for one narrow peak per axis.
steps: Power off, then loosen the two belt tensioner screws with a 2.0 hex key without unscrewing them fully
Move the printhead slowly by hand to each of the four corners so the torsion springs settle the tension
Retighten the screws; users repeat the loosen-move-tighten cycle 2-3 times
Run Vibration Compensation calibration again
In Fluidd open the shaper_calibrate folder and check for a single narrow resonance peak per axis
If the gantry is still out of square, check whether the X axis is parallel to the bed before adjusting skew
facts: One user measured 90 Hz (upper belt) and 82 Hz (lower belt) with a belt tension gauge after the procedure
Broad, multiple or low-frequency peaks in the shaper graph suggest a tension or mechanical problem
Skew correction can be added in printer.cfg via Advanced Mode, which shows a warranty warning

entries.title: Stray colour dots, black streaks and blobs around multi-colour text on the U1
entries.summary: Users report small dots of one colour appearing near other-colour features and black streaks on light walls around inlaid text. Likely causes are ooze or residue on a nozzle, damp filament and printing too hot; contamination shows mainly without a prime tower. Dry the spool, drop the problem colour 5 C, tune retraction and keep the tower. Users disagree on avoid-crossing-walls: it helped some and made it worse for one user.
symptoms: Dots of a second colour near features of that colour
Dark streaks on light walls next to text
Cotton-candy strings on inlays
causes: Ooze or buildup on the nozzle before and after a swap
Damp filament
Nozzle temperature too high
No prime tower, so the nozzle is not cleaned after a swap
Long detour travel letting ooze drop onto the part
steps: Keep the prime tower enabled
Dry spools that have been open for weeks, especially dark colours
Lower the temperature of the oozing filament by about 5 C
Run full filament calibration (temperature, pressure advance, flow, retraction) for that spool
Try Z-hop and compare with avoid crossing walls on and off
Move the model or tower to change travel paths
Advanced users added a nozzle scrub to the change-filament G-code

settings.advice: Reduce 5 C on the colour that drips; users saw less bleed and stringing.
Can keep travel inside the part, but longer detours gave one user more ooze; test both.
A small hop lifts the nozzle off walls during travel; users call it the main workaround for dots.
One user suggested 2-4 mm instead of about 10 mm for a blobbing filament; tune per filament and compare.

sources.title: U1 Toolchanger: Black stringing/blobs on text and color bleed walls (Snapmaker forum)
U1 leaves traces of other colors where it shouldn't (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: U1 Advanced Mode config edits and the community Paxx12 extended firmware
entries.summary: The U1 runs Snapmaker's Klipper fork. Enabling Advanced Mode (Settings > Maintenance) lets you edit and save config files, but firmware updates overwrite them, so keep backups. Many owners use the community Paxx12 Extended Firmware for features such as camera fixes, OpenSpool RFID and Spoolman support. Snapmaker has published a third-party firmware risk notice; users say you can revert to stock and should run full calibration after switching.
steps: Back up printer.cfg and macros before editing in Advanced Mode
Re-apply your edits after each official firmware update
Read Snapmaker's third-party firmware notice and the Paxx12 documentation before flashing
Run a full calibration after installing or leaving custom firmware

entries.title: What U1 Dynamic Flow Calibration measures and how to keep the result
entries.summary: Dynamic Flow Calibration is the U1's automatic pressure advance (K) measurement; it does not set flow ratio, which is preset for Snapmaker filaments and must be tuned manually for others. Snapmaker says results reset when filament is unloaded, but a tester reports engineering confirmed the slicer's profile PA overrides the measurement on later prints. To keep it, read the value in Fluidd during calibration and save it in the filament profile.
steps: Tick Dynamic Flow Calibration in Print Preferences before starting a print
Open the Fluidd console while it runs and note the measured pressure advance per toolhead
Enter that value as the filament profile's pressure advance in Snapmaker Orca
Recalibrate for a new filament brand or type, a new hotend, damp material or new stringing

settings.advice: Store the K value measured by Dynamic Flow Calibration here so later prints use it.
When enabled, the profile value overrides the printer's last measured value.
Not covered by the automatic calibration; tune with Orca's flow tests for third-party filament.

facts: One toolhead takes about 3 min 30 s, all four about 14 min 40 s
Vibration compensation plus homing about 5 min 6 s; without homing about 3 min 41 s

sources.title: U1 FAQ - Official Info Summary (Snapmaker forum)
Snapmaker U1: Official Video Guides (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: U1 error 0003-0530-0002-0008 (calibration anomaly) after fitting new hotends
entries.summary: One owner hit 0003-0530-0002-0008 during build-plate calibration right after installing hardened steel hotends. The suspected cause was contamination on the nozzle tip: toolhead grease from fingers or machining oil on new hotends interfering with probing. Degreasing the nozzle with 99% IPA, running a couple of small prints to flush the hotend and recalibrating cleared it.
symptoms: Calibration Anomaly 0003-0530-0002-0008 during bed calibration after a hotend change
causes: Grease or oil on the nozzle tip affecting probing
Machining residue on brand-new hotends
steps: Let the nozzle cool to warm, then wipe it thoroughly with 99% isopropyl alcohol
Avoid touching the nozzle tip with greasy fingers during hotend swaps
Print two or three small parts to flush residue
Run the full bed calibration again

sources.title: Snapmaker U1 - Error 0003-0530-0002-0008 (Calibration Anomaly) after a hotend swap (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Top surface bulging over infill with the U1 0.08 mm Extra Fine profile
entries.summary: On thin flat parts printed with the default '0.08 Extra Fine @Snapmaker U1 (0.4 nozzle)' process, one user saw the top bulge upward over each infill cell. Snapmaker support reproduced it and fixed it by switching sparse infill to gyroid and setting internal solid infill speed to 250 mm/s. That profile used 9 top layers (0.72 mm); about 12 layers near 1 mm was also recommended. Snapmaker Orca 2.4.0 merged this preset into '0.08mm Standard'.

settings.advice: Gyroid fixed the doming support reproduced with the 0.08 mm profile.
Support set 250 mm/s together with gyroid to remove the bulges.
At 0.08 mm use about 12 layers (close to 1 mm) instead of 9.

sources.title: Domeing of flat surfaces over infill cells (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: U1 firmware 1.5.0/1.5.1 squashed or dragging first layers
entries.summary: After firmware 1.5.0 many owners saw over-squished first layers and nozzle drag; 1.5.1 fixed it for most and a 1.5.2 beta followed. Snapmaker said these updates need a one-time heated bed leveling plus multi-toolhead offset calibration with no filament loaded. Some users downgraded to 1.4.1. Files first printed on older firmware could also show a false nozzle-diameter error on 1.5.
symptoms: Nozzle drags through the first or second layer after updating
First layer squashed although nothing else changed
causes: Changes in 1.5.0 affecting first-layer height
Old calibration data kept after the update
steps: Update to 1.5.1 or newer
Unload filament from all toolheads and run Multi-Toolhead Offset Calibration
Enable Heated Bed Leveling for the first print after the update
If problems persist, export the system log and contact support; some users rolled back to 1.4.1
Re-slice or re-send files that throw a nozzle-diameter mismatch after the update

sources.title: Firmware 1.5.0 - Print Quality Degraded After Update (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Thin or patchy first layer after switching the U1 to hardened steel hotends
entries.summary: After replacing stainless hotends with Snapmaker hardened steel ones, one user saw under-extruded patches on the first layer, while others simply ran nozzle offset calibration and bed leveling and printed fine. That user improved results by raising flow ratio about 2% and using a 0.6 mm first-layer line width. Recalibrate first, then tune flow per filament.
steps: Run multi-toolhead offset calibration and heated bed leveling after the swap
Print a full-bed first-layer test and note whether gaps repeat in the same places
If lines are thin everywhere, raise flow ratio in small steps (for example 1.00 to 1.02)
Try a wider first-layer line width such as 0.6 mm
Check the result with Snapmaker filament to separate hotend issues from spool issues

settings.advice: Raise 1-2% if the first layer shows thin, separated lines after a hotend change.
Wider first-layer lines (around 0.6 mm) helped one user close gaps.

sources.title: First Layer Issues After Installing Original Hardened Steel Hotends (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: U1 vibration compensation (input shaping) and wavy walls
entries.summary: The U1 sweeps the head through a frequency range with its accelerometer and picks input-shaper settings that minimise resonance. Run it from Settings > Maintenance > Device Calibration (about 5 minutes) after setup, belt work or moving the printer. Wavy walls appearing suddenly are often the surface: one owner's waves vanished after moving the printer from a wobbly desk to the floor.
symptoms: Ringing or ghosting after corners
New streaks or waves on walls that were clean before
causes: Outdated shaper results after belt or hardware changes
Printer on a wobbly table or soft mat
steps: Place the printer on a rigid, stable surface (test on the floor if unsure)
Run Vibration Compensation from Settings > Maintenance > Device Calibration
Check the graphs in Fluidd's shaper_calibrate folder for clean single peaks
Re-run after belt tensioning or moving the machine

settings.advice: Lower if ringing remains after input shaping on a stable surface.

sources.title: Snapmaker U1: Official Video Guides (Snapmaker forum)
Printing problem with streaks or waves on my parts (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: When and how to run U1 multi-toolhead offset calibration
entries.summary: The U1 measures XYZ offsets between its four nozzles automatically using an eddy-current sensor; Snapmaker states accuracy within 0.04 mm with clean nozzles. Run it at first setup, after replacing a hotend, after a nozzle scrapes or collides, or when colours misalign or layers shift between heads. It takes about 15-20 minutes and does not need repeating per print. Clean nozzle tips first; after the 1.5.x firmware updates Snapmaker asked users to run it with no filament loaded.
steps: Clean each nozzle tip of plastic and grease
For the 1.5.x firmware update case, unload filament from all toolheads first
Start Multi-toolhead Offset Calibration from the device calibration menu and follow the prompts
Re-run after any hotend change, crash or visible colour misalignment
facts: Offset accuracy target 0.04 mm (official)
Duration about 15-20 minutes
Tom's Hardware found four-head registration accurate on a stacked four-colour test

sources.title: Snapmaker U1: Official Video Guides (Snapmaker forum)
Firmware 1.5.0 - Print Quality Degraded After Update (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: U1 crashes and pickup failures with the 'No sparse layers' prime tower option
entries.summary: Users who enabled the beta 'No sparse layers' wipe-tower option had toolhead collisions and 'extruder pickup failed' (toolhead swapping anomaly, exception 523-1-23). G-code analysis showed tool swaps then happen at the low tower height rather than the print height, with the bed far higher than normal. Leave the option off; one tester avoided crashes with Normal Z-hop and a clear strip in front of the tower.
symptoms: Toolhead hits parked heads or the print near the tower
Pause with extruder pickup failed / exception 523-1-23
causes: Tool changes executed at the tower's own low Z while the print is several mm higher
Slope Z-hop combines XY and Z moves when leaving the tower
steps: Turn off No sparse layers (beta) for U1 prints
If you must use it, set Z-hop type to Normal so lifts are vertical
Keep a strip in front of the tower, at least one printhead deep and across the full X travel, free of the model
Inspect the preview around the first tool change before printing

settings.advice: Keep disabled on the U1; users traced pickup failures and collisions to swaps happening at the low tower height.
Normal (vertical) lift avoids diagonal moves near the tower if experimenting with sparse layers.

sources.title: No sparse layers (beta) - anyone using it? (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: U1 walls rough in only one travel direction (PCTG example)
entries.summary: An owner printing PCTG had rough, blobby walls only when the head moved front-to-back, plus a growling noise, and suspected motors. The same model in PLA came out perfect, so the cause was the PCTG profile. The user suspected cooling, as the duct does not surround the nozzle fully. Test with PLA and a stock profile before suspecting hardware.
steps: Print the same model in Snapmaker or generic PLA with the stock profile
If PLA is clean, tune the problem filament: temperature, fan speed, flow and volumetric speed
Only if PLA shows the same defect, check belts, rods and motors with support

settings.advice: Adjust cooling for PETG-family filaments that blob on one side of the nozzle.
Slow outer walls while tuning a new copolyester filament.

sources.title: Terrible wall finish in one direction (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Snapmaker Orca 2.4.1: nozzle scratches the top during the final U1 tool change
entries.summary: A user found Snapmaker Orca 2.4.1 drops the Z lift before the last travel to the prime tower, so the nozzle can drag across the finished top. The 2.4.0 G-code lifted 0.4 mm before that move. Until confirmed fixed, users can slice with 2.4.0 or check the preview at the final tool change. Version 2.4.1 also changed how the head approaches the tower, detouring and entering through a wall opening.
symptoms: Scratch marks on the top layer of multi-colour prints
Started only after updating to Snapmaker Orca 2.4.1
causes: No Z lift before the final horizontal move toward the prime tower in 2.4.1 G-code
steps: Preview the end of the G-code and look for a lift before the last move to the tower
Compare with a 2.4.0 slice of the same model
Use 2.4.0 for affected prints or report the issue with both G-code files

sources.title: Snapmaker Orca 2.4.1 - Nozzle Scratches Prints During Final Toolchange (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Printing PETG on the U1 textured PEI plate
entries.summary: Owners print PETG directly on the U1 textured PEI plate, one reporting about 40 kg without glue; parts release once the plate cools. Thin first layers, failed starts and brims can over-bond, so some use glue stick, hairspray or a release agent. Users run the bed at about 70-80 C. An early Snapmaker Orca PETG preset with a 0 C bed was fixed in 2.2.3.
steps: Wash the plate with soap and warm water, especially after PLA
Set the bed to about 70-80 C
Let the plate cool fully before removing parts
Use a thin release layer for brims or very thin parts that over-bond
Soak stuck remnants in 90%+ IPA and scrape gently without gouging the PEI

settings.advice: About 70-80 C for PETG; check older presets do not show 0 C.

entries.title: U1 toolhead fails to latch or park, mostly after homing or at print start
entries.summary: Early owners often had heads not docking or not latching during setup, homing or print start while swaps mid-print were fine. Common fixes: repeat the belt tensioning, update firmware (parking coordinates were changed), recalibrate pick and park coordinates per head (support says stay within 1 mm of default), restore grease on the three magnetic points, and refit a loose extruder front cover. The U1 homes sensorlessly against the frame, so check nothing near the homing faces is loose.
symptoms: Toolhead not captured or released during initial calibration
Head misses the dock pin and stops with a swapping error
Lower cover of the carriage knocked off
causes: Uneven XY belt tension after shipping
Old firmware parking coordinates
Pick/park coordinates off for one head
Grease wiped off the magnetic contact points
Loose extruder front cover or internal panel
Frame or panels bent in transit
steps: Update to the latest firmware
Repeat the belt tension procedure, slowly, two or three times
Home, then use the on-screen toolhead coordinate calibration to test and adjust each head separately
Keep any coordinate change within about 1 mm of the default value
Check the three magnetic points on each toolhead still carry the supplied grease
Make sure the extruder front cover and nearby panels are fully seated
Contact support if the frame looks bent; send logs from the touchscreen

sources.title: Failure to launch - Calibration/toolhead parking errors (Snapmaker forum)
Print head is not parked correctly - solution (Snapmaker forum)
Still getting toolhead parking issues! (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Using PETG and PLA as easy-release support interfaces for each other on the U1
entries.summary: PLA and PETG barely bond, so U1 owners use one as the support interface for the other, often at zero top Z distance. Users report clean undersides, but small PETG areas can fail to stick on PLA interfaces at speed. One fix used two ironed interface layers, PETG at 270 C and slower supported areas via a modifier. Bambu's soft Support for PLA/PETG, mostly TPU, was hard to print; one user used a 0.1 mm gap with Support for PLA.
steps: Assign the second material to support interface only, not the whole support
Start with 0 mm top Z distance; try about 0.1 mm if surfaces stick
Use 2 or more interface layers and consider ironing the interface
Slow the first layers printed on the interface with a modifier
Set the prime tower filament to one material so the tower does not mix them
Check the preview: tree supports sometimes omit interface layers

settings.advice: Use PETG under PLA parts or PLA under PETG parts; release is easy because they do not bond.
0 mm is common with dissimilar materials; 0.1 mm worked better for one user with breakaway filament.
Two or more layers give a continuous interface for the part to sit on.
Ironing the interface helped one user get PETG to land on PLA.

sources.title: PLA als Schnittstellenfilament fuer PETG (Snapmaker forum)
Hard time printing Bambu's Support for PLA/PETG (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Caring for U1 toolhead pogo pins and docking contacts
entries.summary: The U1 connects each toolhead through gold pogo-pin contacts rated by Snapmaker for about 1,000,000 swaps. The printer counts swaps and reminds you every 100,000 swaps to clean the contacts on both sides. Dirty or greasy contacts are a common cause of toolhead detection errors; staff suggest scrubbing the toolhead pins with a scouring pad before re-running calibration. Worn pins are replaced by swapping the small PCBA, a job of under 5 minutes.
steps: Check the swap counter on the touchscreen to see how close you are to the 100,000-swap cleaning interval
Remove the toolhead using the official method (H2.0 hex key between the two locating pins until it clicks)
Wipe or lightly scrub the pogo pins and the matching pads on the swapper so no dust or grease remains
Refit the toolhead and confirm the red indicator on the latch is no longer visible
Run a full device calibration after refitting toolheads
facts: Pogo pins rated for about 1,000,000 swaps; cleaning reminder every 100,000 swaps
Snapmaker's example: 600 swaps per print, 7 prints per week gives cleaning roughly every 6 months
A PCBA swap on the toolhead or swapper replaces worn pins in under 5 minutes

sources.title: U1 FAQ - Official Info Summary (Snapmaker forum)
Toolhead 2 detached when its attached? (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: U1 prime tower falls over early because a toolhead was not primed
entries.summary: A user found the tower sometimes fell because a toolhead that had not yet printed laid poor first-layer lines on it. Fixes users discuss are a purge line for every toolhead in the start G-code, or Orca's option to prime all printing toolheads at the start. One person reported that option produced an out-of-range move error on the U1, so preview the G-code first.
steps: Enable priming of all printing extruders in the Multimaterial settings, or add a per-toolhead purge line to the start G-code
Preview the start of the G-code to make sure no move goes outside the bed
Use rib walls and a brim on the tower if it still lifts

settings.advice: Primes every toolhead used by the job at the start; one user reported an axis-limit error with it on the U1, so check the preview.
Increase slightly if the tower base peels on the first layers.

sources.title: Guide: Purge line for every toolhead on the Snapmaker U1 (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: U1 prime tower collapsing when printing PLA with PETG supports
entries.summary: With the tower filament left on Default, Orca may stack PLA on PETG inside the tower; the two do not bond, so the tower turns to spaghetti and can ruin the print. Set the tower to one material, ideally the one present on the most layers, and consider the rib wall type. A community workaround from the OrcaSlicer issue tracker builds one cylinder per material as a private tower.
symptoms: Prime tower lifts or falls apart part-way through
Spaghetti around the tower in PLA+PETG prints
causes: Tower shell printed in whichever filament is convenient, mixing materials that do not adhere to each other
steps: In Multimaterial print settings, change the prime tower filament from Default to the main material
Choose the material used on the highest or most layers, since the tower is printed every layer
Switch the tower wall type to rib for extra stability

Alternative: add one cylinder per material as tall as its last change, assign each a material, place them first in the object list and set intra-layer order to follow the object list, then disable the normal tower

settings.advice: Set to the primary material instead of Default when materials do not bond (PLA with PETG or TPU).
Rib walls resist toppling on tall or mixed-material towers.

sources.title: Hard time printing Bambu's Support for PLA/PETG (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Shrinking the U1 prime tower without losing clean colour changes
entries.summary: Snapmaker's stock U1 profiles prime generously (about 45 mm3 in the Standard process, 40 mm3 and a 40 mm wide tower in the bundled dragon), so the tower can weigh almost as much as the model. Beta testers used about 15 mm3 and users report 15-18 mm3, a 20-30 mm tower and a 10-15 mm3 filament minimum work for PLA. Do not disable the tower: users who did got stringing and stray bits. A few users saw colour specks on white parts at 15 mm3, so raise it again if contamination appears.
symptoms: Prime tower weighs nearly as much as the model
Long print times dominated by tower printing
causes: Conservative default prime volume
Filament profile minimum purge (some profiles default to 60 mm3) overriding a lower process value
steps: Keep the prime tower enabled for any multi-toolhead print
Lower the process prime volume to about 15-18 mm3
Narrow the tower to about 20-30 mm
Lower the per-filament minimum purge on the wipe tower to 10-15 mm3 in each filament profile you use
Print a test with a light colour next to a dark one and raise the values if specks appear
Optionally assign the tower to the filament used most in the model, which users report also cuts print time

settings.advice: Lower toward 15-18 mm3 for PLA/ASA at 0.16-0.2 mm layers; raise if light colours show contamination.
Reduce to about 20-30 mm to shrink the tower; keep it wide enough to stay stable on tall prints.
Set per filament; values of 10-15 mm3 stop a 60 mm3 filament default from inflating the tower.
Users run rectangle for small towers and rib for tall or mixed-material towers that tend to fall.
Pick the dominant model filament for the tower to reduce extra swaps.
One tester used a 5 mm threshold with slower small perimeters to avoid dots from tiny extrusions when priming less.

facts: Thinner layers automatically get longer prime lines because prime is defined by volume
One user cut a print from 13 h 20 min to 11 h 48 min just by shrinking prime volume and tower width

sources.title: U1 how to minimize prime tower in Orca? (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: Where U1 reviews differ from the official specs (tool-change time, abrasives, enclosure)
entries.summary: Snapmaker quotes about 5 seconds per toolhead swap, while Tom's Hardware measured roughly 10-12 seconds per colour change once nozzle priming is included. The same beta-unit review printed PETG-CF on the stock stainless nozzle and ASA without the lid, whereas the official spec sheet lists fibre-filled filaments only with a hardened steel nozzle plus top cover and ASA/ABS only with the top cover. Treat the official limits as the safe baseline.
facts: Official: about 5 s per toolhead switch in Snapmaker lab tests (stated as reference only)
Tom's Hardware (beta unit): about 10-12 s per colour change including priming
Tom's Hardware printed PETG carbon fibre on the stock steel nozzle and ASA with no lid without trouble
Official spec: CF/GF-filled filaments need top cover plus hardened steel nozzle; ABS/ASA/PA/PC need the top cover
Tom's Hardware measured prime-tower waste of about 4-7 g on typical multi-colour prints

entries.title: Snapmaker Orca changes that matter for U1 users (2.3.5 to 2.4.1)
entries.summary: Recent Snapmaker Orca releases changed several U1 workflows. 2.4.0 merged many process presets (for example 0.08 Extra Fine into 0.08mm Standard), added High-Flow Hot End parameters and recommends U1 firmware 2.0.0 or newer first. 2.3.6 added timelapse export (firmware 1.6.0+) and colour-mixing match, recommending a 0.4 mm or smaller hotend at 0.1 mm or lower layers for Full Spectrum. 2.3.5 added top-cover control and filament sync; 2.4.1 changed tower entry.
facts: 2.4.0: update the U1 to firmware 2.0.0 or later before installing
2.4.0: Fine/High Quality/Strength/Draft presets folded into Standard presets per layer height
2.3.6: timelapse export only works with firmware V1.6.0 or newer
2.3.6: Full Spectrum works best with hotends of 0.4 mm or smaller and layers of 0.1 mm or less; larger can show banding
2.3.5: prime tower outer wall gets an opening; top cover control and filament sync added
2.4.1: head detours around the prime tower and enters through the wall opening during tool changes

entries.title: Snapmaker U1 key specifications and material tiers
entries.summary: The U1 is a CoreXY Klipper printer with four independent toolheads, a 270 x 270 x 270 mm build volume, 500 mm/s max toolhead speed and 20,000 mm/s2 max acceleration. Each hotend has a 0.4 mm stainless steel nozzle rated to 300 C and up to 32 mm3/s flow; the PEI steel bed reaches 100 C. Snapmaker grades materials by setup: basic materials run open, engineering plastics need the optional top cover, and fibre-filled filaments also need hardened steel nozzles.
facts: Build volume 270 x 270 x 270 mm; footprint about 584 x 499 x 730 mm; weight 18.2 kg
Max toolhead speed 500 mm/s, max acceleration 20,000 mm/s2
Hotend max flow 32 mm3/s, max nozzle temperature 300 C, standard nozzle 0.4 mm stainless steel, 1.75 mm filament
Heated bed max 100 C, flexible steel sheet with PEI; Snapmaker says the bed heater is 1000 W with one temperature sensor
Basic materials: PLA, PETG, TPU, PVA, PCTG
With the optional top cover: adds PET, ABS, ASA, PA, PC
With top cover plus hardened steel nozzle: adds carbon-fibre and glass-fibre reinforced filaments
Wi-Fi is 2.4 GHz only (802.11 b/g/n); USB flash drive also supported; 26 GB eMMC storage
Max input power 1150 W at 220-240 V, 400 W at 100-120 V
Built-in 2 MP chamber camera at roughly 1 frame per second
Main and auxiliary part-cooling fans; accelerometer-based input shaping

sources.title: U1 FAQ - Official Info Summary (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: U1 supports or small parts coming loose, and a gap between brim and part
entries.summary: For detailed models whose supports break free, forum helpers recommend a brim of 10 mm or more, Z-hop and, in winter without a top cover, a slightly hotter bed. One user found Orca left a gap between brim and part until elephant-foot compensation was set to 0; the dedicated brim-object gap setting also controls this.
steps: Add a brim of about 10 mm on small footprints and support bases
Check the preview for a gap between brim and part; set brim-object gap to 0
If a gap remains, try elephant-foot compensation at 0
Enable Z-hop so travel does not knock over thin supports
In a cold room, raise the bed temperature a few degrees or cover the printer

settings.advice: Use 10 mm or more for small contact areas and tall supports.
Set to 0 so the brim actually touches the part.
One user removed the brim gap by setting this to 0.

sources.title: When U1 printing, the model does not stick to the build plate? (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: U1 nozzle-cleaning move damaging the edge of a third-party build plate
entries.summary: With a BIQU Frostbite plate, one owner's nozzle damaged the plate edge during the pre-probing nozzle clean, which happens on a tab at the plate edge. Slot and tab positions differ slightly between plate brands, and the cleaning offsets are tuned for the Snapmaker plate. The user moved the cleaning point in the macro; staff warned to restore defaults when going back to the stock plate.
steps: Watch the first nozzle-cleaning move on a new plate brand
Compare the plate's slots and tabs with the Snapmaker plate
If the nozzle hits the slot edge, adjust the cleaning offsets in the macro so it lands mid-tab (Advanced Mode)
Restore the default offsets when you return to the official plate
Re-run toolhead offset calibration if the contact point seems wrong on every head

sources.title: U1 - Nozzle cleaning path on bed plate (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: How U1 toolheads park, stay warm and get preheated during multi-colour prints
entries.summary: Per Snapmaker's FAQ, while one head prints the other parked heads sit at a standby temperature of about 70 C and each is heated back to print temperature just before it is picked up, so swaps need no waiting. Heads not used by a print are not heated at all. Extra standby draw for three heads is roughly 10-30 W. Users note that Orca's own idle/standby temperature settings can keep parked heads much hotter, so check what your G-code actually sets.

settings.advice: Filament idle temperature used for parked tools when ooze prevention is on; lower it to reduce ooze and heat exposure of heads that are waiting.
Enable together with an idle temperature so inactive toolheads drop temperature instead of staying at print temperature.

facts: Parked toolheads hold about 70 C standby per Snapmaker FAQ and are preheated shortly before use
Single-colour prints only heat the toolhead in use
Three idle toolheads add roughly 10-30 W in total
Each parked head rests on its own wiper and silicone pad to limit ooze (Tom's Hardware)
One user reported Snapmaker Orca kept finished toolheads at a 175 C idle temperature for the rest of a 26-hour print

sources.title: U1 FAQ - Official Info Summary (Snapmaker forum)
How to turn off finished extruders while keeping others on standby (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: U1 reports a toolhead detached, or a toolhead drops during a print
entries.summary: A 'toolhead detached' error on a seated head was traced by one owner to the 16-pin cable at the mainboard not being fully inserted. After cleaning heads, check the latch red indicator is hidden and run full calibration. Another head fell mid-print after loose PETG interface material lay in the pick-up area; Snapmaker says a detach check runs at each swap but not during printing.
symptoms: Calibration stops saying a toolhead is detached although it is mounted
Toolhead found lying on the bed
Red indicator stays visible on a docked head
causes: 16-pin cable not fully seated at the mainboard
Dirty or greasy pogo pins
Head refitted incorrectly after disassembly
Debris or a detached part blocking the dock area
steps: Power-cycle the printer after reseating the toolhead
Clean pogo pins on the head and swapper
Confirm the round pin sits to the left of the thick vertical bar and the red flag is not showing
Run full device calibration after refitting heads
If one head is never detected, have support guide you to check the 16-pin mainboard connector
Keep the dock and pick-up area clear of loose support or interface pieces

sources.title: Toolhead 2 detached when its attached? (Snapmaker forum)
Toolheads won't seat fully - small red dot never disappears (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: U1 top cover making the chamber too hot for PLA
entries.summary: With the official top cover closed in a warm room, users saw chamber temperatures reach 48-50 C during PLA prints, at which point the U1 pauses with a PLA clogging warning. Staff advise against sealing the top for PLA: half-open in winter, open in summer. The U1 has no chamber heater and the slicer's chamber-wait command was not acted on, though the cavity sensor shows in Fluidd. Staff said removing the purifier block from the start G-code turns off the top-cover fans.
symptoms: PLA print pauses with a clogging warning in a hot room
Soft or deformed PLA after fitting the top cover
causes: Top cover insulation trapping bed heat
High ambient temperature
steps: Open the top cover or front door when printing PLA
Keep the room cooler or move the printer out of a hot garage
Reserve the closed cover for ABS, ASA, PA and PC
To pre-warm the chamber, heat the bed and wait, since there is no active chamber heater
Only edit start G-code fan control if you understand the purifier modes, and keep backups

settings.advice: Informational on the U1; the printer has no chamber heater and users found the wait for chamber temperature not implemented.
