entries.title: U1 nozzle grinding or rippled top surfaces on large flat prints
entries.summary: Some owners got rippled, gouged tops on long flat parts while small curved prints were fine. Snapmaker staff treated it as pillowing and suggested more top layers, rectilinear internal solid infill, slower top layers, a hotter nozzle for third-party filament and keeping default Z-hop. Two hardware causes fixed it for users: a lower front cooling-duct part not fully seated (support confirmed this hurts airflow) and a damaged belt tensioner screw. Layers under 0.16 mm made it worse.
symptoms: Nozzle audibly scrapes the top of flat parts
Top surface shows the infill pattern as ridges
Rippled or wavy top on large flat prints
causes: Part-cooling airflow blocked by a misaligned lower duct cover
Too few top layers over sparse infill
Very thin layers (0.08-0.12 mm) with infill doming
Loose XY mechanics or belt tensioner damage
steps: Check the lower front part of the toolhead duct is fully seated and the airflow path is clear
Increase top shell thickness to about 1 mm
Use 0.16 mm or thicker layers for big flat parts
Switch internal solid infill to rectilinear and slow top surfaces slightly
For third-party filament try +10 C and run flow calibration
Keep the default Z-hop enabled
If nothing changes across filaments, inspect belts, tensioner screws and XY parts with support

settings.advice: Raise toward 1 mm so extra top layers bridge and flatten sparse infill.
Snapmaker suggested rectilinear for the layers under the top.
Lower slightly to reduce pillowing on large flat tops.
Users saw grinding mostly below 0.16 mm; use 0.16-0.2 mm for large flat parts.

sources.title: Extruder nozzle grinding into prints (Snapmaker forum)

entries.title: TPU jams, grinding and buckling on the U1
entries.summary: Snapmaker staff say TPU of 85A and harder prints on the U1 as-is; softer grades (about 80A) need the toolhead side screw backed off to ease gear pressure. One jam came from PTFE tubes butted against the feeder inlet, which added drag on retraction. Users run short retractions (one used 0.4 mm), 2-4 mm on tool change instead of about 10 mm, and avoid overheating very soft TPE. Later U1s have a redesigned runout-sensor block that constrains the filament path.
symptoms: Extruder chews soft TPU
Filament buckles or exits the side of the toolhead
Jams that start on retraction or tool changes
causes: Too much drive-gear pressure for soft TPU
Extra drag from PTFE tubes or dryer feed paths
Long retractions on tool change
Earlier runout-sensor design leaving space for the filament to wander above the gear
steps: Feed TPU directly from a free-rolling spool or use a proper PTFE adapter at the feeder
For TPU softer than 85A, loosen the toolhead side screw slightly
Keep normal retraction short and reduce tool-change retraction to about 2-4 mm
Limit volumetric speed to what the TPU tolerates
If filament escapes beside the gear repeatedly, ask support about the updated runout-sensor part

settings.advice: Keep very short for TPU; one user ran 0.4 mm for a stiff TPU.
Reduce from about 10 mm to 2-4 mm for TPU to avoid buckling on swaps.
Lower for soft TPU; Tom's Hardware's default profile ran about 3.2 mm3/s.

entries.title: ABS and ASA warping, cracking and poor layer adhesion on the U1
entries.summary: ABS and ASA shrink a lot, so uneven cooling builds stress that lifts corners or bends the base once it exceeds bed adhesion. The Top Cover reduces temperature swings (it lowers warping, it doesn't eliminate it). Add glue and a brim, keep the enclosure shut for the whole print and avoid very large parts. For weak layers, raise nozzle temperature, slow down and switch the fan off.
symptoms: Corners lifting off the plate
Warped base
Cracks between layers
Weak layer bonding
causes: High shrinkage with uneven cooling
Open printer exposed to drafts and temperature changes
Part fan cooling layers too fast
Very large footprint
steps: Install the Top Cover before printing and keep the door closed throughout.
Apply glue to the build plate.
Add a brim to enlarge the contact area.
Split or scale down very large ABS/ASA models where possible.
If layers separate, raise nozzle temperature, reduce speed and turn off the part fan.

settings.advice: Enable a brim on ABS/ASA parts to resist corner lift.
Widen the brim on large or sharp-cornered parts.
Set to 0 for ABS/ASA to reduce warping and improve layer bonding.
Raise within 240-280 °C if layers delaminate.

entries.title: Snapmaker ABS: recommended settings, Top Cover requirement and drying
entries.summary: ABS is an impact- and heat-resistant engineering filament (HDT 100 °C) for functional prototypes, tooling, enclosures and car interior parts. With a 0.4 mm nozzle print at 240-280 °C, 90-100 °C bed, 50-200 mm/s with the cooling fan off. On the U1 the Top Cover is strongly recommended to stabilize chamber temperature and filter fumes; the stock stainless hotend is fine since ABS isn't abrasive. Drying is optional (80 °C for 6 h).

settings.advice: 240-280 °C; raise if layers bond poorly.
90-100 °C for ABS, with glue for extra grip.
Keep part cooling off for ABS to prevent warping and weak layers.

facts: ABS smells during printing, so ventilate the room.
Fine for short outdoor use; long sun exposure yellows and embrittles it, so choose ASA for long-term outdoor parts.
Store sealed with desiccant and away from sunlight.
Hardened hotends are only needed for abrasive fills like carbon fiber, glass fiber or glow powder.

entries.title: Snapmaker Artisan 3D printing specs, materials and compatible slicers
entries.summary: The Artisan's 3D printing accuracy is ±0.1 mm per 100 mm with a 0.1 mm layer resolution, and its linear modules allow up to 180 mm/s. The dual-extrusion module prints PLA, ABS, ASA, PETG, TPU (90A or harder), Breakaway Support for PLA, PVA, HIPS, nylon and carbon- or glass-fiber nylon. Besides the free Luban, Cura, PrusaSlicer, OrcaSlicer and Simplify3D are supported.
facts: Artisan linear modules use CNC-ground steel rails, Gates belts with 40 mm lead on X/Y and 8 mm lead screws on Z; 2.0 TMC modules (max 100 mm/s) are not interchangeable with them.
The Artisan dual-extrusion module has no proximity sensor: it levels and calibrates Z and XY offsets by touching the plate with the left nozzle.
A Snapmaker 2.0 dual extruder fitted to the Artisan loses 30 mm of Y travel: 350 × 370 × 400 mm dual, 375 × 370 × 400 left only, 400 × 370 × 400 right only.
The Premium edition includes the Boosted Exhaust Fan and Quick Swap Toolhead Plate; the power supply accepts 100-240 V AC.

entries.title: Artisan dual-sided PEI steel plate kit: textured vs smooth side and conversion
entries.summary: This kit (textured and smooth PEI on a flexible steel sheet with soft magnetic stickers) fits only the Artisan and is sold separately. Parts release once the plate cools and large prints pop off by flexing it. The textured side grips first layers strongly and resists warping, good for large functional parts; the smooth side suits precise small-to-medium parts needing a smooth bottom. Converting from the glass plate is essentially permanent.
facts: The magnetic sticker must be applied by hand following the official instructions; spare stickers are sold separately.
Steel sheet heats quickly, shortening warm-up before printing.
Going back to the glass plate requires complex disassembly and risks damaged or lost parts.

Dual-sided PEI Steel Plate with Soft Magnetic Sticker Kit for Snapmaker Artisan

entries.title: Quick Swap Toolhead Plate for Artisan: which modules it supports
entries.summary: The adjustable Quick Swap Toolhead Plate lets Artisan modules be exchanged quickly. It works with the Artisan dual-extruder 3D printing module and the 10W, 20W and 40W laser modules, but not with the 200W CNC module. The Artisan Premium already includes it.

sources.title: Quick Swap Toolhead Plate (Adjustable Version) for Artisan

entries.title: Snapmaker ASA: recommended settings, Top Cover requirement and outdoor use
entries.summary: ASA is an engineering filament built for long-term outdoor use, with strong UV and weather resistance, good impact strength and HDT of 103 °C. With a 0.4 mm nozzle print at 240-280 °C, 75-100 °C bed, 50-200 mm/s with the fan off. On the U1 the Top Cover is strongly recommended for stable chamber temperature and odor filtering; the stock stainless hotend works. Drying is optional at 80 °C for 6 h.

settings.advice: 240-280 °C; go higher if layer adhesion is weak.
75-100 °C for ASA; add glue against warping.
Keep the part fan off for ASA.

facts: Compared with ABS it resists yellowing and embrittlement in sunlight much better.
Typical parts: outdoor fixtures and enclosures, signs, car exterior parts.
It smells while printing; ventilate and store sealed with desiccant away from sunlight.

entries.title: Horizontal stripes or zebra patterns in Full Spectrum color-mixed prints
entries.summary: Faint horizontal banding is inherent to layered color mixing. It gets worse with taller layers, bigger nozzles, unsuitable filament TD and lopsided ratios: a 90% yellow / 10% cyan mix stripes far more than 50/50. Use a nozzle of 0.4 mm or less, layers of 0.1 mm or below, the Snapmaker PLA Full Spectrum profile and the 0.10 mm color-mixing preset, and confirm with a small swatch first.
symptoms: Visible horizontal stripes in mixed-color areas
Zebra-like bands instead of a uniform blend
causes: Layer height above 0.1 mm
Nozzle larger than 0.4 mm
Very unbalanced mixing ratio
Filament with unsuitable TD, e.g. CMYK Lithophane filament used for 3D mixing
steps: Use a 0.4 mm or smaller hotend.
Slice with 0.1 mm or thinner layers; on a 0.4 mm U1 hotend use the 0.10 mm color-mixing process.
Choose Snapmaker PLA Full Spectrum as the filament profile.
Keep each color between roughly 33% and 67% where possible.
Print a small swatch with the same settings and adjust before the final model.

settings.advice: Reduce to 0.1 mm or less so colors alternate more often.
Enable mix-layer subdivision to give mixed regions finer sublayers and less banding.

PLA Full Spectrum Filament Bundle (White Edition)
SnapSpeed PLA CMYK Lithophane Filament Bundle

entries.title: Choosing between PLA Full Spectrum (White/Gray) and CMYK Lithophane filament bundles
entries.summary: Choose by what you print. The PLA Full Spectrum bundles are tuned for color mixing inside 3D models: the White Edition for most colorful work, the Gray Edition for neutral, subdued palettes. The SnapSpeed PLA CMYK Lithophane bundle has TD values tuned for thin, flat, backlit pieces such as photo lithophanes and light boxes. Don't mix the two families: different TD values cause poor blending, color errors and banding.
facts: CMYK Lithophane filament used for Full Spectrum 3D mixing shows visible horizontal stripes.
Full Spectrum White Edition used for flat lithophanes can give horizontal banding and weaker color.
White and Gray Full Spectrum editions can be combined, but results are less predictable than using one edition per model.

PLA Full Spectrum Filament Bundle (Gray Edition)
SnapSpeed PLA CMYK Lithophane Filament Bundle

entries.title: J1/J1s hot ends (old vs new, PID autotune) and J1 vs J1s differences
entries.summary: The new J1 hot end joins heat sink, heat break, heater block and nozzle by interference fit, so its parts can't be replaced individually. Old and new hot ends can be used together and share fans and temperature sensors, but PID values may differ: update firmware and run Autotune as the manual describes. The J1s adds a print cooling fan so PLA prints without removing the top panel, ships with Breakaway Support for PLA instead of white PLA, and comes with doors and side panels fitted.
steps: When mixing old and new hot ends, update to the latest firmware.
Run the PID Autotune procedure from the manual for the hot ends.

entries.title: Snapmaker J1/J1s specifications and IDEX print modes
entries.summary: The J1 is an IDEX printer with a 300 × 200 × 200 mm volume in Default and Backup modes, 160 × 200 × 200 mm in Copy mode and 150 × 200 × 200 mm in Mirror mode. It reaches 350 mm/s and 10,000 mm/s², 300 °C nozzles and a 100 °C bed with a PEI glass plate, and prints 0.05-0.3 mm layers with 0.4 mm hotends. The idle extruder preheats on standby so switching is seamless.
facts: Materials: PLA, PETG, ABS, ASA, HIPS, PC, PP, PVA, TPU (90A or harder), TPE, PA, PA-GF and PA-CF; PA and fiber-filled PA need a hardened nozzle.
Speed presets by layer height: 0.10 mm 350, 0.12 mm 300, 0.16 mm 250, 0.20 mm 200, 0.24 mm 160 mm/s.
Operating range 10-35 °C at 10-90% RH (non-condensing); storage -20 to 55 °C.
Rail repeatability ±0.03 mm X/Y and ±0.02 mm Z; noise below 50 dBA; rails expected to last over 10 years.
Power 100-240 V AC, 4.4 A max, 24 V 400 W output.
Wi-Fi (2.4 and 5 GHz), USB cable or USB drive; Luban supplied; STL, OBJ and 3MF input.
Ships with two 0.4 mm hotends; 0.2/0.6/0.8 mm and hardened versions are optional. No laser or CNC modules.

entries.title: Snapmaker Liquid Glue for build plates: when to use it and cleanup
entries.summary: Snapmaker's water-soluble Liquid Glue strengthens first-layer adhesion, reduces warping and print failures, and helps parts release afterwards. It suits textured, glass, flexible and other plates and filaments such as PLA, PETG, PET, ABS, HIPS, ASA and TPU. Compared with a glue stick it spreads more evenly, leaves less residue on parts, has little odor and washes off with water or a damp cloth.
facts: It performs the same on different heated bed types.
Snapmaker pages call for glue with PETG HF on the U1 Smooth PEI plate, and suggest it for ABS/ASA warping and stubborn TPU first layers.

sources.title: Liquid Glue for the 3D Printing Build Plate

entries.title: Snapmaker PETG HF: build plates, drying, speed range and stringing fixes
entries.summary: PETG HF is a high-flow PETG with tuned U1 profiles in Snapmaker Orca; it needs neither the Top Cover nor a hardened hotend. It works on the U1 Textured PEI and Graphic Effect plates, and on the Smooth PEI plate only with glue. Dry it before printing and ideally feed it from a dryer such as SnapDryer to avoid stringing, bubbles and poor layer bonding.
steps: For stringing, dry the filament and keep it dry while printing.
Lower the nozzle temperature a little to cut oozing.
Increase retraction distance slightly.

settings.advice: Drop slightly if stringing remains after drying.
Increase a little to control oozing on travel moves.
On the U1 Smooth PEI plate apply glue; PETG HF won't adhere reliably on bare smooth PEI.

facts: Recommended 100-300 mm/s, versus 40-80 mm/s for basic PETG; surface quality and layer adhesion hold up better at high speed.
Easier to tune than basic PETG while keeping standard PETG strength.
Other printers can use it with manual tuning.
Orca V2.2.4 added the profile; V2.4.1 added ten colors such as Chestnut Red, Sage Green, Ice Blue, Iris Purple and Navy Blue.

entries.title: Getting maximum clarity and good layer bonding with PETG Translucent
entries.summary: For the clearest parts, slow down and keep speeds uniform, raise nozzle temperature a little, use thinner layers, nudge the flow ratio up and switch part cooling off. Fewer walls let more light through while more walls diffuse it. Use spiral vase mode for lampshades, or 100% infill on thick solid parts to hide the infill pattern, at the cost of much longer prints. FDM printing can't reach glass-like clarity.
symptoms: Part looks cloudy compared with product photos
Layers splitting or delaminating
causes: Too many walls or thick, complex geometry scattering light
Over-cooling causing uneven shrinkage and weak bonding
High or varying speeds

settings.advice: Enable for lampshades and other single-shell models for continuous extrusion and better light transmission.
Fewer loops raise transmittance; more loops give a softer, diffused glow.
Use 100% on solid thick parts to hide the infill pattern; print time rises a lot.
Raise slightly to close tiny gaps that scatter light.
Turn off or reduce to improve clarity and fix delamination.
Lower layers improve translucency but lengthen the print.

entries.title: PETG Translucent: settings, drying and keeping it dry while printing
entries.summary: PETG Translucent passes up to 90% of light while keeping PETG's toughness, layer adhesion, water and UV resistance and about 77 °C HDT, good for lampshades, diffusers, enclosures and outdoor items. With a 0.4 mm nozzle use 240-260 °C, a 60-85 °C bed, 50-150 mm/s, and the fan off or low. It is highly moisture-sensitive: dry at 65 °C for 6 h and print from a sealed dry box. No Top Cover or hardened hotend needed.

settings.advice: 240-260 °C; raise 5-10 °C if layers separate.
Use 60-85 °C for PETG Translucent.
Keep low or off for clarity and better layer bonding.
Set to 0 since V2.4.1, meaning this filament isn't supported on that plate; use a PEI plate.

facts: Damp signs: popping during extrusion, many surface bubbles, lower translucency, poor finish, stringing.
Store sealed with desiccant, out of sunlight; SnapDryer suits both drying and storage.
Since Orca V2.4.1 it is no longer supported on the Graphic Effect plate (bed temperature 0).

entries.title: Snapmaker PLA-CF: hardened hotend, manual loading and recommended settings
entries.summary: PLA-CF adds chopped carbon fiber to PLA for higher stiffness, very low warping and a matte finish that hides layer lines. Use a hardened steel hotend of at least 0.4 mm: fibers wear stainless hotends and smaller nozzles clog. Load and unload manually, never with the automatic feeder. Recommended: 200-250 °C nozzle, 35-70 °C bed, 50-200 mm/s, max volumetric speed 15 mm³/s, fan on; no Top Cover needed.

settings.advice: Cap at 15 mm³/s for PLA-CF with a 0.4 mm nozzle.
200-250 °C; increase if layer bonding is weak.
35-70 °C for PLA-CF.
Hardened hotend of 0.4 mm or larger only.

facts: RFID reading only works when the spool sits on a holder, since the readers are next to the side spool holders.
Wear gloves when loading, unloading and finishing parts; fibers make edges prickly.
Optional drying 55 °C for 6 h; store sealed with desiccant, away from sunlight.
For weak layers lower the fan speed or raise temperature.
Orca V2.3.5 optimized the PLA-CF profile; V2.4.1 disabled PLA CF on the Graphic Effect plate.

entries.title: PLA Full Spectrum Filament Bundle (Gray Edition): settings and color behavior
entries.summary: Four 1 kg spools (cyan, magenta, yellow, gray; 1.75 mm ±0.02 mm) designed for Full Spectrum color mixing on the U1. Gray suits muted tones and gray shades for architecture or mechanical models. Recommended: 190-230 °C nozzle, 25-65 °C bed, up to 200 mm/s, fan on, nozzle 0.4 mm or smaller and layers of 0.1 mm or less; optional drying 55 °C for 6 h. Select the built-in Snapmaker PLA Full Spectrum profile in Orca V2.4.0+.

settings.advice: 0.1 mm or less for smooth color blending.
Use 0.4 mm or smaller to reduce visible stripes.

facts: At about 50/50, cyan with yellow gives a deep green, magenta with yellow a brick red, and cyan with magenta a muted purple; gray darkens and mutes any color.
It can't mix pure black or pure white, and four-color mixes tend to look dark or gray.
Works best on 3D models with enough volume; not recommended for flat or 2D artwork.
Mixing it with the White Edition works but is less predictable; don't combine it with the CMYK Lithophane bundle.
RFID recognition works only on the U1; filaments print on other FDM printers with manual tuning.

entries.title: PLA Full Spectrum Filament Bundle (White Edition): settings and differences
entries.summary: The White Edition replaces gray with white and uses reformulated, more saturated cyan, magenta and yellow, giving brighter and lighter tones plus real white areas; Snapmaker suggests it as the first bundle to buy. Recommended: 190-230 °C nozzle, 25-70 °C bed, up to 250 mm/s (Gray: 200), fan on, nozzle 0.4 mm or smaller, layers 0.1 mm or less, optional drying 55 °C for 6 h. With a 0.4 mm U1 hotend choose the 0.10 mm color-mixing process preset.

settings.advice: 0.1 mm or lower; the 0.10 mm color-mixing preset is tuned for this bundle.

facts: At about 50/50, cyan with yellow gives green, magenta with yellow orange, and cyan with magenta purple; white brightens and softens a mix but lowers saturation.
Best: two filaments at 33-67% each; three-color mixes are possible, four-color mixes turn darker or grayer.
Pure black can't be mixed; use a separate black filament.
Four 1 kg spools, 1.75 mm ±0.03 mm; tuned TD values help reduce visible stripes.
Using it for flat lithophanes can produce horizontal banding.

entries.title: Snapmaker PLA Glow: hardened nozzle, manual loading and print settings
entries.summary: PLA Glow contains abrasive luminous powder, so use a hardened steel nozzle of 0.4 mm or larger (smaller ones clog) and load and unload by hand instead of with the automatic feeder. Orca has a ready profile; manual starting values for 0.4 mm are 200-230 °C nozzle, 25-70 °C bed, 80% fan, up to 200 mm/s, and drying at 55 °C for 8 h.

settings.advice: About 80% for PLA Glow.
Hardened nozzle of 0.4 mm or more; smaller nozzles clog on the luminous powder.

facts: Prints on Textured PEI, Smooth PEI and Graphic Effect plates; let the plate cool before removing a stuck part.
Charge the glow with a bright lamp or window light for about 10 minutes; it fades to barely visible after about 10 minutes, with faint afterglow up to roughly 40 minutes.
Avoid long light or sun exposure: it ages the material, dulls the color and makes it brittle.
Orca V2.4.0 lists PLA Glow profiles for 0.6 and 0.8 mm nozzles.

entries.title: Silk Dual-Color PLA: colors flipping or uneven color transitions
entries.summary: The filament's two colors sit side by side, so if it twists while feeding the visible color can flip or transitions become uneven. Keep it from rotating: tighten extruder tension, keep feature speeds similar, shorten the feed path and never twist the filament by hand.
symptoms: The visible color swaps sides mid-print
Patchy or uneven color transitions
causes: Loose extruder tension letting the filament spin in the gears
Frequent speed changes causing pressure swings
Long automatic feed path allowing rotation inside the PTFE tube
Filament twisted or tangled during handling
steps: Tighten the extruder's side tension screw if the filament can spin in the gears.
Keep outer wall, inner wall and infill speeds close to each other.
Feed from an external spool mounted near the extruder when possible.
Keep the filament neatly wound, as factory-oriented, during use and storage.

settings.advice: Keep close to the outer wall and infill speeds to avoid pressure swings that twist the filament.
Reduce toward the wall speeds so the extruder pressure stays steady.

entries.title: Silk Dual-Color PLA: recommended settings and tips for maximum shine
entries.summary: Silk Dual-Color PLA gives a glossy, two-tone color-shift finish and hides layer lines better than standard PLA. Recommended: 190-240 °C nozzle, 25-70 °C bed, fan on, 50-150 mm/s, optional drying at 55 °C for 6 h. Use a textured PEI plate; no Top Cover or hardened hotend is needed. For more gloss print slower or hotter, and pick curved, multi-faceted models to show off the color shift.

settings.advice: 190-240 °C; go lower if strings appear, higher for extra gloss.
25-70 °C on the recommended textured PEI plate.
Keep at maximum for the smoothest silk surface.
Slow down for a shinier finish.

facts: Slightly more prone to stringing than plain PLA; clogs are rare at recommended settings.
Running the cooling fan at maximum gives the smoothest surface.
Moderately moisture-sensitive; store dry and out of direct sunlight.
Flat or strictly geometric models don't show the two-tone effect well.
Orca V2.3.1 added profiles for several Silk Dual-Color PLA filaments.

entries.title: Snapmaker Silk PLA: plates, drying and stringing tips
entries.summary: Silk PLA has optimized U1 profiles in Orca and needs no Top Cover or hardened hotend. It prints on Textured PEI, Smooth PEI and Graphic Effect plates. Dry it before printing and keep it dry while printing for consistent results. The key fix for stringing is a lower nozzle temperature, helped by dry filament and slightly longer retraction.

settings.advice: Lower it first when Silk PLA strings; it is the main oozing control.
Increase slightly to reduce stringing on travel.

facts: Other FDM printers can use it with manual tuning.
Orca V2.4.0 added 14 new Silk PLA colors.

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 Bracing Kit: fit, slider looseness and recalibration for 3D printing
entries.summary: The Bracing Kit fits the A150, A250, A250T, A350, A350T, F250 and F350 and reduces linear-module slider looseness, avoiding tedious tension adjustments and repairs. 3D printing modules keep working after it is installed, but the single extruder must be recalibrated and the dual extruder needs the essential calibrations in Guides redone. Compatibility was assessed on firmware v1.18.1 with Luban v4.10.1.
steps: Install the Bracing Kit.
Single extruder: run the calibrations again.
Dual extruder: redo the essential calibrations listed in Guides before printing.

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 A/AT/F series: differences, filaments and heated bed limits
entries.summary: Snapmaker 2.0 covers the A series (A150/A250/A350 3-in-1), the quieter AT series (A250T/A350T) and the F series (F250/F350, 3D printing only but upgradable). It prints PLA, ABS, TPU and PETG; nylon is not possible because the brass nozzle is too soft. Layers can be 0.05-0.3 mm. The bed can reach 80-100 °C but needs about 20-30 minutes to get there; a third-party power module would damage it.

settings.advice: Values above 80 °C are possible on the 2.0 but take 20-30 min to reach; plan longer warm-up.

facts: Storage tips: PLA picks up moisture, so keep it dry; keep PETG cool and dry; ABS gives off strong fumes, so ventilate and wear a mask.
Very small, fine models like jewelry can be hard for an FDM machine such as the 2.0.
Third-party slicers supported: Cura, PrusaSlicer, OrcaSlicer, Simplify3D; Luban is free.
On the 2.0 dual module, a glass plate only works with manual leveling, because probing by nozzle contact would flex the platform.

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 single vs dual extrusion module: flow, temperature, nozzles, work area
entries.summary: The single-extrusion module reaches 9 mm³/s and 275 °C with a fixed 0.4 mm brass nozzle and prints PLA, ABS, PETG and TPU. The dual module reaches 20 mm³/s and 300 °C, uses quick-swap hot ends (0.2/0.6/0.8 mm brass and 0.4 mm hardened optional) and adds Breakaway PLA, ASA, PVA, TPU variants, HIPS, CoPA and PA6/PA12-CF/GF. It switches nozzles by lifting with a motor and needs XY offset calibration besides mesh leveling and Z offset.

settings.advice: Keep at or below about 9 mm³/s on the single module (20 mm³/s on the dual) or extrusion will lag at high speed.
Single module tops out at 275 °C, dual at 300 °C; don't set higher.

facts: Single-module work area: 160 × 160 × 145 mm on the A150, 230 × 250 × 235 mm on A250-size machines (A250, F250, A250T) and 320 × 350 × 330 mm on A350-size machines.
Dual-module work area: A150 135 × 140 × 110 mm (both or right nozzle) or 145 × 145 × 110 (left); A250 class 220 × 235 × 205 mm; A350 class 310 × 325 × 290 (both) or 310 × 330 × 290 (one).
Fans: 2 on the single module, 4 on the dual.

entries.title: SnapDryer filament dryer: compatibility, spool capacity and drying while printing
entries.summary: SnapDryer, built with Polymaker and FabNotion and adapted for Snapmaker printers, dries and stores PLA, PETG, ABS, ASA, TPU, PA, PC, PVA and Breakaway Support for PLA in 1.75 or 2.85 mm (Snapmaker printers take only 1.75 mm). You can pre-dry before a print or use continuous drying mode to keep drying during printing. Each sealed box takes spools up to 205 mm diameter and 78 mm height, enough for any Snapmaker spool of 1 kg or less and most other brands.
facts: In Snapmaker's test at 20 °C and 60% RH the humidity in a closed box changed by under 5% over 30 days, about 1.5 times better sealing than a DIY box.
The color-changing silica gel is reusable: orange when dry, dark green once saturated.
Use the internal spool roller with smaller spools.
Snapmaker-specific extras include a filament tube, filament entry cover, tube connector, round clamp and tape measure; Snapmaker handles after-sales service.

entries.title: Snapmaker filament guide: temperatures, speeds and drying for PETG, TPU, nylon, ABS, PVA
entries.summary: Snapmaker's filament guide gives starting ranges for its other filaments (1 kg spools unless stated). Prefer the built-in Orca profile when one exists and use these ranges for tuning; drying values are for pre-print drying.

settings.advice: Start inside the listed range for the filament and adjust in 5 °C steps for stringing (lower) or weak layers (higher).

facts: Basic PLA: 190-230 °C nozzle, 25-60 °C bed, glue or Magigoo, dry 60 °C for 6 h.
Glow-in-the-dark Green PLA: 190-230 °C, bed 25-60 °C, glue or Magigoo, 50-100 mm/s, dry 60 °C for 6 h.
PETG: 230-240 °C, bed 70-80 °C, no surface treatment, 50-100 mm/s, dry 65 °C for 4 h.
TPU: 210-230 °C, bed 25-60 °C, bare or PVA glue, 30-50 mm/s, dry 65 °C for 4 h.
Black TPU95: 200-220 °C, bed 25-50 °C, PVA plus PVP glue, 20-40 mm/s, dry 70 °C for 4 h.
Black Nylon: 250-270 °C, bed 25-50 °C, PVA glue, 40-100 mm/s, dry 80 °C for 6 h.
Wood PLA (750 g): 190-210 °C, bed 25-60 °C, 30-50 mm/s, dry 60 °C for 6 h.
Breakaway PLA (500 g): 220-230 °C, bed 25-60 °C, 20-40 mm/s, dry 90 °C for 6 h.
Newer product pages give wider ranges for some of these (ABS 240-280 °C, Wood PLA 195-260 °C); follow the page for your exact product.

sources.title: SnapSpeed PLA Filament and Matte PLA Filament

entries.title: SnapSpeed PLA and Matte PLA: temperatures, speeds, drying and storage
entries.summary: SnapSpeed PLA is Snapmaker's high-speed PLA and Matte PLA its matte-finish PLA; both are 1.75 mm on 1 kg spools and rated to about 300 mm/s. The filament guide lists SnapSpeed at 190-210 °C for classic printing (the product text says 190-230 °C) and Matte at 210-230 °C, beds at 25-60 °C with glue only when needed, and drying at 55 °C for 6 h. Both absorb moisture, which causes stringing, bubbles and weak layers.

settings.advice: SnapSpeed PLA about 190-210 °C (go toward 230 °C for very fast printing); Matte PLA 210-230 °C.
Both PLAs work at 25-60 °C bed; add glue only if adhesion is poor.
About 1.23-1.24 g/cm³ for SnapSpeed PLA; never 0.

facts: Guide speeds: SnapSpeed 50-100 mm/s for classic printing, Matte 100-300 mm/s.
SnapSpeed PLA: density 1.23 g/cm³ in the guide (the U1 troubleshooting page uses 1.24 for the RFID version), Tg 59 °C, melt 164 °C, tensile strength 46.0 MPa.
Matte PLA: Tg 61 °C, tensile strength 23.2 MPa, elongation 27.8%.
A brass nozzle is fine; hardened steel resists wear better during long high-speed printing.
Made from food-contact-grade PLA resin, but prints are not certified food-safe.
Store sealed with desiccant and dry in a SnapDryer if the filament has picked up moisture.

sources.title: SnapSpeed PLA Filament and Matte PLA Filament

entries.title: SnapSpeed PLA CMYK Lithophane Filament Bundle: nozzle, drying and image tips
entries.summary: This 4 kg RFID set of SnapSpeed PLA in cyan, magenta, yellow and white has TD values tuned for lithophanes and flat layered-color work, not for Full Spectrum 3D mixing. A 0.2 mm hotend gives the finest image detail (0.4 mm works with less detail); neither a hardened hotend nor the Top Cover is needed. Drying is optional at 55 °C for 6 h. Generate models with Lithophane Makers or follow the same parameters in another generator.

settings.advice: 0.2 mm for the sharpest lithophane detail; 0.4 mm is acceptable.

facts: Pick photos with strong contrast, a clear subject and a plain background; avoid low-contrast or cluttered images.
A finished backlit piece also needs a printed frame and light guide plate plus a purchased backlight (156 × 120 mm USB-C recommended).
Low moisture sensitivity; store dry and out of direct sunlight.
Colors won't exactly match the photo; results depend on TD, generator settings and slicing.

sources.title: SnapSpeed PLA CMYK Lithophane Filament Bundle

entries.title: Snapmaker TPU 90A: recommended settings, drying and manual-only loading
entries.summary: TPU 90A is a softer TPU with U1 profiles in Orca. Print it slowly, 30-50 mm/s, at 210-240 °C nozzle and 25-60 °C bed with the fan on (0.4 mm nozzle basis); it is not suited to high speed. Dry at 70 °C for 6 h and store sealed with desiccant. Loading and unloading must be manual: the automatic feeder is prohibited because the soft filament deforms and jams. No Top Cover or hardened hotend is needed; avoid 0.2 mm nozzles.

settings.advice: 210-240 °C for TPU 90A with a 0.4 mm nozzle.
25-60 °C is enough for TPU 90A.
Keep the part fan on; go to 100% if features deform.
Keep print speeds around 30-50 mm/s; TPU 90A doesn't tolerate high speed.

facts: Compatible with Textured PEI, Smooth PEI and Graphic Effect plates.
If a part sticks too firmly, spray alcohol at the part-plate interface to release it.
For poor first-layer adhesion, re-level, clean the plate, then add glue stick or liquid glue.
Wet TPU 90A shows bubbles, stringing and weak layers.

entries.title: TPU 90A in U1 multi-material prints: flexible-rigid parts with beam interlocking
entries.summary: On the U1, TPU 90A can be combined with rigid filaments for soft grips, overmolded parts, hinges and shock absorbers. Where the pair bonds poorly, enable Use Beam Interlocking in Snapmaker Orca so a mechanical interlock forms at the material boundary. TPU can also be part of a multi-material support strategy where the materials should not bond.

settings.advice: Enable when joining TPU 90A to PLA, PA, PETG or PET to strengthen the bond.

facts: Bondable with beam interlocking: TPU with PLA, PA, PETG or PET.
Not recommended for structural joints: TPU with ABS, ASA or PC, unless validated for the specific use.

entries.title: Snapmaker TPU 95A HF: manual loading, drying, plates and nozzle choice
entries.summary: TPU 95A HF is an easier-flowing TPU with U1 profiles in Orca, printable at 50-110 mm/s versus 20-40 mm/s for generic TPU 95A, with steadier feeding, less stringing and the same elasticity. It needs no Top Cover or hardened hotend, but avoid the 0.2 mm nozzle. Load and unload it by hand rather than with the automatic feeder, and dry it before and during printing because it is very moisture-sensitive.

settings.advice: Use 0.4 mm or larger; a 0.2 mm nozzle gives high back-pressure and frequent clogs with TPU.

facts: Works on U1 Textured PEI, Smooth PEI and Graphic Effect plates.
TPU can stick too well: spray alcohol where the part meets the plate when removing it.
If the first layer fails, re-level and clean the plate, then use a glue stick or liquid glue.
Damp TPU strings, bubbles and extrudes unevenly; SnapDryer is recommended both before and during printing.
Snapmaker suggests watching its TPU loading video before the first TPU print.

entries.title: Fixing TPU stringing and nozzle clogs (TPU 95A HF and TPU 90A)
entries.summary: Moisture is the most common cause of TPU stringing and bubbles, so dry first and print from a dryer. Remaining strings call for a bit more and faster retraction, slower travel and closer part spacing. Clogs have different causes: small nozzles, too much retraction pulling softened TPU up into the hot end, and feed resistance. Balance retraction: enough to stop strings, not so much that it causes jams.
symptoms: Strings or hairs between parts
Bubbles or popping during extrusion
Clogged nozzle or jammed extruder
Thin TPU 90A features sagging or collapsing
causes: Wet filament
0.2 mm nozzle
Excessive retraction leading to heat creep
High drag from the spool or automatic feeding
Too little cooling
steps: Dry the TPU (TPU 90A: 70 °C for 6 h) and keep it in a SnapDryer while printing.
For stringing, raise retraction distance and speed, lower travel speed and place parts closer together.
For clogs, use a 0.4 mm or larger nozzle and shorten or disable retraction.
Feed from a hanging spool with little drag and always load and unload TPU manually.
If TPU 90A details deform, run the part fan at 100% and orient the area toward the airflow.

settings.advice: Raise slightly to reduce strings; reduce or disable if clogs appear, since long retractions drag soft TPU into the heat break.
Increase to reduce TPU stringing.
Lower it to limit oozing during TPU travel moves.
Use 100% for TPU 90A if overhangs or thin features deform.

entries.title: U1 add-ons: hardened hotends, extra build plates and using SnapDryer
entries.summary: U1 add-ons include hardened steel hotend bundles in 0.2/0.4/0.6/0.8 mm (sizes can't be mixed in one print), the Top Cover, the SnapDryer bundle, and double-sided plates: textured PEI (one included), smooth PEI, and a steel plate with a carbon-fiber texture that imprints that pattern on part bottoms. SnapDryer is the recommended dryer; third-party dryers can add enough feed drag to make auto-loading fail, requiring manual loading.
facts: SnapDryer Bundle: 1 Dryer Dock and 4 SnapDryer Boxes, co-branded with Polymaker and FabNotion.
Drying power levels at the dock outlet: level 1 about 50 °C, level 2 about 60 °C, level 3 about 70 °C; temperature alone doesn't reflect drying performance.
RFID recognition doesn't work when feeding from the SnapDryer; enter filament type and color on the touchscreen.

entries.title: U1 Dynamic Flow Calibration vs flow rate calibration: when and how to run it
entries.summary: Flow rate calibration corrects the total amount extruded so line width is right; Dynamic Flow Calibration compensates the pressure lag during acceleration and braking (the K value) to avoid blobs and gaps. On the U1 it is automatic: tap Start, then Next, tick Dynamic Flow Calibration under Print Preferences and tap Print. Results are stored in firmware for the loaded filament and revert to the default K once it is unloaded.

settings.advice: Orca holds only the pre-tested default K; the U1's calibrated K lives in firmware, so recalibrate after changing filament instead of editing this.

facts: Run it for a new filament brand or type, the first print, after a hot end change, when filament got damp or its viscosity changed, or when over-/under-extrusion or stringing appears.
Takes about 3 min 30 s for one toolhead or 14 min 40 s for four; vibration compensation with homing 5 min 06 s (3 min 41 s without homing).
Only toolheads used by the job are calibrated; a single toolhead can't be calibrated alone in a multi-color job.
Orca only shows pre-tested default K values; calibrated values stay in the firmware.

entries.title: Snapmaker U1 hotends: stainless standard, hardened optional, one-piece design
entries.summary: The U1 comes with four 0.4 mm proprietary stainless steel hotends plus a spare. Heat sink, heat break, heater block and nozzle are press-fitted into one unit to limit oozing and thermal resistance, so parts can't be replaced separately. Stainless is enough for common filaments like PLA and PETG; hardened steel hotends in 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 mm are optional for abrasives.

settings.advice: Set to the installed hotend size; all toolheads used in one U1 print must have the same diameter.

facts: Maximum nozzle temperature 300 °C; a thermal-isolation heat break reduces heat creep.
Extruder gears are hardened steel because they wear faster than hotends.
Before each print the nozzle tip is brushed coarse then fine to remove residue and keep leveling accurate; there is no active clog prevention.
Hotends of different sizes can't be combined in the same print.

entries.title: Snapmaker U1 key specifications: build volume, speed, temperatures, accuracy
entries.summary: The U1 is a CoreXY printer with four independent toolheads and a 270 × 270 × 270 mm build volume. It reaches 500 mm/s toolhead speed and 20,000 mm/s² acceleration; hotends go to 300 °C and the bed to 100 °C. Layer heights range from 0.08 to 0.24 mm with 0.2 mm as default, dimensional accuracy is up to ±0.1 mm and repeatability ±0.04 mm on every axis.
facts: Size 584 × 499 × 730 mm and 18.2 kg; with the Top Cover 584 × 510 × 751 mm and 21.8 kg.
Direct-drive extrusion; X uses a carbon fiber rod with oil-free bushings, Y and Z are all-metal; motion via timing belts and lead screws on linear bearings.
Bed is 6.5 mm thick (1.5 mm plate plus 5 mm ribs) with mesh variation usually within 0.4 mm; leveling is fully automatic via a probe in the print head.
Ships with one textured PEI steel plate; recommended room temperature 15-30 °C; about 55 dB at 1 m.
Built-in camera: 2 MP at roughly 1 frame per second.
Filament runout detection, power-loss recovery and thermistor monitoring that stops the printer on overheating or thermal runaway.
Jobs arrive via Wi-Fi or USB flash drive; the U1 is a 3D printer only, with no laser/CNC expansion.
Power input 100-240 V; max 1150 W / 6 A at 220-240 V and 400 W / 4 A at 100-120 V.
Hot end PID tuning is not supported.

entries.title: U1 multi-material bonding chart: which pairs bond and when to use beam interlocking
entries.summary: Snapmaker sorts filament pairs into strong bonding, usable for load-bearing parts without extra settings, and bondable, where weak chemical adhesion can be reinforced with Orca's Use Beam Interlocking. Weak pairs also make easy-release interface supports that leave clean bottom surfaces. PVA gives water-soluble supports for cavities and steep overhangs.

settings.advice: Enable for weak-bonding pairs such as TPU with PLA or PLA with PETG to build a mechanical interlock at the boundary.
Choose a material that bonds weakly to the part (e.g. PETG under PLA) for supports that peel off cleanly.

facts: Strong pairs: PLA+PC; PETG with TPU, PET, ABS, ASA or PC; TPU+PET; PET with ABS, ASA or PC; ABS with ASA, PC or PA; ASA with PC or PA; PC+PA.
Weak (bondable via interlocking) pairs: PLA with PETG, TPU, PET, ABS, ASA or PA; TPU with ABS, ASA, PC or PA; PA with PETG or PET.
The TPU 90A page lists TPU with PETG or PET as bondable with beam interlocking, slightly more cautious than the chart.
Typical uses: rigid plus flexible parts (hinges, overmolds, soft grips), PVA soluble supports, and easy-remove supports from a weakly bonding material.
Orca V2.4.1 prompts a reset when PLA and PETG support each other with non-default base or interface patterns.

entries.title: U1 SnapSwap pogo pin lifespan, cleaning interval and PCBA replacement
entries.summary: The SnapSwap toolhead swapper is rated for 1,000,000 swaps in total and each toolhead's pogo pins for 250,000. The U1 counts swaps (shown on the touchscreen) and reminds you every 100,000 swaps to clean the gold contacts on both sides. If contact-related error codes appear, replace the PCBA on the toolhead or on the swapper; one PCBA takes under 5 minutes.
steps: Check the swap count on the touchscreen.
When reminded (every 100,000 swaps), clean the gold contacts on both mating sides.
If pogo-pin error codes persist, swap the toolhead or swapper PCBA.
facts: Example: about 7 multicolor prints a week at roughly 600 swaps each means contact cleaning around every 6 months and PCBA replacement after about 5 years.

entries.title: Snapmaker U1 power consumption when printing and on standby
entries.summary: During multi-color jobs the three parked toolheads hold about 70 °C, adding roughly 10-30 W in total; all hotends shut off when the print ends. Snapmaker measured about 7.8 W idle on Wi-Fi, 118 W for single-color PLA, 127 W for four-color PLA, and 123-143 W for ABS with the Top Cover.
facts: Test conditions: PLA at 220 °C nozzle and 65 °C bed; ABS at 280 °C and 100 °C with the Top Cover.
A 33-hour job with 30 W of standby heads uses about 1 kWh extra, but faster multi-color printing usually cuts total energy (one test: 0.44 kWh on the U1 vs 2.1 kWh on another printer).
Maximum input: 1150 W / 6 A at 220-240 V, 400 W / 4 A at 100-120 V.

entries.title: Why the U1 still prints a prime tower despite 'Zero Purge'
entries.summary: The U1 is a toolchanger: every filament has its own nozzle, so color changes need no flushing and produce no purge waste, which is why it is marketed as Zero Purge and shows little color bleed. A small prime tower is still printed to clear the bit of degraded filament that sits in a parked, heated nozzle, giving a clean start after each head swap and avoiding oozing or weak layer bonding.

settings.advice: Keep enabled for multi-toolhead U1 prints; it primes nozzles that cooled to standby and prevents oozing and weak bonding after swaps.

facts: Idle toolheads wait around 70 °C and are heated to print temperature just before they are used, so swaps need no waiting.
The 5X faster / 5X less waste claim compares U1 multi-color jobs with single-nozzle filament changers; you can compare by slicing one model for both in OrcaSlicer.

entries.title: U1 software and firmware: Snapmaker Orca, OrcaSlicer, open Klipper-based firmware
entries.summary: Snapmaker recommends Snapmaker Orca for the U1 because its material profiles are tuned for the machine, but standard OrcaSlicer can also generate G-code; Luban is not compatible. The firmware is built on Klipper, Moonraker and Fluidd, Snapmaker published its changes on GitHub on 2026-03-30, and updates arrive over the air. Prints can be watched remotely in the Snapmaker App or Orca.
facts: Repositories: github.com/Snapmaker/u1-klipper, u1-moonraker and u1-fluidd.
Touchscreen languages: English, Simplified Chinese, Russian, German, Hebrew; the Snapmaker App offers English and Simplified Chinese.
Snapmaker Orca is available in 20 languages, among them English, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Japanese, Korean and Chinese.
Download Snapmaker Orca from snapmaker.com/snapmaker-orca.

entries.title: Filaments the Snapmaker U1 supports, with and without Top Cover or hardened hotends
entries.summary: As shipped, the U1 handles PLA, PETG, TPU, PVA and PCTG. Adding the Top Cover opens up PET, ABS, ASA, PA and PC. With both the Top Cover and hardened steel hotends it can also print carbon-fiber and glass-fiber reinforced polymers. Any good-quality 1.75 mm third-party filament works, but RFID recognition only functions with official Snapmaker spools.
facts: TPU must be 90A Shore or harder; softer grades were still under test.
Spool holder limits: 52-60 mm inner diameter, up to 70 mm wide and up to 1 kg.
The RFID system is proprietary; Snapmaker has no plans to open-source it.
PA-CF and PA-GF are listed for parts needing high strength, stiffness and impact resistance.
The printer comes with four 500 g SnapSpeed PLA spools in Red, Pearl White, Black and Yellow; colors can't be chosen.

entries.title: When to run U1 multi-toolhead offset calibration
entries.summary: Run the multi-toolhead offset calibration at first setup, after replacing a hot end, after the nozzle scrapes or hits the bed or other parts, or when layers shift in multi-toolhead prints. It takes about 15-20 minutes and doesn't need repeating before every print.
symptoms: Colors from different toolheads misaligned
Layer shifting in multi-toolhead prints
Nozzle scraped or collided with the bed

entries.title: U1 Top Cover: chamber heating, air filtration and which filaments need it
entries.summary: Out of the box the U1 isn't fully enclosed: it has side panels, a front door and a rear cover. The optional Top Cover passively warms the chamber to as much as 50 °C, switches between hot and cool chamber modes per filament on its own, keeps noise below 50 dB and filters air through primary cotton, a HEPA12 filter and modified activated carbon. It is what enables PET, ABS, ASA, PA and PC.
facts: Don't mix high-temperature and heat-sensitive filaments in one job: the chamber can't change temperature instantly and heat-sensitive filament may soften and clog.
A magnetic front door gives access to the chamber without removing the cover.
Noise below 50 dB was measured at 1 m in internal circulation mode with the fan at 60%.
Snapmaker Orca V2.3.5 added Top Cover controls.

entries.title: Snapmaker U1 box contents and time from unboxing to first print
entries.summary: The U1 needs some assembly, guided by the printed multilingual manual. Expect about 120 minutes to the first print: roughly 15 minutes unboxing, 40 minutes assembling and 65 minutes of largely automatic setup and calibration (placing and removing the PEI sheet is manual), not counting installing the app and Orca.
facts: In the box: printer with textured PEI steel sheet, tool box, 4 toolheads with hot ends, 4 × 500 g SnapSpeed PLA, 4 filament holders, 2 filament feeders, waste collector, 4 toolhead cables, AC cable, safety and quick start guides.
The manual covers nine languages: Turkish, Korean, Japanese, Chinese, Italian, Spanish, French, German and English.
The power cord matches the destination country and the PSU accepts 100-240 V, so no adapter is needed.

entries.title: Wood PLA nozzle clogging and signs that the filament is damp
entries.summary: Wood fibers make Wood PLA more clog-prone and more moisture-sensitive than plain PLA. Frequent clogs call for drying the spool, a slightly lower nozzle temperature and a nozzle of 0.4 mm or more. Damp filament shows as whitish patches, uneven color, extra stringing, popping or crackling at the nozzle and rough surfaces.
symptoms: Recurring nozzle clogs
Local whitening or uneven color
More stringing
Popping or crackling while extruding
Rough, inconsistent surface
causes: Wood fibers in a small nozzle
Moisture absorbed by the fibers
Nozzle temperature on the high side
steps: Dry the filament at 55 °C for 8 h.
Reduce nozzle temperature by a few degrees.
Switch to a nozzle of at least 0.4 mm.
Store the spool sealed with desiccant afterwards.

settings.advice: Reduce a few degrees if Wood PLA keeps clogging.

entries.title: Snapmaker Wood PLA: settings, nozzle size, drying and limitations
entries.summary: Wood PLA blends PLA with natural wood fibers for a matte, wood-like look that sands, paints and stains well. With a 0.4 mm nozzle use 195-260 °C, a 50-65 °C bed, fan on and up to 250 mm/s. Use 0.4 mm or larger nozzles because 0.2 mm clogs easily; no Top Cover or hardened hotend is needed. Dry at 55 °C for 8 h. It softens at roughly 55-60 °C (the page gives both), so avoid load-bearing, outdoor or hot uses.

settings.advice: 195-260 °C; lower a little if clogs recur.
50-65 °C for Wood PLA.
0.4 mm recommended, 0.6 or 0.8 mm also fine; avoid 0.2 mm or smaller.

facts: Good for decor, frames, architectural models, props, trays and chess sets; not for snap-fits, mechanical parts or precise assemblies.
On the U1, RFID recognizes the spool and loads recommended settings automatically.
Long UV exposure can yellow the filament; store sealed with desiccant, cool, dry and out of sunlight.
V2.4.1 raised Graphic Effect plate temperatures for PLA Wood to 70 °C.

entries.title: Adaptive pressure advance for high-speed printing (Orca beta)
entries.summary: Ideal pressure advance usually drops as flow and acceleration rise, so a single value can be wrong at some speeds. Orca's adaptive PA takes several measured PA, flow and acceleration triplets and interpolates a value for each move. It needs calibrated flow and PA and a fixed fallback value.
steps: Run the PA pattern at 3 or more speeds per acceleration (outer wall, inner wall, fastest feature) at your lowest and highest accelerations
Read the flow for each test from the flow colour scheme in preview
Enter one line per test as PA,flow,acceleration (e.g. 0.04,3.96,3000)
Check PA falls as flow rises; if it does not, inspect the extruder

settings.advice: Enable to override the fixed PA with interpolated values.
Paste the PA,flow,acceleration triplets here.
Experimental; leave off unless the model is accurate, since it can mark outer walls near overhangs.
Separate PA for bridges; a lower value reduces slight under-extrusion just after bridges. 0 disables.
Keep a sensible fixed value as fallback and for tool changes.

sources.title: OrcaSlicer Wiki: Flow ratio and pressure advance

entries.title: Avoid crossing walls: reducing stringing and surface marks from travel
entries.summary: Avoid crossing walls routes travel moves inside the part instead of across perimeters and open air, so ooze lands inside rather than on visible surfaces. It is recommended for stringy materials such as PETG and TPU. It lengthens travel slightly; the detour limit controls how far it may go around.

settings.advice: Enable for detailed prints and stringy materials.
Limit the detour (mm or % of direct path); 0 means no limit. Longer detours avoid more crossings but cost time.
Combine with fast travel to minimise ooze time.

facts: A few Prusa users reported layer shifts that went away after turning this off; treat as anecdotal

sources.title: Bambu Lab Wiki: Stringing and Oozing

entries.title: Bed temperature ranges by material and what goes wrong outside them
entries.summary: Bed temperature should sit a little below the material's glass transition. Too cool causes warping and parts coming loose; too hot softens the bottom layers into elephant foot and, in enclosed printers, can overheat the chamber and cause PLA heat creep. Ranges differ by plate type, so check the filament maker's values.

settings.advice: Set within the material range for a smooth or high-temp PEI plate; subtract 5-10 C from the material Tg as a safe upper limit.
Textured PEI often needs a little more heat for PLA (Bambu: about 55-65 C).
Cool plates let PLA print at about 35 C, keeping enclosed chambers cool.
First-layer bed temperature can be slightly higher than later layers for grip.

facts: Orca table: PLA 50-60 C, ABS 90-100 C, ASA 90-100 C, TPU 40-60 C, PC 100-120 C, nylon 90-110 C
Polymaker: PLA 55-60 C, PETG 70-80 C, ABS 90-100 C, TPU 25-60 C
Prusa: PETG 85 C first layer and 90 C after; ASA 105 C then 110 C
Bambu (enclosed printers): PLA 45-60 C with the top glass removed, PETG 60-80 C, ABS/ASA 90-100 C, TPU 35-45 C

sources.title: Polymaker Wiki: Print Not Sticking to Build Plate

entries.title: Brim types, width and mouse ears in OrcaSlicer
entries.summary: A brim adds extra first-layer area around the part to hold edges down. Orca offers Auto, Mouse ears, Painted, Outer, Inner and Outer-and-inner brims. Wider brims hold better but use more material and are harder to clean off; mouse ears only reinforce sharp corners.

settings.advice: Auto sizes from height, footprint and material (capped at 18 mm). Mouse ears or Painted for corner-only help; Outer is easiest to remove.
Increase for warping parts; Bambu suggests 8-10 mm for PLA corner lift. With mouse ears this is the ear radius.
Larger gap is easier to remove but holds less; too large and the brim stops touching the part.
Corners sharper than this get ears; 0 disables ears, 180 puts them on almost every non-straight feature.
Simplifies the outline before detecting sharp corners; 0 disables simplification.

facts: Polymaker suggests 10-30 brim lines for parts that need one
Brims and rafts usually do not need to be more than a few layers tall

sources.title: Bambu Lab Wiki: Model Warping, Falling Off, or Collapsing
Polymaker Wiki: Print Not Sticking to Build Plate

entries.title: Brittle filament snapping on the spool or in the feed path
entries.summary: Filament that snaps before reaching the nozzle is usually fibre-filled (CF/GF), aged, stressed on a tight spool, or affected by storage. Drying often helps, removing the outer windings of a long-stored spool helps, and a short, straight, low-friction feed path matters most for brittle materials.
causes: Fibre-reinforced filaments that are naturally brittle
Long storage or vacuum sealing dehydrating or stressing the outer windings
Moisture absorption
Sharp bends and long PTFE paths, multi-spool feeders
Repeated drying cycles (PC)
steps: Dry the spool at its recommended temperature
Remove the outer roughly 50 g of a long-stored spool
Feed from a straight path; avoid sharp bends and long tubes
Prefer direct feeding over multi-material feeders for very brittle materials
For CF/GF filaments use a hardened nozzle, print a little hotter and 25-50% slower

entries.title: Recommended order of OrcaSlicer calibrations
entries.summary: Orca's calibration tests build on each other. For every new filament run temperature, max volumetric speed, pressure advance, flow ratio, then retraction. Printer-level tests (cornering, input shaping, VFA, adaptive PA, tolerance last) only need repeating after hardware changes. Extruder E-steps or rotation distance must already be right.
steps: Temperature tower
Max volumetric speed (use 10-20% below the result)
Pressure advance
Flow ratio (rerun a quick PA test if flow changed a lot)
Retraction
Optional printer tests: cornering, input shaping (prefer the printer's automatic routine), VFA, adaptive PA, tolerance
Start a new project afterward to leave calibration mode

entries.title: Clogs after switching from high-temperature to low-temperature filament
entries.summary: Leftover ABS, PETG, PC or nylon in the nozzle does not melt at PLA or TPU temperatures and can block flow. Purge the new filament at the old, hotter temperature first, then cool while still extruding until the new material flows cleanly.
steps: Heat to the previous filament's temperature (Bambu: 250-300 C after PA-CF, PET-CF, PPS and similar)
Unload the old filament
Load the new filament and extrude until the colour and flow are clean
Lower to about 220-240 C (or the new filament's range) while extruding until flow is steady
If extrusion still fails, heat further and use a cleaning needle or cold pull
facts: Prusa recommends loading PLA at the ABS or PETG temperature if those were printed before

entries.title: Nothing extrudes: diagnosing and clearing a clog
entries.summary: First find where the blockage is. An extruder-side jam is usually softened or deformed filament stuck above the hotend; a nozzle clog is debris, burnt residue, fibres, or filament that never melted because the nozzle was too cold or the print too fast. Heat to print temperature, push by hand, then unload and inspect the tip before deciding on cleaning or a new nozzle.
causes: Filament softened in the extruder from a hot chamber (PLA, PETG, TPU)
Debris, burnt residue or fibre particles narrowing the nozzle
Nozzle temperature too low or speed too high for melting
Leftover high-temperature material after switching to a lower-temperature filament
Very soft TPU or wet PVA flattened by the drive gears
Kinked, thick or chewed filament section
steps: Check nozzle and bed temperatures match the filament
Heat to print temperature and extrude a little while pushing gently by hand
Unload, cut off the damaged tip and reload
Test with the nozzle at about 220 C and PLA: a long smooth strand dropping straight means the path is clear
If extrusion is weak, clear the nozzle with a cleaning needle or a cold pull
If flow still fails, open the extruder to check gears, or replace the nozzle

settings.advice: Confirm it matches the filament; too low can stop extrusion entirely.
Lower if clogs follow very fast printing.

facts: Bambu recommends 0.6 or 0.8 mm nozzles for fibre-filled filaments and warns against 0.2 mm nozzles with them
Simplify3D mentions pushing debris back with a guitar E string as a last resort

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Clogged Extruder

entries.title: Part cooling fan settings by material in OrcaSlicer
entries.summary: PLA wants full cooling after the first layer; PETG prints best with moderate fan; ABS, ASA, PC and nylon need little or none for layer strength and to avoid warping, with short bursts for overhangs. Orca controls fan by layer time, with separate values for the first layers, overhangs, bridges and support interfaces.

settings.advice: Fan off for the first 1-3 layers for adhesion.
Ramp the fan up gradually until this layer (e.g. 0% at layer 1 to full by layer 4-5).
PLA up to 100%; PETG about half (Prusa); ABS/ASA low or 0.
Base fan for layers slower than the layer-time thresholds; 0 for ABS/ASA.
Layers faster than this get fan between min and max.
Extra cooling on overhangs and bridges; Prusa suggests only 10-20% for ABS/PC overhangs.
Keep fan always on at least minimum speed to avoid start-stop cycling.

facts: Prusa says PLA and PETG generally should not be printed in a closed enclosure because they need cooling
Polymaker: fans are usually turned off for low-density polymers such as ABS and HIPS

entries.title: Cracks in tall ABS and ASA prints
entries.summary: Tall ABS or ASA parts crack between layers when upper layers cool and shrink while the lower part is still warm. The stress exceeds the layer bond. Keep the whole part warm in an enclosure, turn the part fan off, avoid drafts and print slower and hotter. For very large parts, PETG or a tougher PLA may be the practical choice.
causes: Open printer or drafts cooling one side
Part cooling fan on
Low nozzle temperature giving weak bonds
Large cross-sections building high shrink stress
steps: Print enclosed; aim for a warm chamber (about 40-50 C or more)
Turn part cooling off
Use a draft shield on open printers
Raise nozzle temperature and slow down (Polymaker prints ABS near 260 C at about 35 mm/s with a 0.6 mm nozzle)
Avoid opening the enclosure until the part has cooled
Consider PETG for very large parts

settings.advice: 0 or very low for ABS/ASA to keep layers fusing.
Set 0 so the fan does not start on short layers.
Enable on open-frame printers.
About 50-70 C for ABS/ASA on printers with active chamber heating.
Use the upper part of the range for stronger bonds.
Slow down to give layers more time to fuse.

sources.title: Layer separation and splitting (FDM) - Prusa Knowledge Base

entries.title: Parts measuring too large or too small
entries.summary: Measure away from the first layer, then sort the error. A fixed offset at every size points to flow or a contour offset; an error that grows with size is material shrinkage. Fix elephant foot and flow first, then use X-Y contour compensation for fixed errors and filament shrinkage for proportional ones.
steps: Print a tall test part and measure the top 20 or so layers, not the base
Fix elephant foot and calibrate flow ratio
Same error at 20 mm and 100 mm: apply X-Y contour compensation (e.g. -0.1 mm if always 0.1 mm too big)
Error proportional to size: set filament shrinkage (e.g. 99.5% if 100 mm measures 99.5 mm)
Use Inner/Outer/Inner order or Precise wall for tighter outer dimensions
Check Z height with Precise Z height if the part must match exactly

settings.advice: Negative shrinks outer contours, positive grows them; use for constant offsets.
Enter measured size as a percent of nominal (94% if 100 mm prints as 94 mm); Orca scales XY to compensate.
Same idea for height on high-shrink materials.
Improves outer dimensional accuracy with inner/outer wall order.
Adjusts the last layers so total height matches the model.
Too high makes parts oversized; calibrate before compensating.

facts: Prusa expects ABS to shrink about 1-2%
Simplify3D example: 0.1 mm error on a 20 mm part = 0.5% shrinkage

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Dimensional Accuracy

entries.title: Elephant foot: bulging first layers and how to compensate
entries.summary: Elephant foot is a flared bottom where the first few layers are wider than the rest. It comes from a nozzle set too close and a bed hot enough to soften the lower layers under the weight above. Fix Z offset and bed temperature first, then use Orca's elephant foot compensation; a raft or a small chamfer in the model also hides it.
causes: First layer over-squished (nozzle too close)
Bed temperature above or near the material's softening point (e.g. PLA bed over 60 C)
Hot first-layer nozzle temperature
Over-extrusion on the first layer
steps: Check Z offset; lines should be flattened but not smeared
Lower bed temperature toward the low end of the material range
Enable elephant foot compensation, start around 0.1-0.2 mm and measure
Spread compensation over 1-5 layers if the flare goes up several layers
If it persists, use a raft or add a small chamfer to the bottom edge in CAD

settings.advice: Shrinks the first layer inward; start about 0.1-0.2 mm and match your measured bulge. Not applied on rafts.
Taper the compensation over 1-5 layers if the bulge spans several layers.
Lower 5 C at a time; keep the bed a little below the material's glass transition. Use the key for your plate type.
A very hot first layer promotes elephant foot; bring it closer to the normal print temperature.
Raise slightly if the first layer is visibly smeared.

sources.title: Polymaker Wiki: Elephant Foot (Smooshed First Layer)

entries.title: Extruder clicking, skipping or grinding filament
entries.summary: Clicking means the extruder cannot push filament through as fast as asked, so the motor skips or the gear chews the filament. Common causes are a nozzle too close on the first layer, printing faster than the hotend melts, low temperature, a partial clog, aggressive retraction, or idler tension that is wrong.
symptoms: Periodic click or knock from the extruder
Plastic shavings near the drive gear
Filament with a ground notch
Under-extrusion or gaps following the clicks
causes: First layer too close, blocking the nozzle
Requested flow above the hotend's melt rate
Nozzle temperature too low
Partial clog or heat creep
Retraction too fast or too long
Idler too tight (flattens filament) or too loose (slips)
Small nozzle (0.25 mm and below) or binding filament path
steps: If it clicks only on the first layer, raise Z offset
Test by reducing retraction speed 50%; if grinding stops, retraction was the cause
Raise nozzle temperature 5-10 C (not if heat creep is suspected)
Lower print speed or max volumetric speed (Simplify3D tests at half speed)
Check for clogs and do a cold pull if flow is weak
Clean the gears and set idler tension per the extruder's guide; check spool and tube friction

settings.advice: Lower if grinding happens during retractions.
Reduce if long retractions grind the same spot.
Raise 5-10 C within the material range.
Lower so speeds stay within melt capacity.
Raise slightly if clicking happens on the first layer only.

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Grinding Filament

entries.title: Bulges after speed changes: extrusion rate smoothing
entries.summary: Sudden jumps in flow, for example when the slicer slows down for an overhang or switches from inner to outer wall, leave bulges or thin spots. Extrusion rate smoothing limits how fast flow may change (mm3/s per second) by ramping speed. It only affects slicer-requested speed changes, not firmware cornering slowdowns.

settings.advice: 0 disables. Start at 60-80% of the acceleration-based max (e.g. about 35-50 at 1000 mm/s2 accel for 0.42 x 0.16 mm). Bowden or no PA: about 8-10.
Default 3 mm; lower is smoother but heavier G-code. Raise to 3-5 if the printer stutters or Klipper reports Timer too close.
Enable to apply smoothing only to outer and overhang walls and avoid slowing hidden features.

facts: Any non-zero ERS value disables arc fitting
Tune by reducing 10% if bulges remain at sharp overhangs, or raising 10% if none appear
On Klipper direct drive, Orca suggests pressure advance smooth time around 0.02 s before tuning ERS

entries.title: Filament drying temperatures and times by material
entries.summary: Dry filament in a forced-air dryer or convection oven below the spool's and filament's softening point. Bambu's convection-oven values are a good reference. Do not use a microwave or a kitchen oven with hot spots; turn spools and store them sealed straight after drying.
steps: Check the spool's own temperature limit before heating
Dry at the material temperature for the listed time, turning the spool midway if heating from one side
Let it cool, then store immediately in a sealed box or bag with desiccant
Monitor storage humidity with a hygrometer
facts: Convection oven, Bambu values: PLA 50 C for 8 h; PLA Silk 55 C for 8 h
PETG and PETG-CF: 60-65 C for 8 h
ABS and ASA: 75-85 C for 8 h
TPU: about 70 C for 8 h
PC: 75-85 C for 8 h; PVA and PA/nylon blends: 75-85 C for 8-12 h
PPA-CF and PPS-CF: 100-140 C for 8-12 h
Nylon left in open air for about 3 months becomes very hard to dry at 80-90 C
PC can become brittle on the spool after repeated heat-cool drying cycles; keep it sealed instead of re-drying often

entries.title: First layer not sticking to the build plate
entries.summary: Poor first-layer grip is usually a dirty plate, a nozzle that starts too high, the wrong plate type in the slicer, or a bed that is too cool. Clean first, check the squish, then slow the first layer and keep the fan off. Use glue or a brim only after the basics are right.
causes: Skin oil, dust or residue on the plate
Nozzle too far from the bed (Z offset too high or stale bed mesh)
Slicer plate type does not match the installed plate, so bed temperature or offset is wrong
First layer printed too fast or with the part fan on
Bed too cool for the material
steps: Clean with 90%+ IPA; if adhesion fades over time wash with warm water and dish soap, then dry
Re-run bed leveling, then adjust Z offset until lines are slightly flattened with no gaps
Confirm the bed type selected in the slicer
Slow the first layer to about 30-45 mm/s or less and turn the fan off for it
Raise bed temperature 5-10 C for materials that will not stick
Add a brim, then glue stick for PETG, ABS, ASA, PC, nylon and flex (not needed for PLA on PEI)

settings.advice: Lower in small steps (about 0.02-0.05 mm) if first-layer lines are round and separated; never crush the nozzle into the plate.
Reduce for better grip; around 30-45 mm/s or less is common.
At least 1; 3 for warp-prone parts.
Raise 5-10 C if the first layer will not grip; use the key for your plate type.
A thicker first layer (up to about 75% of nozzle diameter) tolerates small leveling errors better.
Add a brim for small or sharp-cornered parts before reaching for adhesives.

facts: Prusa warns against cosmetic alcohols or tissues with softeners because they leave oils
Bambu notes its textured PEI plate profile lowers the nozzle 0.04 mm automatically, so picking the wrong plate leaves the first layer too high

sources.title: First layer issues - Prusa Knowledge Base
Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Print Not Sticking to the Bed
Polymaker Wiki: Print Not Sticking to Build Plate
Bambu Lab Wiki: Model Warping, Falling Off, or Collapsing

entries.title: First-layer slicer settings for reliable adhesion
entries.summary: The first layer should be printed slower, slightly thicker and wider than the rest, with the fan off, so it bonds firmly and tolerates small leveling errors. Orca keeps separate initial-layer values for speed, height, line width, nozzle temperature, bed temperature and acceleration.

settings.advice: Keep low (about 30-45 mm/s or less) even on fast printers; Simplify3D's example runs it 50% slower than other layers.
Also keep slow; the first-layer solid fill needs time to bond.
Thicker first layer (up to about 75% of nozzle diameter) is more forgiving.
Slightly wider than normal improves contact.
Lower acceleration reduces dragging and tearing of first-layer lines.
Orca recommends matching nozzle diameter for stable base walls with Arachne.
Keep the fan off for the first layer (1-3 layers).

sources.title: Polymaker Wiki: Print Not Sticking to Build Plate
Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Print Not Sticking to the Bed

entries.title: Reading the first layer: nozzle too close vs too far
entries.summary: The first layer shows whether Z offset is right. Too close gives thin, transparent or rough ridged lines, little extrusion on the first 1-2 layers, extruder clicking and elephant foot. Too far gives round, separated lines with gaps that peel up and can lead to spaghetti. Adjust Z offset in small steps and re-check.
symptoms: Too close: almost no plastic on layers 1-2, then normal from about layer 3-4
Too close: rough, scraped surface, clicking extruder, plate marks
Too far: visible gaps between round lines, weak grip, lines lift when touched
One area too close and another too far: bed not level or mesh stale
steps: Re-run automatic bed leveling (always after moving the printer or changing the plate or nozzle)
Clean residue off the nozzle before leveling; blobs on the tip skew probing
Print a single-layer test and adjust Z offset by about 0.02-0.05 mm per step
If only part of the plate is off, check plate seating, debris under the sheet and bed mesh
Do not lower the nozzle to fix poor adhesion caused by a dirty plate; it can damage the sheet

settings.advice: Positive moves the nozzle up (fixes over-squish); negative moves it down (fixes gaps). Change in 0.02-0.05 mm steps.
A slightly wider first-layer line helps fill small gaps and grip.
If the first layer must stay squished for grip, compensate the bulge here.

sources.title: First layer issues - Prusa Knowledge Base
Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Not Extruding at Start of Print
Bambu Lab Wiki: First Layer Printing Optimization Guide (P2S)

entries.title: Calibrating flow ratio in OrcaSlicer (YOLO and 2-pass)
entries.summary: Flow ratio scales all extrusion for a filament. Orca's YOLO test prints eleven blocks with offsets around the current value; pick the smoothest top with no gaps and add its offset. The older 2-pass method uses percentage modifiers. Save the result in the filament profile, and recheck pressure advance if flow changed a lot.
steps: Select the right printer and filament profile first; YOLO builds on the current filament flow ratio
Calibration > Flow ratio > YOLO (recommended); default range -0.05 to +0.05, step 0.01
Pick the block with the smoothest top, no gaps between arcs and little line at the inner spiral
New flow = old flow + block offset (e.g. 0.98 + 0.01 = 0.99)
2-pass: Pass 1 nine blocks, Pass 2 ten blocks from -9 to 0; new = old x (100 + modifier) / 100
Save to the filament profile

settings.advice: Store the calibrated value here; typical range 0.95-1.05.
Process-level multiplier applied on top of the filament ratio; keep at 1 unless you need a per-process tweak.
Fine-tune top surfaces only after the base flow is calibrated.

facts: Flow results depend on correct E-steps or rotation distance and on temperature
On Bambu printers leave the printer's own Flow calibration option unchecked when running Orca's test

sources.title: OrcaSlicer Wiki: Flow ratio and pressure advance

entries.title: Gaps between infill or top skin and the perimeters
entries.summary: A visible gap where infill or top skin meets the walls means the two are not overlapping enough to fuse, or infill is printed too fast or under-extruded. Increase infill/wall overlap a little, slow the infill and check flow.
steps: Confirm flow is calibrated
Increase infill/wall overlap a few percent
For top surfaces, set top/bottom infill-wall overlap around 25-30%
Slow infill (Simplify3D tests at half speed, then speeds back up)

settings.advice: Default 15%; raise a few percent if sparse infill pulls away from walls. Too high can show infill on outer walls.
Orca suggests about 25-30% to close pinholes where top skin meets walls.
Lower if infill does not bond to walls.
Fix under-extrusion first.

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Gaps Between Infill and Outline
OrcaSlicer Wiki: Top and bottom shells

entries.title: Gaps inside thin walls and missing small features
entries.summary: Walls only a few line widths thick can leave a gap down the middle, and features thinner than the nozzle may not print at all. Orca's Arachne wall generator varies line width to fill thin walls; Classic needs Detect thin wall or a line width that divides the wall evenly. Features thinner than the nozzle need a redesign or a smaller nozzle.
causes: Wall thickness not a clean multiple of line width (e.g. 1.0 mm wall with 0.4 mm lines)
Classic wall generator without thin-wall handling
Minimum feature size set high enough to drop small details
Feature thinner than the nozzle diameter
steps: Check the preview for gaps or missing features before printing
Switch the wall generator to Arachne
Lower minimum feature size if small details disappear
With Classic, enable Detect thin wall or set line width so the wall divides evenly (e.g. 0.5 mm lines for a 1.0 mm wall)
Thicken the feature in CAD or use a smaller nozzle (e.g. 0.3 mm or below)

settings.advice: Arachne adapts line width to thin and tapering walls; Classic keeps fixed widths.
Lower so thin details are kept; features below it are skipped.
Width used for lines that replace thin features; affects how thin features are printed.
Classic only: prints walls too thin for two lines as a single line. Orca suggests Arachne instead.
Adjust so wall thickness divides evenly by line count when using Classic.
Controls where gap fill is applied; make sure small gaps are filled where you need them.

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Gaps in Thin Walls
Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Small Features Not Printed

entries.title: Holes and gaps in top surfaces
entries.summary: Holes in the top skin usually mean too few solid top layers for the infill spacing below, very low infill density, or under-extrusion. Aim for at least about 0.5-1 mm of total top thickness, raise infill if needed, and check flow.
causes: Too few top shell layers, especially at small layer heights
Very sparse infill (around 10% or less) leaving long spans
Under-extrusion
Poor cooling on the first top layer
steps: Set at least 3 top layers and a minimum top thickness around 0.5-1 mm
If gaps remain, increase top layers (e.g. 3 to 5)
Raise infill density (e.g. 15% to 25-30%)
Calibrate flow

settings.advice: At least 3; increase until the preview shows a closed top.
Set a minimum thickness (about 0.5-1 mm) so thin layer heights get more layers automatically.
Raise if the first top layer sags into large infill gaps.
Monotonic line is recommended for even top surfaces.
Raise slightly only if the top is under-filled after base flow is calibrated.

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Gaps in Top Layers
OrcaSlicer Wiki: Top and bottom shells

entries.title: Ghosting and ringing: ripples after corners and features
entries.summary: Ghosting shows as faint repeated waves on a wall just after a sharp corner, hole or letter. The toolhead or bed vibrates after quick direction changes. Fix loose belts and frame issues, use input shaping where the firmware supports it, and otherwise lower acceleration, jerk and outer wall speed.
symptoms: Echoes of corners, holes or embossed text repeated along the wall
Worse on the axis with more moving mass (bed axis on bed slingers)
Gets worse at higher speed and acceleration
causes: Acceleration or jerk too high for the frame
Loose belts or loose screws
No or poorly tuned input shaping
Printer on a wobbly surface; heavy moving mass
steps: Check belt tension and tighten loose frame and carriage screws
Place the printer on a firm surface
Run input shaping (accelerometer or ringing tower)
Lower outer wall acceleration and speed as a test
Use resonance avoidance if a specific speed band rings

settings.advice: Lower to reduce ringing on visible surfaces.
Lower overall if ringing appears everywhere.
Slower outer walls ring less.
Lower jerk reduces the shock at direction changes.
Enable to keep outer wall speed outside a resonant band; turn it off while testing ringing.

facts: Polymaker's example: 3000 mm/s2 accel and 30 mm/s jerk ghosted; 500 mm/s2 and 12 mm/s did not, at about 15% more print time

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Vibrations and Ringing
