entries.title: Heat creep: clogs that start partway through a print
entries.summary: Heat creep is heat rising past the heat break so filament softens and swells where it should stay solid, jamming the extruder or hotend. It usually shows as a print that starts fine and then under-extrudes or stops. Hot enclosures with PLA, high bed temperatures in closed printers, a failing heatsink fan and long retractions are typical triggers.
symptoms: Good first layers, then thinning and stopped extrusion after a while
Extruder clicking with filament that will not move
Unloaded filament with a swollen or mushroomed section above the melt zone
causes: Chamber too warm for low-Tg filaments (PLA, TPU; PETG if very hot)
High bed temperature heating a closed chamber
Hotend heatsink fan stopped, blocked or reversed
Hot room in summer
Long or slow retractions and low-flow moves (e.g. ironing) keeping filament in the transition zone
steps: Print PLA and TPU with the door open or lid removed on enclosed printers
Keep the chamber at least 10 C below the filament's glass transition temperature
Use a lower bed temperature (or a cool plate) for PLA in enclosed printers
Check the hotend fan spins whenever the nozzle is hot and the heatsink is clean
Shorten retraction on direct drive
Clear the jam, then reseat any PTFE liner fully

settings.advice: Set 0 (no chamber heating) for PLA, PETG, TPU and PVA.
Keep PLA bed temperature modest in closed printers (Bambu: about 55 C on textured PEI); use the key for your plate type.
Reduce on direct drive; long retractions pull soft filament into the cold zone.
Filament softening temperature; Orca warns to open the door or lid when the bed is at or above it.

entries.title: Infill pattern showing through walls or top surfaces
entries.summary: Seeing the infill pattern on the outside means the skin is too thin, infill is pressing outward, or the filament is translucent. Add walls and top layers, avoid printing infill before walls, keep infill/wall overlap modest, and with multi-colour prints avoid flushing into infill under light or clear filaments.
causes: Too few walls or top layers
Infill printed before walls pushing them out
Infill/wall overlap too high
Light or translucent filament
Purged colour flushed into infill showing through thin walls
steps: Add a wall loop (more walls reduce infill ghosting)
Increase top shell layers
Turn off Print infill first, or pair it with Precise wall / Inner-Outer-Inner
Lower infill/wall overlap a little
Disable Flush into objects' infill for light or translucent colours

settings.advice: Increase by one; more walls hide infill and add strength.
Raise if infill shows through top surfaces.
Disable; infill-first tends to show through external surfaces.
Reduce slightly if infill imprints on outer walls.
Disable for transparent or light filaments or parts with few walls.

sources.title: Bambu Lab Wiki: Reduce Wasting During Filament Change

entries.title: Input shaping calibration with Orca's ringing tower
entries.summary: Input shaping cancels the printer's resonant vibrations in firmware. If the printer has an accelerometer, use its automatic routine. Otherwise Orca's ringing tower tests frequency and then damping; enter the result in firmware and restore normal speeds afterward. MZV is a good default shaper; EI tolerates more variation.
steps: Use glossy opaque filament with max volumetric speed of at least 10 mm3/s
Frequency test: default 15-110 Hz range, damping 0.1-0.2 (or 0 for firmware default)
Measure X and Y heights with least ringing and read the frequency
Run the damping test at those frequencies
Klipper: SET_INPUT_SHAPER; Marlin: M593 then M500; RRF 3.4+: M593 P<type> F<freq> S<damping>
Restore normal acceleration and jerk; redo after belt, motor or frame changes
facts: Klipper: resonance below about 20-25 Hz suggests stiffening the printer or reducing moving mass first
Klipper sets max_accel to the lower of the acceptable-ringing and over-smoothing limits

entries.title: Smoothing top surfaces with ironing
entries.summary: Ironing makes a second, very low-flow pass over top surfaces to melt ridges flat. It adds print time and runs filament slowly through the hotend, which raises heat-creep and clog risk on some printers. Use Top or Topmost mode for flat visible tops.

settings.advice: Top irons all top surfaces; Topmost only the last; Solid also irons internal solid layers and adds a lot of time.
Low flow (around 10-20%); raise if gaps remain, lower if the surface gets rough.
Keep at or below nozzle diameter.
Keep the pass away from edges to avoid over-extruding there; 0 uses half the nozzle diameter.
Rectilinear or concentric; pick what covers the shape best.
Lower fan can reduce clogging from low flow and smooth the surface; -1 disables.

entries.title: Layer separation and weak layer bonding
entries.summary: Layers that split apart did not fuse well. Common causes are a nozzle that is too cold, too much cooling, a layer height too large for the nozzle and under-extrusion. Raise temperature, cut fan for materials that dislike it, keep layer height at or below about 80% of the nozzle and check flow.
symptoms: Clean breaks between layers, sometimes with a slight upward bend
Parts snap along layer lines with little force
Cracks appearing as the part cools
causes: Nozzle temperature too low for the material or speed
Excess cooling from the part fan or drafts
Layer height above about 80% of nozzle diameter
Under-extrusion
Printing too fast for good fusion
steps: Raise nozzle temperature in 5-10 C steps
Reduce part cooling (off for ABS/ASA)
Keep layer height at or below about 0.32 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle
Calibrate flow; Prusa suggests trying +5% flow steps for stronger bonding
Slow down; a larger nozzle and slower walls increase bond strength

settings.advice: Raise 5-10 C; Simplify3D notes ABS needs about 220-235 C or more to bond.
Reduce for ABS, ASA, PC and nylon; too much fan weakens layers.
Keep at or under about 80% of nozzle diameter.
Correct any under-extrusion.
Slower walls give more fusion time.

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Layer Separation and Splitting
Layer separation and splitting (FDM) - Prusa Knowledge Base

entries.title: Layer shifting: belts, pulleys and other mechanical causes
entries.summary: A layer shift is a sudden sideways offset where the rest of the print continues misaligned. The axis lost steps or a belt slipped. Check belt tension, pulley grub screws, obstructions in the axis path and binding rods or bearings before changing slicer speeds. A staircase pattern usually means a loose or misaligned pulley.
symptoms: Upper part offset in X or Y from the lower part
Repeated small shifts forming a staircase
Clicking from an axis motor just before the shift
causes: Belt too loose (slips) or too tight (binding)
Loose pulley set screw so the pulley turns on the motor shaft
Obstructions: filament caught near a pulley, cables hitting the frame
Dry or scratched rods, worn bearings, overtight rollers
Stepper driver overheating or failing motor
steps: Power off and move each axis by hand; feel for tight or rough spots
Pluck belts: a low bass note with slight resistance is about right; follow the maker's tension spec
Hold the motor shaft and try to move the axis; any slip means a loose belt or pulley
Tighten pulley grub screws with one seated on the shaft flat
Clear debris and reroute cables; clean and lubricate rods
If one motor still skips, swap connectors to isolate motor versus driver
facts: Prusa MK3 belt status target is about 250 on X and 275 on Y, plus or minus 15
Simplify3D notes overheated motor drivers can stop the motors temporarily

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Layer Shifting

entries.title: Layer shifts from excessive speed, acceleration or nozzle collisions
entries.summary: If the mechanics check out, shifts usually come from moving faster than the motors can follow or from the nozzle hitting something on the part, such as a curled overhang, a bump where infill lines cross, or a blob. Lower speed and acceleration, add Z-hop, and fix the curling that the nozzle is catching.
causes: Travel or print acceleration above what the machine can handle (common on older bed slingers)
Nozzle striking upward-curled overhangs or edges
Crossing infill patterns (grid, triangles) building small bumps
Over-extrusion leaving ridges
steps: Reduce print and travel speed by 20-50% as a test
Lower acceleration; Polymaker suggests staying near 1000 mm/s2 on older Cartesian printers unless they have input shaping
Enable Z-hop so travel clears the part
Fix curling with more cooling on overhangs and slowdown for curled perimeters
Switch infill to gyroid or a non-crossing pattern
Check flow; reduce if top surfaces have ridges

settings.advice: Lower if shifts happen on long travels.
Lower overall acceleration on printers without input shaping.
Reduce if motors skip during travels.
A few tenths of a millimetre lifts the nozzle over curled edges during travel.
Use gyroid or another pattern whose lines do not cross within a layer.
Enable to slow where perimeters tend to curl up, such as sharp overhang corners.

facts: Prusa community reports that enabling Avoid crossing perimeters occasionally caused shifts on some printers; this is anecdotal

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Layer Shifting
Bambu Lab Wiki: Model Warping, Falling Off, or Collapsing

entries.title: Random horizontal lines on walls from extrusion or temperature swings
entries.summary: Occasional lines on the side of a print, not tied to lead-screw pitch, often come from extrusion changing: filament diameter variation, nozzle temperature drifting more than about 2 C, or a spool that snags. Check temperature stability and filament quality before mechanics.
causes: Filament diameter tolerance too loose (a 5% variation can widen a line by about 0.05 mm)
Hotend temperature oscillating from poor PID tuning or a fan blowing on the block
Spool snags or tangles causing momentary under-extrusion
Mechanical Z backlash or bed wobble (check after the above)
steps: Watch the temperature graph; more than about 2 C swing calls for PID tuning
Make sure the part fan or a draft is not cooling the heater block (use a silicone sock if available)
Check the spool turns freely and the filament path has low friction
Try a good-quality spool to rule out diameter variation
Then check Z mechanics

settings.advice: Set to the measured average; a big mismatch shows as consistent over or under-extrusion.

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Lines on the Side of Print
Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Inconsistent Extrusion

entries.title: Under-extrusion at high speed: max volumetric speed limit
entries.summary: A hotend can only melt so many cubic millimetres per second. Above that, walls and infill thin out, layers bond poorly, the surface may turn from glossy to matte and the extruder can click or clog. Calibrate the limit per filament and set it in the filament profile; Orca then caps speeds so flow stays below it.
symptoms: Gaps and thin lines only on fast features (infill, long walls)
Glossy surface turning matte at speed
Clicking extruder during fast moves
Clogs after sustained high-speed printing
causes: Requested flow (line width x layer height x speed) above what the hotend can melt
Nozzle temperature too low for the speed
Spool value printed on the box overstated
steps: Run Calibration > Max volumetric speed (defaults 5 to 20 mm3/s, step 0.5)
Measure the height where defects start; value = start + height x step (e.g. 5 + 19 x 0.5 = 14.5 mm3/s)
Enter 10-20% below the measured value in the filament profile
If you need more flow, raise temperature toward the top of the range and retest

settings.advice: Set 10-20% below the calibrated limit. It caps print speed automatically; 0 is not allowed.
Higher temperature raises melt capacity; use the upper part of the range for fast printing.
Infill is usually the highest-flow feature; lower it if infill under-extrudes.
Keep outer walls well below the flow limit for surface quality.

facts: Example: with a 0.4 mm line, 0.2 mm layer and a 12 mm3/s limit, max speed is about 150 mm/s
Bambu notes very high speed modes can push filament through before it fully melts, causing clogs

sources.title: OrcaSlicer Wiki: Max volumetric speed calibration

entries.title: Missing layers or gaps at random heights
entries.summary: A few layers with gaps or holes, while the rest prints fine, means extrusion briefly dropped. Typical causes are a loose drive gear set screw, weak idler grip, a PTFE tube not seated against the nozzle, spool snags, or a short skip from a partial clog.
steps: Check the drive gear set screw grips the motor shaft flat
Make sure the idler holds the filament firmly; filament should not slide easily when tensioned
On PTFE-lined hotends, push the tube fully down to the nozzle
Check the spool and feed path for snags
Raise nozzle temperature slightly if gaps appear at random
Look for extruder clicking during the print

sources.title: Polymaker Wiki: Missing Layers and Holes in Prints
Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Inconsistent Extrusion

entries.title: Colour bleeding and contamination in multi-colour prints
entries.summary: Streaks of the previous colour mean not enough material was purged after a filament change. Dark to light changes need the most flushing. Raise the flushing volume for the affected pairs or the multiplier, and keep flushing into infill or objects only where the mixed colour stays hidden.
causes: Flush volume or multiplier too low for a dark-to-light change
Flushing into infill under light or translucent filament with few walls
Ooze from the inactive filament or nozzle
steps: Open the flushing volumes table and raise the values for the problem colour pairs
Or raise the global flush multiplier (e.g. back to 1.0 if lowered)
Turn off flush into infill for transparent or light parts, or add walls
Use flush into objects only for parts where mixed colours do not matter
Run a small test before cutting purge to save filament

settings.advice: Increase the from/to pairs that show contamination, especially dark to light.
1.0 is the default; values like 0.8-0.9 save filament but may show discoloured layers.
Saves filament but can show through light or clear walls.
Prints the whole object with transition material; use only for sacrificial or non-visual parts.
Safe place to purge since supports are removed.

sources.title: Bambu Lab Wiki: Reduce Wasting During Filament Change

entries.title: Ooze from idle nozzles on multi-tool and IDEX printers
entries.summary: A parked nozzle held at print temperature keeps leaking, leaving blobs and strings on the part, degrading the melt and risking clogs. Enable ooze prevention so inactive tools drop in temperature, set a filament idle temperature, prime on a tower after each change and keep filament dry, since moisture raises nozzle pressure.
causes: Ooze prevention disabled so all tools stay at print temperature
Idle temperature set too high for the filament
Wet filament increasing pressure in the nozzle
No prime tower or too little purge after a tool change
steps: Enable ooze prevention
Set an idle temperature in each filament profile (it overrides the temperature variation)
Use preheat time so the next tool reaches temperature without long waits
Enable the prime tower and set minimal purge (Prusa: 15 mm3 PLA, 35 mm3 others, up to 70 mm3 for TPU)
Dry filament; fit nozzle wipers if the printer supports them

settings.advice: Enable so inactive extruders cool down.
Nozzle temperature for parked tools; only used with ooze prevention on, and overrides the standby delta when non-zero. Too high still oozes.
Temperature change for inactive tools when idle temperature is 0; default -5 C. Use a larger negative value if parked tools still ooze.
Seconds of preheating before a tool change to avoid long waits.
Raise if the first lines after a change are thin or contaminated.
Gives each fresh tool a place to prime before returning to the part.

entries.title: Different materials not bonding in multi-material parts
entries.summary: Some material pairs bond weakly, for example PLA with PETG, which is why they make good support interfaces for each other but poor structural joints. Where two materials must hold together, use Orca's interlocking beams or segmented-region interlocking so the materials mesh mechanically instead of relying on a flat bond.
causes: Chemically incompatible materials sharing a flat boundary
Contamination at the interface from too little purge
Different shrink rates pulling the joint apart
steps: Check whether the pair is known to bond (PLA/PETG do not bond well)
Enable interlocking beams on the boundary between materials
Keep interlocking depth at a few cells; too few gives weak adhesion
Alternatively use segmented-region interlocking depth for painted regions
Make sure purge volumes are adequate at material changes

settings.advice: Enable to generate an interlocking structure where filaments meet; disables segmented-region interlocking.
Distance from the boundary in cells; too few cells gives poor adhesion.
Fewer layers are stronger but more prone to defects.
Width of the interlocking beams.
Keeps interlocking away from the outer surface (in cells).
Alternate painted-region depth every other layer so layers interlock; 0 disables.

facts: Prusa reports PETG with PLA supports, and PLA with PETG supports, working well as easy-release pairs
Prusa notes rigid filament printed on TPE or TPU can shift the soft layers; more minimal purge helps

entries.title: Using a second material or soluble filament for support interfaces
entries.summary: On multi-material printers, printing only the support interface in a non-bonding or soluble material gives clean undersides that peel off easily. With such interfaces the top Z gap can be zero. Keep the support body in the cheaper main material to save time and purge.

settings.advice: Choose PETG for PLA parts (or PLA for PETG), or a soluble filament.
Keep the support body in the model material to reduce changes and purge.
Enable so the interface filament is not used for the support body.
0 for direct contact with soluble or non-bonding interfaces.
Sets how many dense layers sit under the part, and therefore how many layers use the interface material.
Can be smaller (Simplify3D suggests about 0.1 mm) with dissolvable supports.

facts: Prusa advises removing the solid sheath around soluble supports for easier removal

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Poor Surface Above Supports

entries.title: No plastic comes out at the start of a print
entries.summary: If the first lines are missing, the nozzle has either drained by oozing during heat-up, is pressed too close to the bed, or is blocked by ground filament or a clog. Prime with a skirt or purge line, raise Z offset if extrusion only starts a few layers up, and check the extruder if the filament is chewed.
causes: Nozzle drained while heating, so it needs priming before the part
Nozzle starts too close and blocks its own outlet
Filament stripped by the drive gear
Partial or full clog
steps: Use a purge line in start G-code or a skirt with 2+ loops
Set a minimum skirt extrusion length if the printer has no prime line
If extrusion starts around layer 3-4, raise Z offset in small steps (e.g. 0.05 mm)
Look for shavings or a notch in the filament; if present see the grinding entry
If nothing extrudes when pushing by hand at temperature, treat it as a clog

settings.advice: Use 2 or more loops to prime the nozzle before the part.
Set a minimum filament length for the skirt when there is no prime line; default 0 is off.
Raise slightly if the first layers are empty but later layers print normally.

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Not Extruding at Start of Print

entries.title: Nozzle scraping or knocking into the print
entries.summary: A nozzle that clips the part makes a scraping or ticking noise, leaves marks and can shift layers or knock parts off. The usual causes are edges or overhangs curling up, bumps where crossing infill lines overlap, and over-extrusion. Fix the cause, then use Z-hop as insurance.
causes: Overhangs or corners curling upward from poor cooling
Grid or triangle infill crossing itself in one layer, building bumps
Over-extrusion or too-thin layers leaving ridges
Warped parts lifting off the bed
steps: Watch where the contact happens: overhang edges, infill, or top surfaces
Improve overhang cooling and enable slowdown for curled perimeters
Switch infill to gyroid, line or rectilinear and slow infill
Calibrate flow ratio
Enable Z-hop; limit it to top surfaces if stringing increases
Fix any warping that lifts the part

settings.advice: A few tenths of a mm (Simplify3D example: 0.5 mm); larger lifts clear more but can add stringing.
Auto chooses based on overhangs; Spiral lift can reduce stringing; Slope lifts while moving.
Top only limits hops to top surfaces, reducing strings elsewhere.
Avoid grid and triangles if the nozzle catches on infill.
Raise (up to 100% for PLA) so overhang edges do not curl into the nozzle path.
Enable to slow where curling is likely, e.g. sharp overhang corners.

sources.title: Bambu Lab Wiki: Model Warping, Falling Off, or Collapsing

entries.title: Rough or uneven outer wall surface finish
entries.summary: Rough outer walls usually trace back to speed (ringing, VFA or flow limits), wall order, flow or pressure advance, or wet filament. Print the outer wall slower and at steady speed, use Inner/Outer/Inner order when overhangs allow, and calibrate flow and pressure advance.
causes: Outer wall too fast or too high acceleration (ringing, VFA)
Outer wall squashed against inner walls (Inner/Outer order)
Flow or pressure advance not calibrated
Wet filament causing bubbles and fuzz
Infill printed first pushing out the walls
steps: Lower outer wall speed and acceleration
Use Inner/Outer/Inner (needs 3+ walls) or enable Precise wall
Calibrate flow ratio and pressure advance
Dry the filament
Keep outer wall speed constant with Don't slow down outer walls
Disable Print infill first if the outer wall shows bulges

settings.advice: Slow for visible parts; avoid VFA speed bands.
Lower to reduce ringing.
Inner/Outer/Inner gives the best outer finish and accuracy; Inner/Outer is better for overhangs.
Sets zero overlap between outer and inner wall with inner/outer order for cleaner, more accurate walls.
Keeps outer wall speed constant during cooling slowdowns for consistent sheen.
Leave off for visual parts; infill-first can push walls out and show through.

entries.title: Over-extrusion: blobby walls, rough tops and oversized parts
entries.summary: Over-extrusion pushes more plastic than the toolpaths have room for. Top surfaces bulge or look rough, walls get lumpy, parts measure oversize and the nozzle can drag through the excess and scar the surface. Lower the flow ratio after confirming the filament diameter and first-layer height are right.
symptoms: Top layers bulge or show ridges
Walls wavy or blobby, edges not sharp
Parts and holes measure oversize or tight
Nozzle scrapes or leaves marks on top surfaces
causes: Flow ratio too high
Filament diameter set too small in the profile
Nozzle too close on the first layer, oversizing the bottom
Top surface flow too high
steps: Check filament diameter and Z offset
Run the Orca flow ratio calibration and pick the smoothest block
If only top surfaces are rough, reduce top surface flow slightly
Re-measure a test part after changes

settings.advice: Lower in small steps (about 0.01-0.02) or use the calibrated value.
Slightly below 1 can smooth top surfaces; calibrate base flow first.
Verify it matches measured filament.

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Dimensional Accuracy

entries.title: Overhangs and edges curling upward
entries.summary: Overhang edges that lift upward have not cooled fast enough and shrink as they set. This differs from warping off the bed. Give overhangs more fan, slow down where perimeters curl, lower the temperature a little and avoid printing PLA in a hot enclosure. Curled edges can catch the nozzle and cause shifts.
causes: Part fan too weak or off for PLA
Hot enclosure or ambient air for PLA
Nozzle temperature at the top of the range
Fast overhang printing on sharp corners
Very thin layers that are less rigid
steps: Run PLA at full fan after the first layer
Open the enclosure door or lid for PLA
Enable forced cooling for overhangs and Slow down for curled perimeters
Lower temperature 5-10 C
Check overhang speed settings
Consider supports from about 55 degrees for PLA and 45 degrees for ABS/ASA

settings.advice: Enable forced cooling for overhangs and bridges.
Raise toward 100% for PLA; keep moderate for ABS/ASA.
Lower (e.g. 10-25%) so the fan kicks in on milder overhangs; 0% cools all outer walls.
Enable to slow where perimeters tend to curl, like the front of a Benchy hull.
Keep enabled so steeper overhangs print slower.
Lower 5-10 C if overhangs stay soft.

sources.title: Polymaker Wiki: Curling of Layers and Angles
Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Curling or Rough Corners

entries.title: Drooping steep overhangs: Orca overhang and wall-order settings
entries.summary: Overhangs steeper than about 45 degrees at 0.2 mm layers start to droop. Besides cooling, Orca can print inner walls first so the outer wall leans on them, add extra perimeters over steep areas, alternate wall direction on even layers, or reshape the model so overhangs become printable cones. Thinner layers raise the printable angle.

settings.advice: Inner/Outer gives the outer wall something to lean on and is best for overhangs; Inner/Outer/Inner gives a better outer finish but weaker overhangs.
Keep on; other overhang features depend on it and 100% overhangs use bridge settings.
Enable to add wall paths over steep overhangs; requires Detect overhang wall.
Reverses overhanging perimeters on even layers; helps steep overhangs and warping in ABS, ASA, TPU but can texture the outer wall.
Reverse only inner walls for a smoother outer surface.
Reshapes steep overhangs into printable cones; changes the geometry.
45-60 degrees suits most printers; 90 leaves the model unchanged.
Halving layer height (0.2 to 0.1 mm) can raise the printable overhang from about 45 to about 60 degrees.

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Poor Surface Above Supports

entries.title: Partial clog: cold pull cleaning procedure
entries.summary: A cold pull drags residue out of the nozzle on a cooled plug of filament. Use it when some plastic still comes out but flow is weak or uneven; a fully blocked nozzle needs other methods. PLA works best because it keeps the nozzle's shape. Repeat until the pulled tip is clean.
steps: Heat to the current filament's print temperature (or hotter if the previous material was higher-temp) and push PLA through until it flows clean
Stop heating and keep pushing as the nozzle cools so it stays filled (Prusa: until about 170 C)
Let it cool into the soft-solid range: Prusa pulls at about 100 C; Polymaker gives about 90-140 C depending on material
Pull the filament straight out in one firm, steady motion
Inspect the tip: a clean nozzle-shaped imprint means done; dark specks or another colour means repeat
facts: Prusa says not to use cold pulls on its Nozzle X; use cleaning filament instead
Pulling sideways can snap the filament inside the hotend
Polymaker suggests a cold pull when changing from ABS to PLA, cooling to about 130 C before pulling

sources.title: Cold pull (MK4/S, MK3.9/S, XL) - Prusa Knowledge Base

entries.title: PETG stringing and oozing: what is normal and what to change
entries.summary: PETG strings more than PLA even when well tuned, so a few fine wisps that a heat gun removes are normal. Heavy strings usually mean the filament is wet, the nozzle is too hot, or the part is slightly over-extruded. Lower temperature, a bit more retraction, part cooling and avoiding wall crossings help most.
causes: Moisture: PETG is fairly hygroscopic
Nozzle temperature at the hot end of the range
Slight over-extrusion
PETG residue building up on the nozzle during long prints
steps: Dry the spool before judging stringing
Lower nozzle temperature 5-10 C
Increase retraction modestly and test with the retraction tower
Turn on Avoid crossing walls
Use moderate part cooling after the first layers; cooling reduces strings
Clean PETG build-up off the nozzle before printing
Remove leftover fine strings with a heat gun passed over for 1-2 s

settings.advice: Lower in 5 C steps; Prusa's PETG profile uses about 230 C first layer and 240 C after.
PETG usually needs a bit more than PLA; raise gradually, but stay at or under about 2 mm on direct drive.
Enable; Orca recommends it for stringy materials such as PETG and TPU.
Moderate cooling (around half) reduces stringing and keeps detail; turn it down if layer bonding gets weak.
Calibrate; even small over-extrusion makes PETG string more.

facts: Prusa recommends a bed of 85 C first layer, 90 C after for PETG
PETG bridges and overhangs less cleanly than PLA

sources.title: Polymaker Wiki: Hairy or Stringy Prints

entries.title: Pillowing: bumpy, pitted top surfaces over infill
entries.summary: Pillowing is a lumpy top skin with dips or holes between infill lines, most common on wide flat tops. The first top layers sag into the gaps and later layers cannot cover them. More top layers, a bit more infill, an even infill pattern and good cooling on top layers fix it.
causes: Too few top layers for the infill spacing
Low infill density (0-10%)
Weak cooling on top layers (worse with ABS, ASA, TPU)
Very thin layers giving weak bridging lines
steps: Make total top thickness at least 4-6 times layer height (about 1 mm is a common target)
Raise infill to roughly 15-30% for wide flat tops
Switch from grid to gyroid for more even support
Make sure the fan runs on top layers; slow top layers for low-fan materials
Enable an extra bridge layer under top skins

settings.advice: Increase (e.g. 5-6 at 0.2 mm layers).
Set about 0.8-1 mm minimum.
Raise to about 15-30% for big flat tops.
Gyroid spreads support more evenly than grid.
Use at least external bridge only; internal or all adds a second bridge layer that reduces pillowing.
Slow down if cooling is limited.
Make sure the fan runs fully on top layers for PLA; slow top layers instead for low-fan materials.

sources.title: Polymaker Wiki: Pillowed/Pitted Top of Print
5 Ways How To Fix Pillowing in 3D Prints - 3D Printerly

entries.title: Sagging or drooping bridges
entries.summary: Bridge lines sag when they are too hot, too slow to cool, or carry too much plastic. Use strong cooling, slower bridge speed, slightly lower bridge flow and a few degrees less temperature. For long spans, use thick bridges or add a support in the middle, or reorient the part.
steps: Max out the part fan for bridges (PLA)
Slow bridges to about 15-30 mm/s
Lower bridge flow slightly (about 0.9-0.95)
Drop nozzle temperature 5-15 C if bridges stay soft
Enable thick bridges for long external spans
Add a support enforcer under the middle of very long bridges, or rotate the part
Dry the filament if bridges bubble

settings.advice: Reduce for sagging external bridges; below 1 pulls lines tighter but can weaken contact.
Slow down (about 15-30 mm/s).
Fan speed for overhangs and external bridges; 100% for PLA.
Enable so bridges get forced cooling.
Uses nozzle-height lines; stronger for long spans but rougher.
Up to about 125% gives smoother bridges but risks over-extrusion; lower speeds cooling but may sag.
0 = automatic; set an angle to span the shortest distance.

entries.title: Pressure advance: bulging or rounded corners and how to tune it
entries.summary: Pressure advance pushes extra filament while accelerating and pulls back while decelerating so nozzle pressure follows speed. Too low leaves blobs and bulges at corners and seams; too high rounds corners and starves the line after them. Tune it per filament with Orca's line, pattern or tower test and enable it in the filament profile.
symptoms: Too low: bulging corners, blobs at loop ends and seams
Too high: rounded corners, gaps or thin lines just after corners
Very high values with high accel can make the extruder skip
steps: Calibrate temperature and flow first (rotation distance must already be right)
Pick a method: Line (fast, needs a good first layer), Pattern, or Tower (slower, ignores first-layer quality)
Tower: PA = start + step x best height (e.g. 0 + 0.002 x 8 = 0.016)
Choose the value with the sharpest corners and even lines; when unsure pick the lower one
Save to the filament profile and tick Enable pressure advance
On Marlin, Linear Advance must be enabled in firmware (M900)

settings.advice: Enable in the filament profile so the value is written to G-code.
Set to the calibrated value. Klipper sees typical values from 0.05 to 1.0; direct drive sits low in that range, Bowden high.
Optional beta feature for high-speed printers; still set a fixed PA as fallback.

facts: Klipper: if no clear improvement appears up to 1.0, pressure advance is unlikely to help
After PA is tuned, a small retraction (about 0.75 mm in Klipper's example) plus wipe usually handles remaining ooze

sources.title: OrcaSlicer Wiki: Flow ratio and pressure advance

entries.title: Prime (wipe) tower toppling, detaching or getting knocked over
entries.summary: Prime towers fail when they are narrow and tall, have poor bed grip, are built from filaments that do not bond to each other, or get hit by the nozzle or blobs. Give the tower a brim and a wider or ribbed base, keep its speed moderate, and avoid modes that leave it short while the nozzle travels down to it.
causes: Narrow tall tower with a small footprint
Weak bed adhesion at the tower base
Layers of poorly bonding materials (e.g. PLA and PETG) stacked in the tower
Purge blobs or ooze catching the nozzle
High tower print speed
No sparse layers mode leaving the tower low so the toolhead reaches down
steps: Add or widen the prime tower brim
Use the Rib or Cone wall type for a more stable base
Increase tower width if ribs are not used
Keep tower speed at or below the default 90 mm/s
Keep Z hop when moving to tower enabled
Turn off No sparse layers if the tower or part gets hit
Dry filament and tune ooze control to reduce blobs

settings.advice: Increase for better grip; Bambu notes negative values auto-size from tower height.
Rib (four ribs) or Cone give more stability than Rectangle.
Larger angle gives a wider, steadier base (cone type).
Wider is more stable but uses more filament; not adjustable with Rib type.
Keep at or below 90 mm/s unless ooze is well controlled.
Disable if collisions occur; it makes the toolhead descend to a short tower.
Keep enabled to lift over the tower when moving to it.

facts: Bambu Studio splits poorly bonding filaments (e.g. PLA and PETG) into separate tower blocks and slows the first layer after a material switch to improve tower stability

entries.title: Print sticks too well or damages the PEI plate (PETG, TPU)
entries.summary: Over-adhesion comes from an over-squished first layer, a bed that is too hot, or materials such as PETG, CoPE and TPU that bond chemically to PEI. Use glue stick or a release agent as a barrier, raise Z slightly, drop the bed a few degrees and let the plate cool fully before removal.
causes: Nozzle too close, flattening the first layer into a shiny sheet
Bed hotter than needed
PETG on smooth PEI, or TPU on textured PEI, bonding chemically
No release layer
steps: Apply a thin even layer of glue stick before PETG, CoPE or TPU prints
Raise Z offset in 0.02-0.05 mm steps until lines stay distinct
Lower bed temperature 5-10 C after the first layers
Let the bed cool below about 40 C before removing; flex the sheet
For stubborn parts, Polymaker suggests 5-10 minutes in a freezer so the plate contracts away from the print
Use plastic scrapers, not metal

settings.advice: Raise slightly (0.02-0.05 mm, TPU up to about 0.1 mm extra) to stop over-compression.
Drop 5-10 C after the first layer if parts are hard to remove; use the key for your plate type.
For TPU, a slow first layer around 15-20 mm/s with a little extra Z gap avoids suction-like bonding.

facts: Prusa advises against printing PETG directly on smooth PEI; use a textured or satin sheet or glue stick
Prusa says acetone is only for occasional cleaning of smooth PEI and never textured sheets; Polymaker advises no acetone on PEI at all

sources.title: Polymaker Wiki: Print Sticking Too Well to Build Plate
First layer issues - Prusa Knowledge Base

entries.title: When to use a raft and how to set raft layers and gap
entries.summary: A raft is a sacrificial base printed under the part. Use it for warping materials, very small contact areas, or an uneven or worn plate; try a brim first because it is faster. Rafts also hide elephant foot, but the part's underside is rougher and elephant foot compensation is skipped on rafts.

settings.advice: 2-4 layers for most prints, more for an uneven bed or strong warping. 0 disables.
Larger gap releases easier but leaves a rougher underside; smaller gap is smoother but sticks harder.
Widen to spread warping forces; costs material and plate space.
Widens only the first raft layer for grip; defaults give about 3.5 mm reach around the part.

facts: All objects must use the same raft layer count when a prime tower is used
Polymaker uses a raft as the reliable fix for persistent elephant foot

sources.title: Polymaker Wiki: Elephant Foot (Smooshed First Layer)

entries.title: Calibrating retraction length with the Orca retraction tower
entries.summary: OrcaSlicer's retraction test prints a tower whose retraction length changes with height. Pick the shortest length that gives a clean section. Run it after temperature, flow ratio and pressure advance are tuned, because those change how much the nozzle oozes.
steps: Calibrate temperature, max volumetric speed, pressure advance and flow ratio first
Open Calibration > Retraction test
Direct drive: start 0 mm, end 2 mm, step 0.1 mm; Bowden: start 1 mm, end 6 mm, step 0.2 mm
Print, find the lowest section with no strings and measure its height
Use the Calib_Retraction_tower comment in the G-code preview to map height to length
Save the value as the printer retraction length or as a filament override

settings.advice: Set to the shortest length that printed clean on the tower. Low-ooze PLA or ABS may only need 0.2-0.4 mm.
Keep fixed while testing length; change speed separately afterward if strings remain.

facts: If the tower strings even near the top, dry the filament and check the nozzle for leaks rather than retracting further
Orca's calibration guide orders filament tests as temperature, max volumetric speed, pressure advance, flow ratio, retraction

entries.title: What each OrcaSlicer retraction setting does
entries.summary: Retraction pulls filament back before travel to relieve nozzle pressure. Length and speed do most of the work; the travel threshold decides which moves retract at all. Too little retraction strings, too much can pull soft filament into the cold zone and clog. Find values with the retraction tower and override per filament when materials differ.

settings.advice: Main lever against stringing. Direct drive usually 0.2-2 mm, Bowden more. PETG and TPU differ from PLA, so use filament overrides.
Faster cuts ooze; too fast can grind filament or skip steps.
Reload speed after travel; 0 uses the retraction speed.
Travels shorter than this do not retract. Lower it if short hops string.
Forces a retraction at each layer change; keep on.
Extra filament pushed after a retraction; rarely needed. Negative trims blobs, positive fills gaps at restarts.
Skips retraction for travel entirely inside infill, saving time where ooze is hidden.
Separate retraction for tool or filament changes on multi-material printers.

sources.title: Stringing and oozing - Prusa Knowledge Base

entries.title: Rough or droopy surfaces on top of supports
entries.summary: The gap that makes supports removable also leaves the surface above them rough, and sparse interfaces let it droop. Balance with 3-4 interface layers, a tighter interface spacing and a smaller top gap, treat the surface like a bridge with good cooling, or use support ironing. Reorienting or splitting the part avoids the issue altogether.
steps: Reorient or split the model to reduce supported areas
Increase top interface layers to 3-4
Reduce interface spacing (denser interface)
Reduce top Z distance one step (removal gets harder)
Make sure bridge cooling applies to the first layer over supports
Try support ironing for a smoother interface

settings.advice: 3-4 layers give a solid top for the part to sit on.
Smaller spacing gives a smoother underside.
Smaller gives a smoother surface but harder removal.
Irons the top interface and makes it solid for a smoother underside.
Surfaces above supports behave like bridges; strong cooling helps.

sources.title: Bad looking surface above supports - Prusa Knowledge Base
Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Poor Surface Above Supports

entries.title: Scarf joint seam: when it helps and how to set it
entries.summary: The scarf joint ramps flow up at the loop start and down at the end so the two ends overlap smoothly instead of leaving a notch or bump. It works best on smooth curved walls, adds some print time, and does little on sharp corners and overhangs. It is never used on the first layer or in vase mode.

settings.advice: Set to Contour (outer walls) or Contour and hole to enable; None disables it.
Enable to scarf only smooth curves and keep normal seams on sharp corners and overhangs.
Corners sharper than this (default 155 degrees) get a normal seam when conditional scarf is on.
Print the scarf slowly, under about 100 mm/s; default 100% of wall speed. Use extrusion rate smoothing if speeds differ a lot.
Scarf length; default 20 mm. 0 disables the scarf.
Default 10 segments is usually enough.
Keep at 1; lower values risk under-extrusion at the joint.
Usually leave off; wrapping the whole wall adds time for little gain.
Leave off unless inner seams matter; small visual benefit.

entries.title: Making the Z seam less visible in OrcaSlicer
entries.summary: Every closed wall loop has a start and end point that forms a seam. In Orca, seam position decides where it goes, seam gap trims the loop end to avoid a bulge, and wipe options tuck the end inside. Aligned, Aligned Back or Back usually look best; Random spreads seams out but leaves bumps all over.
steps: Calibrate pressure advance and retraction first; seam tuning cannot fix bad PA
Pick seam position Aligned or Back (or paint seams onto a hidden edge)
Set seam gap around 0-15% of nozzle size on a tuned printer
Enable Role based wipe speed and Wipe on loops
For round parts with a visible seam, try the scarf joint seam

settings.advice: Aligned hides seams in concave corners; Back puts them on the rear; Nearest scatters them; Random spreads bumps over the surface but can add strength to pins.
Default 10%. Increase if the seam bulges, decrease if a gap or notch shows.
Enable to offset inner wall seams from the outer one; spreads weak points and helps watertightness.
Enable to move slightly inward at loop end (about 20% of nozzle width); needs 2+ walls.
Enable to de-retract just inside the part so restart over-extrusion is hidden.
Enable so the wipe moves at the speed of the feature just printed.

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Blobs and Zits

entries.title: Small parts and pointed tops melting or deforming
entries.summary: Tiny layers finish so quickly that the next layer lands on still-soft plastic, so tips, spires and small parts sag or blob. Give each layer more time to cool: enable layer-time slowdown, raise the fan, or print several copies so the nozzle moves away between layers.
steps: Enable Slow printing down for better layer cooling
Raise the target layer time (Simplify3D's example slows layers under 15 s; Polymaker uses 3-5 s minimum)
Increase fan speed for materials that allow it
Lower nozzle temperature 5-10 C
Print two or more copies spaced apart

settings.advice: Enable so short layers are stretched to the target layer time.
Raise if tips still deform.
Floor for the slowdown; if reached the layer finishes early. Print extra copies in that case.
Layers faster than this get more fan; raise to cool small layers harder.
Increase for PLA and similar materials.

facts: Very slow nozzles over tiny layers can still overheat them; extra copies avoid this and avoid ooze from pauses

sources.title: Polymaker Wiki: Ugly Tops of Prints or Ugly Thin Prints

entries.title: Print detached mid-print and turned into spaghetti
entries.summary: A mess of loose filament means the part came loose, toppled or was knocked over, and the printer kept extruding in mid-air. Work out which: the whole part slid (adhesion), a corner lifted first (warping), a tall thin part fell (stability or collisions), or the upper part shifted (layer shift).
causes: Weak first-layer adhesion: oily plate, nozzle too high, wrong plate type or bed temperature
Warping lifting the part until the nozzle catches it
Tall thin models knocked over by vibration or the nozzle
Bumps from crossing infill catching the nozzle
Loose belts causing collisions or shifts
steps: Clean the plate, re-level, and check the first layer squish
Confirm the plate type in the slicer matches the physical plate
Add a brim; enable supports for tall or thin models
Reduce speed and acceleration by 20-30% for tall parts
Use non-crossing infill such as gyroid
Check belt tension

settings.advice: Add a brim for small footprints and tall parts.
Lower slightly if the first layer is not squished.
Reduce 20-30% for tall, thin models.
Avoid grid and triangles that cross within a layer.
Supports can brace tall thin features against toppling.

sources.title: Bambu Lab Wiki: Model Warping, Falling Off, or Collapsing
First layer issues - Prusa Knowledge Base
Bambu Lab Wiki: First Layer Printing Optimization Guide (P2S)

entries.title: Extrusion stops or thins out partway through a print
entries.summary: When extrusion fades mid-print while the axes keep moving, check the simple things first: empty or tangled spool, ground filament, a clog or heat creep, then an overheating extruder driver. Dusty filament can also build up into a clog.
causes: Spool ran out or filament tangled and cannot unwind
Filament ground away by the drive gear after a slowdown or clog
Heat creep or a gradual clog from dust or burnt residue
Extruder motor driver hitting its thermal cutoff
Too much friction in a Bowden tube
steps: Check filament still reaches the extruder and the spool spins freely
Look for a ground notch; if present, follow the grinding entry
Unload and inspect the tip for a swollen section (heat creep) or debris
Let electronics cool if the extruder stops while X/Y continue; improve driver cooling
Keep filament clean and dust-free

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Stops Extruding Mid-Print
Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Inconsistent Extrusion

entries.title: Stringing and oozing between parts: causes in order and fixes
entries.summary: Thin hairs or cobwebs between features come from molten plastic leaking out of the nozzle during travel moves. The usual culprits, in order, are wet filament, too little retraction, a nozzle temperature that is too high, and long or slow travel moves over open air. Fix moisture first, because wet filament will keep stringing no matter how retraction is tuned.
symptoms: Fine strands spanning gaps between towers or separate parts
Small blobs where travel moves start or end
Popping or hissing at the nozzle together with heavy stringing (points to moisture)
causes: Damp filament: steam makes the melt foam and leak
Retraction length or speed too low for the extruder type
Nozzle temperature too high, so the melt is runny
Long travel moves across open space or between widely spaced parts
Slow travel speed giving the nozzle time to ooze
Worn or wrong-size nozzle selected in the profile
steps: Dry the spool (see the drying entry) and retest before touching settings
Lower nozzle temperature by 5-10 C and check the result
Raise retraction length in small steps; run the Orca retraction tower to find the shortest clean value
Enable Avoid crossing walls and place multiple parts closer together
Increase travel speed if the machine handles it
Keep Wipe while retracting on
If strings persist, inspect the nozzle for wear and make sure the profile nozzle size matches the installed one

settings.advice: Increase in small steps (0.1-0.2 mm direct drive, 0.2-0.5 mm Bowden). On direct drive keep it around 2 mm or less; very long retractions can cause clogs.
Raise if oozing persists; too fast can grind filament. Roughly 20-100 mm/s is a common working range.
Lower 5-10 C at a time while watching for weak layers or under-extrusion.
Increase so the nozzle spends less time over open air; back off if you get ringing or skipped steps.
Enable to route travel inside the part instead of over gaps; costs a little print time.
Keep enabled so the nozzle wipes along the last path while retracting.
Lower so short travel moves also retract; higher values save time but string more.

facts: Simplify3D cites 0.5-2.0 mm retraction for direct drive and up to about 15 mm for some Bowden setups
Bambu Lab advises keeping retraction length at or under 2 mm on its printers because longer retractions tend to clog
Foaming low-density PLA (e.g. PLA Aero) oozes unless temperature and flow are lowered; Bambu suggests a flow ratio of 0.5-0.7

sources.title: Stringing and oozing - Prusa Knowledge Base
Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Stringing or Oozing
Bambu Lab Wiki: Stringing and Oozing

entries.title: Stuttering, pauses or blobs from heavy G-code (arc fitting, smoothing)
entries.summary: If the printer hesitates on curves, leaving blobs or zits, the controller may be struggling with the G-code stream. Arc fitting adds CPU load and is not a quality improvement, and a very short extrusion-rate-smoothing segment length floods the controller with commands. Disable arc fitting on Klipper and raise the smoothing segment length.
causes: Arc fitting enabled on firmware that handles arcs poorly (Klipper splits arcs into coarse 1 mm lines by default)
Extrusion rate smoothing segment length too short for the printer
Weak 8-bit controller boards
steps: Disable arc fitting, especially on Klipper
Raise the extrusion rate smoothing segment length to 3-5 mm if stutters or Timer too close errors appear

settings.advice: Disable on Klipper; on Marlin only with ARC_SUPPORT enabled. It cannot be combined with extrusion rate smoothing.
Raise from 1 toward 3-5 mm to reduce controller load.

entries.title: Choosing support type and style (normal, tree, organic)
entries.summary: Normal supports project straight down and are stable under large flat overhangs; tree supports branch from a trunk and use less material, leaving fewer marks on curved models. The threshold angle decides which overhangs get support, and Build plate only keeps supports off the model surface.

settings.advice: Normal for big flat overhangs; Tree for organic shapes and fewer scars. Manual uses only enforcers.
Grid is most stable; Snug saves material and reduces scarring; Organic, Tree Slim, Tree Strong and Tree Hybrid suit different loads.
Overhangs below this slope get supported; lower allows steeper unsupported overhangs. About 45 degrees is a common start at 0.2 mm layers.
Enable to avoid supports landing on (and marking) the model.
Skips tiny overhangs that print fine unsupported.
Branch density; raise if tree supports fail or tops sag.

facts: Polymaker suggests supports from about 55 degrees for PLA and 45 degrees for ABS/ASA because of limited cooling

sources.title: Polymaker Wiki: Curling of Layers and Angles
Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Poor Surface Above Supports

entries.title: Supports breaking, toppling or detaching during the print
entries.summary: Supports fail when thin isolated towers or branches lack a base, print too fast, or use a pattern that is easy to remove but weak. Densify the support, add a brim or wider first layer under it, slow support printing, and choose sturdier styles. Reorienting the model can remove the weak supports entirely.
causes: Tall isolated support towers with a small footprint
Sparse support pattern spacing or low tree branch density
Support printed fast so the nozzle knocks it
Poor bed adhesion of support bases
steps: Reorient or split the model to cut support height
Decrease support base pattern spacing, or raise tree branch density
Add a brim under supports (or tree support brim)
Slow the support speed
Choose sturdier styles: Grid for normal supports, Tree Strong or Hybrid for heavy overhangs
Use a sturdier base pattern such as rectilinear grid

settings.advice: Reduce for denser, sturdier supports.
Rectilinear-grid or honeycomb are sturdier than plain rectilinear but harder to remove.
Lower so the nozzle does not knock thin supports.
Add a brim under tree supports, or enable the auto brim width.
Grid is more stable for normal supports; Tree Strong for heavy overhangs; Snug saves material.
Increase to 1-2 walls for stiffer tree branches.
Widens the first support layer for better grip.

entries.title: Supports fused to the part and hard to remove
entries.summary: Supports weld to the part when the gap between support and model is too small for the material, interfaces are too dense, or the support sits too close to vertical walls. Increase top Z distance and XY distance, use fewer or concentric interface layers, add fan on interfaces, or use a different interface material.
causes: Top Z distance zero or too small with the same material
Dense interface and many interface layers
Support XY distance too small next to walls
Hot, slow interface printing with little cooling
steps: Raise top Z distance by one layer height step
Increase support/object XY distance
Use the Concentric interface pattern so it peels off in one piece
Reduce interface layers or widen interface spacing
Raise support interface fan speed
For multi-material printers, use PETG interfaces for PLA (or vice versa) or a soluble interface with zero gap

settings.advice: Increase for easier removal; it rounds to layer height unless independent support layer height is on. 0 only for soluble or different-material interfaces.
Increase so supports do not bond to vertical walls (Simplify3D suggests about 0.2-0.4 mm).
Concentric peels off cleanly without line ends on the surface.
Fewer interface layers release more easily but leave a rougher underside.
Wider spacing loosens the bond; 0 is solid.
Higher fan on interfaces weakens the bond for easier removal.
Pick a non-bonding or soluble filament for interfaces on multi-material printers.

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Poor Surface Above Supports

entries.title: Tall, thin models wobbling, breaking or being knocked over
entries.summary: Slender parts sway as the nozzle moves, so walls get messy near the top and the part can snap or tip over. Reduce speed and acceleration, add a brim and supports or a helper structure, give small layers time to cool, and lay the part down if the design allows.
steps: Reduce print speed and acceleration by 20-30%
Add a brim for a wider base
Enable supports or add a sacrificial stabiliser in the model
Enable layer cooling slowdown so thin tops are not soft
Reorient the model to lie flat when possible
Print several copies so each layer gets cooling time

settings.advice: Lower for tall slender parts.
Lower so the part is not pushed around.
Add a brim to anchor the base.
Keep enabled so short upper layers cool before the next one.

sources.title: Bambu Lab Wiki: Model Warping, Falling Off, or Collapsing
Polymaker Wiki: Ugly Tops of Prints or Ugly Thin Prints

entries.title: Choosing nozzle temperature with a temperature tower
entries.summary: A temperature tower prints the same features at different nozzle temperatures. Lower temperatures string less and bridge better; higher temperatures bond layers better and allow more flow. Choose the middle of the good range, or the upper part if you print fast.
steps: Open Calibration > Temperature and keep Auto-scale for nozzle on (layer height = half the nozzle)
Print and inspect each block for stringing, bridges, overhang sag, surface and layer strength (try snapping the tower)
Pick the middle of the range that looks good; go higher for high-speed or high-flow printing
Save as the filament nozzle temperature

settings.advice: Set to the chosen tower value.
Record the lowest acceptable temperature for the filament.
Record the highest acceptable temperature for the filament.

facts: Orca typical nozzle ranges: PLA 180-220 C, ABS 230-250 C, ASA 240-260 C, TPU 220-245 C, PC 270-310 C

entries.title: Holes printing too small and parts not fitting together
entries.summary: Printed holes usually come out smaller than modelled. Run Orca's tolerance test to see how much clearance your printer needs, then enlarge holes with X-Y hole compensation, and convert round holes to polyholes for more reliable diameters. Check flow and elephant foot first, since both shrink holes.
steps: Calibrate flow and elephant foot compensation
Print the Orca Tolerance Test (holes at 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 mm clearance; fits a 6 mm hex key)
Note the smallest clearance that fits and measure holes with calipers
Set X-Y hole compensation to enlarge holes by the measured shortfall
Enable polyholes for round holes; enable twist to avoid stacked corners

settings.advice: Positive values enlarge holes; tune from the tolerance test.
Converts round holes to polygons that print closer to size; convex holes with 8+ points only.
Larger margin detects more holes as circular.
Rotates polygons layer to layer so corners do not line up.
Prevents the first layers closing holes at the base.

entries.title: Scratches and scars on top surfaces from travel moves
entries.summary: Lines dragged across finished top surfaces come from the nozzle travelling at print height over plastic that is slightly too high, usually because of over-extrusion. Check flow first, then add Z-hop. In Orca, Z-hop happens only with a retraction, so short travels below the retraction threshold will not lift.
steps: Confirm flow ratio is not too high
Enable Z-hop (Simplify3D's example uses 0.5 mm)
Set Z-hop to Top surfaces if you only see marks on tops
Lower the travel distance threshold so short travels also retract and lift
Enable Avoid crossing walls to route travel inside the part

settings.advice: Raise to about 0.2-0.5 mm to clear top surfaces.
Choose Top only to hop over top surfaces without extra stringing elsewhere.
Lower so more travel moves retract (and therefore lift).
Lower slightly if the top surface itself is over-filled.
Enable so travels avoid crossing walls and finished surfaces.

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Scars on Top Surface

entries.title: TPU and flexible filament jamming or tangling in the extruder
entries.summary: Soft filament buckles and wraps around the drive gears when pushed too fast or too hard. Print slowly, keep retraction minimal and slow, loosen the idler a little, keep the filament dry and use a harder TPU on Bowden or long-path printers. Very soft grades (about 85A) may not feed reliably on some extruders.
causes: Print speed or volumetric flow too high for a soft filament
Long or fast retractions
Idler pressure too high, deforming the filament
Long Bowden or feeder path with gaps where it can buckle
Very soft grades or wet filament
steps: Print around 20 mm/s and no more than about 30-40 mm/s (Prusa guidance)
Start with retraction off, then add a little if needed
Loosen the idler so gears push gently
Raise nozzle temperature about 5 C to lower resistance
Use a harder TPU on Bowden machines; expect some stringing in exchange for reliable feeding
Dry TPU before printing

settings.advice: Set low for TPU so all speeds are capped (slow printing is the main fix).
Minimal or 0 for soft TPU; add small amounts only if stringing is unacceptable. Long retractions cause tangling and clogs.
Keep slow; fast retraction makes soft filament buckle in the extruder.
About 230-245 C per Prusa; +5 C reduces back-pressure.
Keep low; the volumetric cap will also limit other features.

entries.title: TPU print settings: supports, infill, travel and bed release
entries.summary: TPU strings easily, bonds strongly to PEI and can fuse to its own supports. Give supports a larger Z gap, use simple infill patterns, avoid crossing walls to cut stringing, and use glue stick or a textured sheet as a release layer. Fewer walls and less infill keep parts flexible.

settings.advice: Prusa suggests about 0.3 mm for flexible materials.
At least 100% of line width for TPU.
Grid or another simple pattern; complex patterns cause defects with flexibles.
Enable; recommended for stringy materials like TPU.
Fewer walls and less infill make parts softer; more add strength.
Slow first layer (about 15-20 mm/s) with slightly higher Z offset avoids over-compression.

facts: Prusa lists TPU nozzle 230-245 C and bed 60-75 C; Orca's table lists 220-245 C nozzle and 40-60 C bed
Very soft flex can bond too strongly to PEI; use glue stick or a textured sheet

sources.title: Problems with infill - Prusa Knowledge Base
Polymaker Wiki: Print Sticking Too Well to Build Plate

entries.title: Under-extrusion: gaps, thin lines and weak parts
entries.summary: Under-extrusion means less plastic leaves the nozzle than the slicer expects, leaving gaps between walls, holes in top surfaces and weak parts. Check the simple causes first: wrong filament diameter or flow ratio, a partial clog, printing faster than the hotend can melt, too low a temperature, and extruder grip or spool drag.
symptoms: Gaps between perimeters, visible at the top of a 20 mm test cube with 3 walls
Holes or rough patches in top surfaces
Thin, wavy lines and fragile parts
Problem worse on fast sections such as infill
causes: Flow ratio too low or wrong filament diameter in the profile
Partial clog or worn nozzle
Requested flow above the hotend's melt capacity
Nozzle temperature too low (hardened or steel nozzles often need 5-10 C more)
Extruder idler too loose or too tight, or dirty drive gears
Spool or tube friction, tangles, wet or out-of-tolerance filament
First layer nozzle so close it blocks flow
steps: Confirm filament diameter (1.75 or 2.85 mm) matches the profile; measure with calipers
Hand-extrude at temperature: a thin, curling or weak strand suggests a partial clog
Slow down or lower max volumetric speed and see if gaps disappear
Raise nozzle temperature 5-10 C within the material range
Clean and check extruder gears and idler tension; make sure the spool turns freely
Calibrate flow ratio with the Orca flow test

settings.advice: Calibrate; typical values sit around 0.95-1.05. Raise only after ruling out clogs and speed limits.
Must match the real filament; a wrong value scales all extrusion.
Lower if under-extrusion appears only at high speed.
Raise 5-10 C if the melt cannot keep up, especially with hardened nozzles.

entries.title: Vertical fine artifacts (VFA) and speed-dependent wall ripples
entries.summary: VFAs are fine, evenly spaced vertical ripples on walls that appear only at certain speeds. A common cause is stepper motor resonance, plus belt, pulley and jerk effects. Print Orca's VFA speed tower, find the bad speed band, and keep outer walls out of it with resonance avoidance or a different outer wall speed.
steps: Calibration > VFA: cover your outer wall speed range (e.g. 20-200 mm/s, step 10)
Inspect which speed blocks look rough or smooth
Enter the bad band as the resonance avoidance range, or pick an outer wall speed outside it
Keep outer wall speed steady: Don't slow down outer walls stops layer-time slowdowns from moving it into the bad band
If ripples remain at all speeds, check belts, pulleys and motors

settings.advice: Enable to skip a resonant speed band for outer walls.
Lower edge of the bad speed band from the VFA tower.
Upper edge of the bad speed band.
Choose a speed outside the rough band.
Enable to keep outer wall speed constant during cooling slowdowns, which helps avoid VFAs.

entries.title: Warping with ABS, ASA, PC and nylon: enclosure, chamber and fan
entries.summary: High-shrink materials warp because of the large gap between bed and room temperature. They need a closed, warm enclosure, little or no part cooling, a hot bed and good adhesion. Without an enclosure, large flat parts in these materials will usually warp; a draft shield helps but switching to PETG or a PLA blend may be the practical fix.
causes: Open-frame printer or open doors letting the part cool unevenly
Part cooling fan running on ABS/ASA
Bed or chamber too cool
Printing too fast, leaving more internal stress
steps: Close the enclosure and let the bed heat-soak 5-10 minutes before starting
Aim for a warm chamber: Bambu suggests 40 C or more, Polymaker about 50 C for ABS/ASA
Turn part cooling off or very low; use a little only for steep overhangs
Raise bed temperature 10-15 C within the material range
Add a wide brim, or a raft for small-footprint parts
Without an enclosure, enable the draft shield
Print slower and at the upper end of the nozzle range to relax stress

settings.advice: On printers with chamber heating, set about 50-70 C for ABS/ASA per Orca's table; never for PLA, PETG or TPU.
Enable only if the printer has a chamber heater and firmware support.
Keep low for ABS/ASA; Prusa mentions 10-20% only to help steep overhangs.
Enable on open-frame printers so a full-height skirt wall shields the part from drafts.
Use a wide brim on large or sharp-cornered parts.
2-4 layers for small contact areas or a worn plate; try a brim first.
ABS/ASA typically 90-110 C; larger parts need the higher end.

facts: Prusa expects ABS parts to shrink about 1-2% after cooling
Simplify3D cites ABS printed at 230 C shrinking almost 1.5% at room temperature

entries.title: Corners lifting and warping off the bed (PLA, PETG and general)
entries.summary: Corners curl up because the outer edges cool and shrink faster than the middle, pulling the part off the plate. Most cases are fixed by a clean plate, correct first-layer squish and a slightly hotter bed, then a brim or mouse ears. Drafts, a cold room and dense grid-type infill make it worse.
symptoms: Corners or edges rise off the plate during the print
A horizontal ripple on the side where the nozzle re-hit a lifted corner
Bottom surface not flat; slight lift mistaken for a flow problem on top layers
causes: Oily or dirty plate (fingerprints are the top cause)
First layer too high, or wrong plate type selected in the slicer
Bed temperature too low for the material and plate
Cold room (below about 20 C) or drafts from windows, AC or fans
Large flat parts with high, grid-style infill that shrink unevenly
Part cooling or auxiliary fan too strong on low layers
steps: Wash the plate with warm water and dish soap (or wipe with 90%+ IPA) and avoid touching it
Re-level and check the first layer is slightly squished
Make sure the slicer bed type matches the physical plate
Raise bed temperature 5-10 C
Add a brim (about 8-10 mm) or brim ears on sharp corners
Turn part cooling off for the first 3 layers
Block drafts; on large flat parts switch to gyroid at 25% or less infill

settings.advice: Raise 5-10 C if corners lift; Bambu suggests about 55-65 C for PLA on textured PEI. Use the key matching your plate type.
Use about 8-10 mm for parts with sharp corners or large footprints.
Mouse ears or Painted put brim only on corners that lift and are easier to remove.
Set to about 3 so the first layers stay warm and grip the plate.
Gyroid shrinks more evenly than grid or triangles on large flat parts.
Lower (25% or less) on big flat parts to reduce shrink stress.
Reduce the auxiliary fan by 20-30% if outer walls of small or overhanging parts warp.

facts: Bambu ranks shrinkage risk, worst first: PC, PA-CF, PA, ABS, ASA, PETG, PLA
Prusa notes too much fan can lift the whole object and weaken layers

sources.title: Bambu Lab Wiki: Model Warping, Falling Off, or Collapsing

entries.title: Weak, stringy or broken-up infill
entries.summary: Infill is often the fastest feature, so it is the first to under-extrude, leaving thin, broken lines. Slow infill or respect the volumetric limit, choose a stronger pattern, and consider wider infill lines. Complex patterns are harder to print, especially in flexible filament.
steps: Check infill flow in the preview flow view against your max volumetric speed
Lower infill speed (Simplify3D tests at half speed)
Use stronger 3D patterns such as gyroid or cubic for mechanical parts; grid for flexible filaments
Use a wider infill line width and adjust density to compensate

settings.advice: Reduce if infill lines are thin or broken.
Gyroid or cubic for strength; grid for TPU and other flexibles.
Wider lines are stronger per pass; space them further apart.
Make sure it is calibrated so infill speed is capped automatically.

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Weak Infill
Problems with infill - Prusa Knowledge Base

entries.title: Signs of wet filament and what moisture does to prints
entries.summary: Moisture in filament turns to steam in the nozzle, so extrusion foams and sputters. Expect popping or hissing, heavy stringing, rough or bubbly surfaces, pits, weak brittle layers and inconsistent lines. Nylon, PVA, TPU and PETG absorb water fastest; PLA is least sensitive but still affected over time.
symptoms: Popping, crackling or hissing at the nozzle
Much more stringing and oozing than usual
Rough, fuzzy or bubbly surfaces, pitted walls
Weak, brittle layers and inconsistent extrusion
Cloudy look on translucent PETG
steps: Dry the spool at the material's drying temperature (see drying entry)
Store dried filament sealed with desiccant; aim for under about 20% RH
Print hygroscopic filaments straight from a dry box
Dry any spool that has been open a long time before important prints
facts: Bambu: at about 55% RH, freshly dried filament can pick up enough moisture to affect prints within 2-12 hours
Bambu: in a 20% RH environment filaments generally stay dry for 2-7 days

entries.title: Wipe while retracting and related wipe settings
entries.summary: Wiping moves the nozzle back along the path it just printed while retracting, so leaked plastic is smeared onto the part instead of forming a blob or string at the next start. Orca lets you split retraction into a quick part before the wipe and the rest during it.

settings.advice: Enable to reduce blobs at travel starts; Prusa and Klipper both recommend wipe when available.
How far the nozzle wipes; retraction not covered by the wipe is done before or after it.
Percent of retraction done quickly before wiping (example 20%); higher suits Bowden setups.
Used when role-based wipe speed is off; absolute or percent of travel speed.
Enable to wipe at the speed of the feature just printed.
Keep on to avoid ooze at layer changes.

sources.title: Stringing and oozing - Prusa Knowledge Base

entries.title: Worn nozzle and abrasive filaments (CF, GF, glow, wood)
entries.summary: Fibre-filled and other abrasive filaments wear brass nozzles quickly. A worn, widened nozzle oozes and strings more and loses detail, and filler particles clog small nozzles. Use a hardened nozzle, 0.6 mm or larger for fibre-filled or wood filaments, and replace a nozzle that is visibly worn. Make sure the slicer profile matches the installed nozzle size.
causes: Brass nozzle used with CF, GF or other abrasive filaments
Small nozzle (0.2-0.4 mm) with particle-filled filament
Profile set for a different nozzle diameter than installed
steps: Inspect the nozzle tip; compare with a new one for widening or rounding
Swap to a hardened steel or similar nozzle for abrasive materials
Use 0.6 or 0.8 mm for fibre-filled filaments; avoid 0.2 mm
Set the nozzle diameter in the printer profile to match
Hardened nozzles may need 5-10 C more nozzle temperature

settings.advice: Must match the installed nozzle or the slicer will over- or under-extrude.
Raise 5-10 C with hardened or steel nozzles, which conduct heat less well than brass.

facts: Prusa: wood-filled filaments may need at least a 0.6 mm nozzle and about 0.2 mm layers; carbon or Kevlar-filled filaments need a hardened nozzle

sources.title: Bambu Lab Wiki: Stringing and Oozing

entries.title: Z-hop types and trade-offs in OrcaSlicer
entries.summary: Z-hop lifts the nozzle during retracted travel so it does not drag over the part. It protects tall or curling prints but can add stringing because the nozzle pulls a thread upward. Use the smallest height that prevents collisions, restrict it to surfaces that need it, and consider spiral or slope lift.

settings.advice: Use the smallest lift that avoids collisions; Prusa notes a lower lift reduces stringing.
Normal lifts straight up; Slope and Spiral lift while moving (spiral can reduce stringing); Auto picks by overhangs.
Angle for slope and spiral lift; 90 degrees equals normal lift.
All, Top only, Bottom only, or Top and bottom surfaces.
Only hop above this Z height.
Only hop below this Z height.

facts: Klipper's pressure advance guide suggests disabling z-lift on retract when tuning for ooze
Polymaker found Z-hop caused squashed layer bulges on some older single-leadscrew printers

sources.title: Stringing and oozing - Prusa Knowledge Base

entries.title: Z-wobble and Z-banding: regular ridges on walls
entries.summary: Evenly repeating ridges or a wavy wall usually point to mechanics: a bent or misaligned lead screw, a loose coupler, play in the carriage, hotend or bed, or a bed heater cycling widely. Rule these out by hand before blaming slicer settings. Layer heights that land on whole motor steps can help on some printers, though this is debated.
causes: Bent or misaligned lead screw, or one binding in its nut
Loose coupler, motor mount, carriage, rollers or bearings
Hotend or nozzle loose when hot
Bed temperature swinging (bang-bang control) and moving the bed slightly
Inconsistent extrusion from a partial clog
steps: If bands are evenly spaced at a distance matching the lead screw pitch or lead, suspect the screw
Roll the screw on a flat table to check it is straight; replace rather than bend
Check the screw drops straight into the coupler; a flexible coupler helps
Tighten carriage, hotend (when hot) and bed mounts; adjust eccentric rollers
Clean and lightly grease the lead screw
PID-tune bed and hotend

settings.advice: On 8 mm lead screws with 1.8 degree motors, one full step is 0.04 mm; 0.08, 0.12, 0.16 or 0.20 mm layers stay on full steps.
On older single-leadscrew printers, disabling Z-hop has removed periodic layer bulges.

sources.title: Z-Banding and Z-Wobble in Your 3D Prints - Clever Creations

entries.title: Zits and blobs on outer walls at start and end points
entries.summary: Small bumps on the outer surface form where a loop starts or stops, because pressure in the nozzle is not matched to the motion. A blob at the start of a loop points to too much re-priming after retraction; a blob or gap at the end points to leftover pressure. Tuning pressure advance, wipe and seam placement fixes most cases.
symptoms: Raised dots or a vertical line of bumps on outer walls
Blobs where travel moves rejoin the wall
Bumps scattered everywhere when seam position is Random
causes: Pressure advance not tuned, so pressure lags at starts and stops
Too much filament pushed back after retraction
Unneeded retractions inside the part
Long pauses (e.g. minimum layer time waits or per-layer power-loss saves) letting the nozzle ooze
steps: Calibrate pressure advance first
If the blob is at the loop start, try a small negative Extra length on restart
Enable wipe while retracting and Wipe on loops
Set seam position to Aligned or Back instead of Random
Enable Reduce infill retraction so travels inside infill do not retract and re-prime
Disable per-layer power-loss recovery on printers where it pauses every layer

settings.advice: Tune with the Orca PA test; too low leaves blobs at corners and loop ends.
Default 0. A small negative value (about -0.1 to -0.2 mm) trims priming blobs at loop starts; positive adds material.
Enable so retraction happens while the nozzle moves along the path.
Enable to tuck the loop end slightly inward; needs more than one wall.
Use Aligned, Aligned Back or Back to gather the start points in one hidden line.
Enable to skip retractions for travels entirely inside infill, where ooze is hidden.

sources.title: Simplify3D Print Quality Guide: Blobs and Zits

entries.title: First aid for 3D printing burns, fume inhalation and irritant filaments
entries.summary: Hot nozzles, hot ends, beds, build plates and molten filament can burn skin. For a burn, move away from the heat, cool it under running water, take off nearby jewelry or clothing, cover with a clean dry dressing and get medical help if needed. For breathing irritation from fumes, get to fresh air and seek medical care. Check the SDS before handling soluble filaments that may irritate skin.
steps: Burn: move away from the heat source.
Rinse the burned area right away under cool running water.
Remove clothing or jewelry near the burn.
Cover it with a clean, dry bandage; use pain relief or seek medical help if needed.
Fume irritation: move the person into fresh air and arrange medical attention promptly.
Prevention: ventilate or use air purification, wear a mask if needed, and read the SDS of soluble or unfamiliar filaments.

entries.title: 3D printing safety basics: hot surfaces, fumes and material data sheets
entries.summary: Never touch the nozzle, glass build plate or heated bed while the printer is printing, heating or just finished. Some filaments release odors or fumes when melted, so print in a ventilated room or with an air purifier, and read each material's safety data sheet, taking extra care with third-party filaments.
facts: Nozzle, build plate and bed stay hot for several minutes after printing; use heat-insulated gloves if you must handle them.
ABS fumes and particles irritate the respiratory system; ventilate or use air purification.

entries.title: ABS recommended print settings and bed limits on Snapmaker 2.0
entries.summary: Snapmaker's reference for ABS: nozzle 245-265 C, bed 90-100 C, part-cooling fan off, 30-50 mm/s. Use the PEI-coated side, or glass with glue. ABS releases fumes and particles that irritate the airways, so print with good ventilation or an air purifier. On Snapmaker 2.0 the bed tops out at 80 C on A350/A350T/F350 and 100 C on A250/A250T.

settings.advice: Target 90-100 C, but no more than 80 C on A350-size Snapmaker 2.0 beds.
Set to 0 or very low; Snapmaker prints ABS with the part fan off.
About 160 C for the parked nozzle.

facts: Nozzle 245-265 C; bed 90-100 C; speed 30-50 mm/s.
Retraction 0-2 mm at 20-50 mm/s; part-cooling fan off.
Standby temperature 160 C; drying 80 C for 8 h.
Plate: PEI-coated side; the glass side works if glue is applied.
Max bed temperature: A350/A350T/F350 80 C; A250/A250T 100 C.

entries.title: Artisan uneven support platform: adding shims or silicone bed shims
entries.summary: On the Artisan, if the printing platform does not sit flush on the support platform below it, or rocks clearly when you press the two together at a left or right corner, the support platform is uneven. One or two 0.5-0.8 mm shims at the marked spot, or the two silicone bed shims from the replacement kit, fill the gap, stiffen the bed and make leveling more reliable.
