Helpful tips for J1/J1s new users to avoid common pitfalls

entries.title: J1 first layer not sticking or print moving during printing
entries.summary: If the J1 first layer will not stick or the part shifts mid-print, causes include inaccurate or incomplete calibration, too fast a first layer, degraded filament or a small footprint. Recalibrate, check plate clamps for cracks, slow the first layer below 20 mm/s, add a brim or raft, fine-tune Z offset live on the screen, try another filament, or print on the glass side with a thin layer of glue stick.
symptoms: First layer does not adhere to the plate.
Part moves during printing.
causes: Calibration inaccurate or not completed.
Print speed too high for the first layer.
Filament has degraded.
Too little contact area between the model and the plate.
steps: Repeat the calibration steps from the touchscreen Calibration page.
Inspect every plate clamp and its base on the heated bed for cracks.
Set the initial layer speed below 20 mm/s and re-slice.
Add a brim or raft for parts with a small footprint.
Once printing starts, adjust Z offset from the print screen to move the nozzle closer or further.
Try a different, fresh filament.
Flip the plate to the smooth glass side and apply a thin coat of solid glue before the bed heats.
Clean grease and dust off the plate (water, or alcohol) and make sure the clamps hold it firmly.

settings.advice: Lower to under 20 mm/s.
Enable an outer brim for parts with a small contact area.
Widen if edges still lift.
Add a raft when a brim is not enough.
Use the filament's recommended bed temperature, e.g. PLA 50-65 °C, PETG 70-80 °C.

entries.title: J1 first layer uneven: one side or corner too close or too far
entries.summary: Inconsistent J1 first layers (too far on one side and squashed on the other, or a high back-right corner where the nozzle drags) can come from residue on the nozzle or bed PCB spoiling calibration, cracked plate clamps or bases, play in the Z guide rail bearings, an uneven glass plate or bed PCB, or a wrong bed temperature. Work through each, then fine-tune corners with the knobs under the bed.
symptoms: Nozzle too far on one side and too close (under-extruded) on the other.
Back-right corner high, nozzle drags there while front and left print fine.
causes: Filament residue on the nozzle or bed PCB corrupting calibration.
Cracked or damaged plate clamps or clamp bases.
Play in the Z-axis guide rail bearings.
Uneven glass plate or bed PCB.
Wrong bed temperature.
steps: Clean residue off the nozzle and heated bed PCB before calibrating, without scratching the bed.
Inspect every plate clamp and base for cracks; a loose bed produces bad calibration data.
Raise Z to the top and gently rock the bed bracket up and down; looseness or clicking means play in a Z guide rail bearing.

Z play fix: loosen the guide rail screw with a socket wrench, shift the rail forward or back along Y until the wobble improves, then loosen the four linear bearing flange screws to let it settle and retighten them.
Rotate the glass plate 180°, recalibrate and reprint; if the bad corner moves with the plate, check the plate with a long straight edge on a flat surface.
Check the bed PCB with a straight edge, also after heating it to 70 °C and waiting 15 minutes.
Print the four-corner test, measure each corner and turn the knobs (10 notches, 0.05 mm each) until all read 0.2 mm.

sources.title: First layer has poor adhesion or appears uneven at the corners.

entries.title: Checking the J1 glass plate clamps
entries.summary: If the J1 plate clamps drift out of position, the glass plate is not held firmly, which hurts print quality and calibration. Every three months, with plate and bed cool, open and close the clamps on both sides and try to push the plate around; if it moves, adjust the clamps by hand and repeat until it stays put. Also look for cracked clamps or clamp bases.
steps: Let the glass plate and heated bed cool to room temperature.
Unlatch and relatch the clamps on each side, then try to slide the plate by hand.
If it shifts, reposition the clamps by hand and test again until it no longer moves.
Replace or report cracked clamps or bases; a loose bed corrupts calibration data.

sources.title: First layer has poor adhesion or appears uneven at the corners.

entries.title: Setting the glass plate thickness on the J1 touchscreen
entries.summary: The J1 combines the stored plate thickness with bed-levelling data to work out the Z working height. Change it only after replacing or modifying the glass plate, or when switching to a third-party plate. Measure the plate, enter the value under Settings > Machine Settings > Glass Thickness (4.7-5.5 mm allowed), tap Done, then redo heated bed levelling.
steps: Measure the thickness of the plate you will print on.
Tap Settings > Machine Settings > Glass Thickness.
Enter the value (only 4.7-5.5 mm is accepted) and tap Done.
Run Heated Bed Leveling again so the new value takes effect.
facts: Values outside 4.7-5.5 mm are refused because they could damage the machine or cause print faults.

sources.title: Modifying the glass plate thickness value on the Touchscreen
Choosing the proper build plate side

entries.title: J1 heated bed levelling with the leveling wheel
entries.summary: Heated bed levelling makes the PEI glass plate even under the nozzle so first layers stick uniformly. Start it from Calibration > Heated Bed Leveling > Start; the touchscreen has you turn the leveling wheel under the heated bed while the left extruder measures Z at two points. Clean nozzle and bed first: during calibration the nozzle should spring back quickly after touching a calibration point.
steps: Clean residue off both nozzles and the heated bed; calibrating without filament loaded is recommended.
Tap Calibration > Heated Bed Leveling > Start.
As the screen directs, rotate the leveling wheel under the bed until the left extruder's Z offset at the two points is aligned.
Continue with Z offset and XY offset calibration (the wizard order).
Print a first-layer test; if corners still differ, fine-tune with the hand-twist knobs under the bed.
Redo levelling after changing the glass thickness value, the plate or a hot end.
facts: The calibration card in the box is used for bed levelling and Z offset calibration in manual mode.

sources.title: How to resolve J1(s) heated bed calibration failures

entries.title: Installing the official high-speed hot end fan on a J1/J1s print head
entries.summary: The official high-speed hot end fan (3.74 CFM, 12300 RPM versus the stock 3.31 CFM, 9600 RPM) gives faster cooling for overhangs, bridges and quick prints. It comes with two ducts marked L and R for the left and right heads. You need a PH1 Phillips screwdriver and the supplied tweezers; work with the printer switched off and unplugged.
steps: Switch off and unplug, remove the top panel and move the head to an accessible spot.
Remove the four screws on the head's outer casing and ease it apart carefully; the fan lead is short and still attached to the board.
If there is glue around the fan connector, pick it off with tweezers without touching the board.
Press the connector latch to unplug the fan, remove the four fan screws and take out the old fan and duct.
Fit the new fan with its outlet pointing down and the matching L or R duct beneath it, then screw both to the casing.
Plug the fan firmly into the board, close the casing and refit the top panel. Repeat on the other head.

sources.title: Installing the high-speed hot end fan
Snapmaker J1/J1s Upgrades and Mods Community Resources

entries.title: J1 Homing Stall Detection: protecting objects under the heated bed
entries.summary: Homing Stall Detection (Settings > Machine Settings > Homing Stall Detection) halts the heated bed if something blocks its Z homing path at print start/end or during calibration. When it trips, the job or calibration is cancelled and the printer freezes; clear the obstruction and restart. It does not watch the heads' X/Y homing path. Snapmaker recommends leaving it on, but it can be switched off if it trips falsely.
steps: If the printer freezes during homing, power it off (immediately if the bed or heads are still pushing against something).
Remove any object under the bed or in the heads' path.
Power on again and restart the job or calibration.
facts: Only obstacles in the bed's Z homing path are detected; with something in the heads' X/Y path the heads keep trying to home, which can damage the object or printer before it freezes.
With detection off, the bed keeps homing into an obstacle; switch the printer off at once and remove the object.
If you disable it because of false triggers, keep the space under the bed completely clear.

entries.title: Clearing a clogged J1 hot end (filament stuck at the PTFE junction)
entries.summary: Filament can jam inside the J1 hot end, which has a 15 mm PTFE liner: long retractions pull molten filament up to the junction of the metal throat and PTFE, where it swells and sticks. Poor filament with impurities and fast-printed special filaments (e.g. silk PLA) also cause it. Rule out the sensor, drive gear and extruder clog first, then push the plug through at high temperature.
causes: Retraction too long, softening filament at the metal-throat/PTFE junction.
Low-quality filament containing impurities.
Special filaments such as silk PLA printed too fast or too cold.
steps: Motors off, move the head off the wiper, open the idler latch and cut the filament at the extruder with diagonal pliers.
Pull the remaining filament out from the top of the print head.
Heat the nozzle to about 250 °C (roughly 30 °C above the loaded filament's print temperature).
Push the pink H2.0 or grey H1.5 hex key down through the filament entry on top of the head to force the plug out of the nozzle; do not push so far that the hot end is damaged.
If the plug comes out, load some PLA to purge the path. If not, treat it as a nozzle clog.

settings.advice: Keep at 2 mm or less so soft filament is not drawn into the PTFE section.

sources.title: The hot end or nozzle is clogged (J1)

entries.title: When and how to swap J1/J1s hot ends (0.2-0.8 mm, hardened steel, all-metal)
entries.summary: Swap the hot end when you need another nozzle size or a harder nozzle, when the stock 0.4 mm brass nozzle is worn or has a blockage you cannot clear, or when it clogs repeatedly. Hot ends are told apart by nozzle shape and colour. Unload filament first and wait until the nozzle reads below 40 °C (about 15 minutes); nozzles reach up to 300 °C.
steps: Unload the filament (aided or manual).
Return to the home screen and do not start until the displayed nozzle reading is under 40 °C; wear insulated gloves.
Follow the left or right hot end guide for the type you are fitting.
0.2/0.4/0.6/0.8 mm or 0.4 mm hardened steel hot ends: redo heated bed levelling and XY and Z offset calibration before printing.
0.4 mm hardened steel all-metal hot ends: update the touchscreen firmware, run hot end PID auto-tune, then redo bed levelling and XY/Z offset calibration.
In the slicer, set nozzle diameter and type to match each head.

settings.advice: Match the hot end on each extruder (0.2, 0.4, 0.6 or 0.8 mm) and pick the matching Snapmaker J1 printer variant.
Set to hardened steel when the hardened steel hot end is fitted.

sources.title: Installing Hot Ends (0.2mm/0.4mm/0.6mm/0.8mm) or Hot Ends (0.4mm, Hardened Steel)
Installing Hot Ends (0.4mm, Hardened Steel, All-metal)

entries.title: Replacing the J1 hot end silicone sock
entries.summary: The silicone sock around the J1 heater block keeps hot end temperature stable and stops leaking plastic from fouling the block; a missing sock can contribute to extruder temperature errors. Replace it when torn or dirty beyond cleaning: power off, unplug, wait until the hot end is at room temperature, pull off the old sock and fit a new one with its logo facing you.
steps: Power off and unplug.
Wait until the hot end is fully cool to avoid burns.
Pull off the old sock.
Fit the new sock (spares are in the tool box) with the hot-surface logo facing you.

sources.title: Enhanced edition - Troubleshooting abnormal extruder temperature control (J1/J1s)

entries.title: J1 'Hotend detection abnormal' alert (hotend may not be installed correctly)
entries.summary: This J1 alert means the printer cannot detect the hot end correctly, even after reinstalling it as the manual describes. Likely causes: hot end not fully seated, a faulty hot end or hot end adapter board, a bent or damaged FFC cable, poor FFC contact at the adapter board, or a faulty print head adapter board, FFC adapter board or mainboard.
steps: Reinstall the hot end several times, pushing it firmly all the way up and making sure its cable lies in the groove.
Try a spare hot end; if the alert disappears, the original hot end is faulty.
Inspect the FFC ribbon cable for bends or damage and check it is seated straight and tight.
Confirm both FFC ends are secure at the adapter board; press lightly on the FFC adapter board and see whether the alert clears.
Gently exchange the two FFC cables at the adapter board: a fault that follows the print head means the head or hot end; one that stays on the same channel means the adapter board or mainboard.
Send your findings to Snapmaker support.

entries.title: J1 IDEX print modes: Normal, Copy (Duplication), Mirror and Backup
entries.summary: J1/J1s has four print modes. Normal prints whatever the slicer assigns to each head (multi-material, multi-colour or several models split between heads). Copy (called Duplication in Luban) prints two identical parts at once; Mirror prints a part plus its left-right reversed twin on a slightly smaller usable area. Backup keeps the second head on standby to take over if the active one runs out or clogs. As both heads share Y and Z, they cannot build two different shapes simultaneously.
steps: Luban: open 3D Printing with J1 chosen as the machine, pick a mode in the pop-up and close it; switch later via Mode in the main toolbar.
Third-party slicers (e.g. Snapmaker Orca): on the touchscreen tap the G-code file, then tap the lower-left corner of the file info screen to choose a mode. Default Mode is preselected.
If a mode was chosen both in Luban and on the touchscreen for the same file, Luban's choice wins.
Tap the question-mark icon next to the selector for a short description of each mode.
facts: Copy and Mirror run both extruders at the same time with identical parameters, which roughly doubles output for batch parts.
Mirror suits paired parts such as a left and a right shoe.
Backup: one wiki page says the standby head takes over when the working head runs out of filament; the Luban guide also mentions clogs.
Because the heads cannot move apart in Y or Z, a head that has finished its layer and waits next to the part can leave marks on the surface.
Luban does not draw the second (right-side) model on the plate in Duplication or Mirror mode.

sources.title: Selecting the print mode of J1

entries.title: J1 layer shifting: speed, acceleration, belts and loose heads
entries.summary: Layers sliding out of place on the J1 come from printing too fast, acceleration set too high, loose belts, a print head with play on the X rail, or a loose hot end. Compare slicer speeds with Snapmaker's recommendations, keep acceleration at or below 10000 mm/s², restore firmware defaults with M502/M500 if needed, tension the belts, then shake the head and hot end to find play.
symptoms: Layers offset sideways from the layers below.
causes: Print speed too high.
Acceleration too high.
Loose belt.
Print head loose on the X rail.
Hot end loose in the print head.
steps: Compare outer wall, inner wall and infill speeds with Snapmaker's recommended values and slow them down.
Reset acceleration to factory defaults: connect Luban over USB and send M502, then M500, in the Console.
Tension the X and Y belts with the printed gauges.
Shake the print head gently; if it moves, tighten the screws holding it to the X rail and the fixing plate screws. If play remains, film it and contact support (possible X rail fault).
Shake the hot end; if loose, loosen its two retaining screws, reseat the hot end and tighten them firmly.
Do not loosen the thumb screws on the back during other work; slack belts cause shifts.

settings.advice: Keep at or below 10000 mm/s², Snapmaker's recommended maximum; lower it further if shifts continue.
Reduce together with print acceleration if shifts happen on travel moves.
Lower toward the recommended J1 speeds if layers shift.
Lower toward the recommended J1 speeds if layers shift.
Fast infill is a common trigger; reduce it first.

sources.title: Adjusting the tension of the belts

entries.title: Unusual noise from J1 X or Y linear rails
entries.summary: Noisy X or Y motion on the J1 usually comes from dry rails or sliders fitted on the wrong mounting holes, but a motor or other part can also be the source. Turn the motors off and move the rail by hand: if it is still noisy, lubricate and then check slider installation; if it is quiet by hand, the noise comes from the motor or another component and support should be contacted.
causes: Not enough lubrication on the linear rails.
Sliders not aligned with the correct installation holes.
Noise actually coming from the motor or another part.
steps: Power off or disable the motors on the screen and move the noisy rail by hand.
Still noisy by hand: lubricate the X/Y rails with white lithium grease.
If greasing does not help, check that the sliders are installed correctly and are not catching on the rails.
Quiet by hand: the motor or another part is the source; send photos or video to Snapmaker support.

entries.title: Lubricating J1 X/Y linear rails and the Z lead screw
entries.summary: Grease the J1's X and Y linear rails and Z lead screw every three months, when the old grease has turned black-brown, after about 100 km of slider travel, or when sliders bind or rails get noisy; X and Y need it most. Use NLGI 2 white lithium grease (TENGKE GREASE PS2 for the rails, NIKI FG 107M for the Z screw, or Permatex 80345 for both), and test that new and old grease are compatible first.
steps: Compatibility test: mix old and new grease 1:1 and let it stand; use it only if it stays smooth without lumps or particles.
Turn the motors off (Control > Motor), power off and unplug.
Wipe all old grease from the X and Y rails.
Brush new grease into the upper and lower grooves and the front face of the X rail, then slide the heads to spread it.
Grease the grooves of both Y rails and move the X rail back and forth.
Wipe the Z lead screw, apply new grease, power on and jog the bed up and down (Control > Move) to spread it.
facts: TENGKE GREASE PS2 (synthetic + mineral oil, lithium soap) works from -50 to 110 °C; NIKI FG 107M (PAO base, for a metal screw in a plastic nut) from -40 to 130 °C.

entries.title: J1/J1s maintenance schedule and intervals
entries.summary: Snapmaker's intervals for J1/J1s: clean the nozzle at every calibration and before each print; clean the glass plate, heated bed, extruder gears and base panel at least monthly; and every three months update firmware, check belt tension, grease the axes, and check the nozzle wiper and glass plate clamps. Replace the hot end sock when it is torn or badly soiled.
facts: Every print and calibration: wire-brush the nozzle at 200 °C.
Monthly or as needed: glass plate residue, glue and grease; heated bed surface; extruder drive and idler gears; base panel.

Every 3 months: firmware update; belt tension (also after long transport, belt noise, layer shifts or poor adhesion); lubrication (also when grease darkens or after about 100 km of travel); nozzle wiper position; plate clamps.
As needed: hot end sock replacement.

entries.title: Loading filament manually on the J1 (idler latch open)
entries.summary: In manual loading you push filament through the opened J1 extruder yourself until it flows from the nozzle. It doubles as a diagnostic: if hand-pushed filament extrudes but Load does not, suspect the drive gears or the filament sensor rather than a blocked hot end.
steps: Tap Control > Motor to switch the motors off, then slide the head off the nozzle wiper by hand.
Heat the extruder via Control > Extruder (default 200 °C).
Remove the top panel, hang the spool, cut the tip at 45° and thread it through the guide tube.
Press the idler latch on the front of the print head to open it.
At temperature, push the filament into the extruder by hand until it flows out of the nozzle.
Close the latch, seat the guide tube in the extruder and clip, refit the top panel and brush the nozzle clean.

sources.title: Extruder drive gears are not aligned/Extruder driving gear set screw is loose (J1)

entries.title: Finding the maximum volumetric speed of the J1/J1s
entries.summary: Snapmaker gives no fixed maximum volumetric speed for the J1s. It depends on nozzle size, material, how fast the hot end can melt filament, the condition of the extrusion mechanism, and ambient temperature and humidity. Snapmaker suggests measuring it with OrcaSlicer's Max Volumetric Speed test and using the result as the filament's flow limit.
steps: Run Orca's Max Volumetric Speed test for each filament and nozzle combination you use.
Inspect the printed test and find where extrusion starts to fail; note the matching flow value.
Enter a value slightly below that as the filament's max volumetric speed.

settings.advice: Set from the test result, a little below the failure point, so the slicer slows features that would exceed the J1 hot end's melt rate.

sources.title: What's the maximum volumetric speed of the J1S?

entries.title: J1/J1s new-user checklist: FFC connectors, lubrication, stickers and firmware
entries.summary: Snapmaker's tips for new J1/J1s owners: lift the roughly 28 kg printer with two people, confirm the linear bearings are greased before running, check that the two small FFC connectors at the top centre of the back are locked, update firmware, finish every touchscreen calibration and verify auto-levelling with a test print. Also check that the PEI glass plate is flat.
steps: FFC check with power off: the black line on each cable should run parallel and close to the line printed on the PCB, and the connector bar should sit against the white housing; a gap of about 1 mm means it is not locked.
Peel the yellow stickers slowly. Remove residue with silicone remover and an eraser, or rubbing alcohol on a soft cloth; never acetone, which can cloud the front doors.
Thread filament this way: pull the PTFE tube off the top of the toolhead, feed filament through the tube from the back, insert it into the toolhead, then refit the tube.
Check for firmware updates at Settings > Firmware Update.
Redo calibration after nozzle or hot end swaps and firmware updates; auto-levelling can be off, so confirm with a test model.
On the PEI side, let the plate cool to room temperature before removing the print.

sources.title: Helpful tips for J1/J1s new users to avoid common pitfalls

entries.title: Clearing a clogged J1 nozzle (debris, carbon build-up, wear)
entries.summary: J1 nozzle clogs come from dust or debris carried in on the filament, plastic carbonised after long periods at temperature, or a worn nozzle whose outlet has narrowed. Heat slightly above print temperature and push the blockage back up with a needle thinner than the nozzle (under 0.4 mm for the stock nozzle), then test by loading PLA. Replace the hot end if it keeps clogging.
causes: Foreign matter such as dust on the filament blocking the nozzle.
Filament held hot too long, carbonising and raising flow resistance.
Nozzle wear reducing the outlet diameter.
steps: Heat the nozzle a little above printing temperature, e.g. about 220 °C for PLA.
Insert a nozzle-cleaning needle or wire thinner than the bore (stock nozzle 0.4 mm) from the tip and push the plug backwards; wear heat-resistant gloves, since hot plastic can spurt.
Load PLA (Control > Extruder > Heat > Load) and check that it flows smoothly and steadily.
If the strand is still thinner than normal, repeat the cleaning.
If clogs persist, replace the hot end (or the nozzle on threaded hot ends) or contact support.

sources.title: The hot end or nozzle is clogged (J1)
How to determine if the nozzle is clogging and replace it
Installing Hot Ends (0.2mm/0.4mm/0.6mm/0.8mm) or Hot Ends (0.4mm, Hardened Steel)

entries.title: Replacing a worn or carbon-clogged J1 nozzle (thin extrusion, gaps between layers)
entries.summary: A J1 nozzle partly blocked by carbonised plastic or metal debris gives a very thin strand, gaps between layers although loading looks normal, and extruder clicking even with correct settings and no jam. On threaded hot ends the nozzle can be replaced on its own: hold the heater block with one wrench and turn the nozzle with another.
symptoms: Extruded strand is much thinner than normal.
Filament comes out when loading, but layers show gaps or under-extrusion during printing.
Extruder clicks during printing although slicer settings are right and nothing is jammed.
causes: Leftover filament carbonised by long heating builds deposits that narrow the nozzle bore.
Metal debris inside the nozzle raises extrusion resistance or partly blocks the opening.
steps: Unload the filament, power off and remove the hot end.
Pull off the silicone sock.
Tools: two adjustable wrenches; or an adjustable wrench plus a 6.5 mm (or 7 mm) open wrench; or a vice plus either wrench.
Hold the heater block with one tool and unscrew the nozzle counter-clockwise with the other.
Screw in the new nozzle clockwise and tighten to about 4 N·m.
Refit the sock and hot end, then redo bed levelling and XY/Z offset calibration as after any hot end change.
facts: Interference-fit hot ends cannot have the nozzle replaced separately; replace the whole hot end instead.

sources.title: How to determine if the nozzle is clogging and replace it
Snapmaker J1/J1s Upgrades and Mods Community Resources

entries.title: Checking the J1 nozzle wiper position
entries.summary: A homed J1 head parks on the nozzle wiper, which stops the idle nozzle oozing onto the print. The wiper can drift with use or knocks, so check it every three months: home both heads via Control > Move > Home and confirm each nozzle tip sits fully in the wiping pad, pressed about 1-2 mm into it. If not, pull the wiper back into position by hand.
steps: Tap Control > Move, then the Home button.
When both heads are parked, check that each nozzle tip is fully inside the wiping pad and pressed in about 1-2 mm.
If not, move the nozzle wiper by hand back to its standard position.

entries.title: J1 performance modes (Silent, Default, Fast): speed and acceleration limits
entries.summary: While printing, Adjust > Performance on the touchscreen switches between Silent, Default and Fast. The modes differ in TMC silent driver mode, top print speed and top acceleration, and the firmware holds slicer speeds to the active mode's ceiling. Every new job starts in Default; after power-loss recovery a job resumes in the mode it had before.
steps: During a print, tap Adjust.
Scroll the left menu and tap Performance.
Pick Silent, Default or Fast.

settings.advice: Keep at or below 10000 mm/s² (the Fast cap); anything above the active mode's limit is not reached.
Speeds above 490 mm/s (Fast) or 280 mm/s (Default) are not reached; slicing for the mode you will use gives realistic time estimates.

facts: Silent: TMC silent mode on; max 130 mm/s for combined XY moves, 105 mm/s single-axis; max acceleration 3000 mm/s²; lowest noise.
Default: TMC silent mode on; max 280 mm/s combined, 200 mm/s single-axis; max acceleration 8000 mm/s².
Fast: TMC silent mode off; max 490 mm/s combined, 350 mm/s single-axis; max acceleration 10000 mm/s²; loudest.
Most print noise comes from fast, high-acceleration travel and infill moves.
The selected mode applies only to the current job and is not remembered for the next one.

sources.title: Adjusting the work speed of J1 on the Touchscreen

entries.title: PLA clogs on the J1 when the top panel and doors are closed
entries.summary: With the top panel fitted and doors shut, heat trapped in the J1 enclosure can soften PLA until it deforms in the extruder drive gears or the nozzle, often during the first layer while the bed is heating the chamber. For PLA, remove the top panel and leave the front doors open, or print on the glue-coated glass side with the bed unheated. Community top-panel risers are another way to vent the chamber.
symptoms: Extrusion stops partway through a PLA print or on the first layer.
"Failed to Load Filament" pause.
Soft, bent PLA found around the drive gears when the idler latch is opened.
causes: Closed enclosure gets too warm for PLA.
Heated bed warming the closed chamber during long prints.
steps: For PLA and other low-temperature filaments, take off the top panel and open the front doors.
If a clog has already formed, clear it with the J1 extruder-clog or hot end-clog procedure.
Optionally print PLA on the glass side with glue and the bed heater off.
Keep the panel and doors closed only for materials that like a warm chamber, such as ABS, ASA and nylon.

settings.advice: Keep PLA within 50-65 °C; on the glued glass side the bed can stay unheated to limit chamber heat.
Avoid running PLA hotter than needed (50-65 °C range) in a closed J1.

sources.title: Helpful tips for J1/J1s new users to avoid common pitfalls
Snapmaker J1/J1s Upgrades and Mods Community Resources

entries.title: Fitting the J1 Print Cooling Fan accessory (back panel and PCB swap)
entries.summary: Installing the Print Cooling Fan accessory means unloading filament, letting the nozzles cool below 40 °C (about 15 minutes), unplugging the printer, removing the back panel, swapping the original rear PCB for the new one and mounting the fan. A video guide is also available. Leave the thumb screws on the back alone: loosening them slackens the belts and can cause layer shifts.
steps: Heat and unload the extruders, stop heating, wait until the nozzles fall below 40 °C, then power off and unplug.
Remove the filament holders, top panel, guide-tube holder (H2.0) and back-panel screws, then lift off the back panel.
Loosen the two screws near the ribbon connectors, nudge the clips with the flat end of the hex key without removing them, and unplug the ribbon cables and other leads.
Unscrew the original PCB (H2.5) and keep its shims if it may be reused; mount the new PCB with three M4×8 screws.

Plug cables in the right orientation. For each ribbon cable, flip the clip up by hand, push the cable straight in to the stop and press the clip down until it clicks; never lever the clip with a tool.
Pass the fan lead through the hole, lock the fan with M3×10 screws, clip the cable, refit the back panel (pre-tighten the corner screws first), the holders and the top panel.

entries.title: Sending prints to the J1 from Snapmaker Luban over the network
entries.summary: With the J1 and the computer on the same network, slice in Snapmaker software, then choose Export > Load G-code to Workspace and Start Job > Start on Luban in the Preview window. Watch the first layer closely and stop if it does not stick. A Wi-Fi dropout during printing does not interrupt the job. Luban accepts STL, OBJ and 3MF models, and J1 support needs Luban 4.5.0 or newer.
steps: Connect the printer and the computer to the same network.
Slice the model and click Export > Load G-code to Workspace.
In Preview, click Start Job > Start on Luban.
Watch the first layer; if it fails to adhere, stop and follow the first-layer troubleshooting.

entries.title: Replacing a J1/J1s print head FFC ribbon cable
entries.summary: Replace the print head FFC cable when it is visibly damaged or deeply creased, or when an extruder temperature-control fault has been traced to it. With the printer off, loosen the FFC clamp bolts (H2.0), unplug the cable from the FFC adapter board (pull it on PCBA V1.1, rotate it on V1.2), unscrew the print head's four rear bolts while supporting it, then swap the cable following Snapmaker's video.
steps: Switch the printer off.
Slightly loosen the bolts clamping the FFC cable with an H2.0 driver; they do not need to come out.
Read the PCBA version on the adapter board: on V1.1 pull the FFC cable straight out, on V1.2 rotate it out.
Hold the print head and remove the four H2.0 bolts on its back to take it off the X rail.
Replace the FFC cable in the head as shown in the wiki video and reassemble.

sources.title: Replacing the FFC cable of the print head

entries.title: Replacing the J1/J1s mainboard
entries.summary: Raise the heated bed to the top (from the touchscreen, or by turning the lead screw clockwise with power off), power off and unplug, remove the 14 bottom cover screws (H2.0), disconnect every mainboard cable, remove the 10 mainboard screws (H2.5) and fit the new board. Replacement boards usually ship without the blue thermal pad, so move it over from the old board. Never plug or unplug anything with power on.
steps: Raise the bed fully via the touchscreen controls, or turn the lead screw clockwise by hand with power off.
Power off and unplug.
Remove the 14 bottom cover screws (H2.0) and take the cover off.
Disconnect all cables from the mainboard, noting their positions.
Remove the 10 mainboard screws (H2.5) and swap the board, transferring the blue thermal pad.
Reconnect cables in the correct orientation and refit the cover.

entries.title: Replacing the J1/J1s touchscreen
entries.summary: To replace the J1 touchscreen, raise the bed, power off and unplug, remove the bottom cover (14 H2.0 screws) and carefully unplug the touchscreen FFC cable from the mainboard. Loosen the four H2.0 screws at the front bottom that hold the screen bracket, take out the screen assembly and remove its four H1.5 screws, open the casing (four Phillips screws) and disconnect the antenna and screen FFC before fitting the new screen.
steps: Raise the bed to the top, then power off and unplug.
Remove the bottom cover (14 H2.0 screws) and gently unplug the delicate touchscreen FFC cable from the mainboard.
Loosen the four H2.0 screws at the front bottom holding the screen bracket and take out the screen assembly.
Remove the four H1.5 screws securing the screen and the four Phillips screws on the casing.
Open the casing slowly, disconnect the antenna and screen FFC cable, and fit the new touchscreen.

entries.title: Replacing the J1 X linear rail (torques and alignment)
entries.summary: To replace the J1 X rail, take off the top cover and withdraw the filament tubes, take both print heads off (four H2.0 bolts each, support the head), remove the head mounts and unscrew the old rail. Wipe the bracket, degrease the new rail with gloves on, apply white lithium grease and slide it 2-3 times. Position it with the printed J1 Linear Rail Installer, then torque the rail bolts left to right to about 1 N·m, the head mounts to about 1 N·m and the print heads to about 0.6 N·m.
steps: Take off the top cover and withdraw the filament tubes from the feed ports.
Holding each print head, remove the four H2.0 bolts on its back and take it off; then remove the head mount screws.
Unscrew the X rail and lift it out; wipe the bracket clean.
Wearing gloves, wipe the factory grease off the new rail, apply white lithium grease and slide the carriage 2-3 times.
Fit the rail with screws snug but not tight, set its height with the printed J1 Linear Rail Installer, then tighten left to right to about 1 N·m.
Refit the head mounts (about 1 N·m) and print heads (about 0.6 N·m), then reinsert the filament tubes.

sources.title: J1 X linear rail replacement guide

entries.title: Replacing the J1/J1s Y motor (4240 or 4248)
entries.summary: J1 Y motors come as 4240 (42×40 mm) or the slightly larger 4248 (42×48 mm); both install the same way. Raise the bed, power off, remove the bottom cover (14 H2.0 screws), unplug the Y motor, loosen the knurled M4 belt-tension nut at the back, slip the belt off the idler pulley, remove the bearing block and motor screws (H2.5), loosen the rigid coupling and slide it aside, then lift out the motor with its bearing bracket and move the timing pulley and bearing block to the new motor.
steps: Raise the heated bed to the top, then power off and unplug.
Remove the 14 bottom cover screws (H2.0) and disconnect the Y motor cable from the mainboard.
Loosen the knurled M4 nut at the back (belt tensioner) and take the timing belt off the Y idler pulley.
Remove the screws of the bearing blocks at both ends and the Y motor screws (H2.5).
Loosen the two rigid coupling screws (H2.5), slide the coupling right, route the motor cable up the column and lift the motor assembly out.
Loosen the two timing pulley screws (H2.0), move the pulley and bearing block to the new motor and install it.

entries.title: J1/J1s safety: hot surfaces, pinch points, fumes and labels
entries.summary: Never touch the nozzle, PEI glass plate or heated bed while the printer is printing or heating, and switch off and unplug it before maintenance. Use it in a ventilated area because some molten plastics release harmful substances, and read each material's Safety Data Sheet. Machine labels warn about hot surfaces, the fragile PEI glass plate, pinch points on moving parts and not piling items where motion could hit them.
facts: Wait until prints have cooled completely before touching them.
Keep hands clear of moving axes to avoid pinching.
A label warns against printing directly on the heated bed surface, which can damage it; always print on the plate.
ABS gives off fumes and particles that irritate the lungs; print it with ventilation or an air purifier.
Use insulated gloves for hot nozzle work, and wait until the nozzle reads below 40 °C (about 15 minutes) before swapping hot ends.

sources.title: Installing Hot Ends (0.2mm/0.4mm/0.6mm/0.8mm) or Hot Ends (0.4mm, Hardened Steel)

entries.title: J1/J1s first power-on setup and calibration wizard
entries.summary: On first boot the touchscreen runs initial setup. The J1 asks for language, acceptance of the terms and user experience program, a printer name and a Wi-Fi network; the J1s instead guides you through fitting the remaining screws. Both then run the wizard: heated bed levelling, Z offset, XY offset, offset check and vibration compensation. Re-run it any time from Settings > Machine Settings > Wizard.
steps: Step 1: level the heated bed by turning the leveling wheel as prompted.
Step 2: set the right head's Z offset with its thumb wheel.
Step 3: let the printer measure the XY offset between the heads automatically.
Step 4: print the offset check model and inspect it.
Step 5: print the vibration compensation test and pick the best region.
Repeat the calibrations after swapping nozzles or hot ends and after firmware updates.

sources.title: Helpful tips for J1/J1s new users to avoid common pitfalls

entries.title: Printing Silk PLA on the J1 without clogging
entries.summary: Silk PLA and most silk filaments need slower speeds and a hotter nozzle than standard PLA; running them at the J1's high speeds is a known clog cause. With any official hot end, Snapmaker suggests at most 100 mm/s and a nozzle of 220 °C or higher, which also gives a better silky sheen. The all-metal hot ends were designed partly to reduce clogging with silk and high-speed PLA.

settings.advice: Set 220 °C or higher for silk PLA.
Keep at or below 100 mm/s.
Keep at or below 100 mm/s.
Keep at or below 100 mm/s; fast infill is where silk filaments usually jam.

sources.title: Snapmaker J1/J1s Upgrades and Mods Community Resources
Inappropriate print settings cause a clog

entries.title: Snapmaker J1/J1s specifications and hardware overview
entries.summary: Snapmaker J1 and J1s are enclosed desktop IDEX printers: two print heads travel independently on one X rail and share the Y and Z axes, enabling dual-material, dual-colour, copy, mirror and backup printing. The wiki's spec table is only an image, so these facts are gathered from the manual and troubleshooting pages. The wiki documents J1 and J1s with the same procedures; the only stated difference is first setup (J1s has you fit remaining screws, J1 asks for language, name and Wi-Fi).
facts: IDEX layout: left and right extruders move independently along a shared X-axis linear rail; Y and Z motion is common to both heads.
Nozzle temperature up to 300 °C. Stock hot end: 0.4 mm brass nozzle; optional 0.2/0.4/0.6/0.8 mm, 0.4 mm hardened steel and 0.4 mm hardened steel all-metal hot ends.
Standard (non all-metal) hot ends contain a 15 mm PTFE liner, so long retractions can jam them; the all-metal versions aim to cut clog risk with silk and high-speed PLA.
Build surface: double-sided glass plate (PEI-coated face and bare glass face) locked by plate clamps on the heated bed; the glass thickness setting accepts 4.7-5.5 mm.
Bed levelling and XY/Z offset calibration work by electrical contact: the nozzle touches gold-plated pads on the heated bed.
Homing order is Z, then X, then Y. X and Y use optical limit switches with light-blocking plates; Z uses a spring-type limit switch.
Performance modes cap acceleration at 3000 (Silent), 8000 (Default) and 10000 mm/s² (Fast); Fast allows up to 490 mm/s for combined XY moves.
The filament sensor checks that filament is advancing, so it reports clogs, runout and tangles and pauses the print.

Hot end sensor is a PT100 (about 110 Ω); heater cartridge about 14 Ω. Print heads connect through FFC ribbon cables to an FFC adapter board; extruder motors use mainboard ports E0 (left) and E1 (right).
Stock hot end fan: 24 V, 3.31 CFM, 9600 RPM, 40.3 dB. Official high-speed fan: 3.74 CFM, 12300 RPM, 44.2 dB.
The machine weighs almost 28 kg (lift with two people). The Wi-Fi antenna sits inside the touchscreen. The Y motor is a 4240 or the newer 4248 stepper.
Recommended room: 10-35 °C and 10-90% relative humidity without condensation. Flexible filament must be TPU 90A or harder.

entries.title: J1 stringing: oozing during travel moves
entries.summary: Stringing is plastic oozing from the nozzle during travel and leaving fine strands on the part. On the J1 the causes are print parameters (usually temperature), damp filament, and retraction that is off or set wrong. Lower the nozzle temperature (never below the maker's minimum), travel faster, dry the filament, and enable retraction but keep it at 2 mm or less to avoid hot end jams.
causes: Print parameters, especially nozzle temperature, set too high.
Moist filament.
Retraction disabled or badly set.
steps: Reduce nozzle temperature in small steps, staying above the maker's minimum.
Increase travel speed.
Dry the filament and store it dry.
Turn on retraction, limited to 2 mm.

settings.advice: Lower gradually, not below the filament's minimum.
Raise so the nozzle spends less time over gaps.
Enable, but no more than 2 mm on the J1 to avoid clogs.
20-50 mm/s for PLA, PETG and ABS per the J1 filament library.

facts: J1 drying guide: PLA 55 °C/6 h, PETG 65 °C/6 h, ABS and ASA 80 °C/8 h, HIPS 60 °C/3 h, PVA 80 °C/12 h, TPU 65-70 °C/8 h, nylon and CF/GF nylon 100 °C/8 h.

entries.title: J1 wizard stuck on 'Moving' at the 'Fix Print Cooling Fan' step (homing failure)
entries.summary: If J1 setup hangs on 'Moving' during 'Fix Print Cooling Fan', the printer could not finish homing (order Z, X, Y). Causes: packaging blocks or zip ties left on the X/Y axes setting off stall protection, X/Y optical switches never triggering or always triggered, or the spring-type Z switch stuck, bent or damaged.
symptoms: Wizard sits on the 'Moving' page and never advances.
X or Y keeps driving noisily into the switch end (switch not triggering).
X or Y backs off slightly, then stops silently (switch stuck triggered).
Bed keeps lowering with noise (Z switch not triggering).
causes: Shipping blocks or zip ties obstructing the X or Y axis.
X/Y light-blocking plates not reaching the optical switches, or X rail out of square.
Loose limit switch cable, bad solder joint or loose switch mount.
Z spring switch held pressed, or its spring bent or damaged.
steps: Remove all packaging blocks and zip ties from the X and Y axes, then rerun the wizard.
Check that the light-blocking plates sit in the optical switches after homing and that the X rail is square (see the Y-homing stall fix).
Power off, unplug and reconnect the limit switch cable; wiggle the switch mount to find loose soldering or a loose mount.
Z: with power off, turn the Z lead screw by hand to raise the bed about 10 mm, restart and rerun the wizard.
Inspect the Z switch's metal spring for bending; press it by hand and listen for a clear click (no click means a faulty switch).
Contact support with photos or video if unresolved.

entries.title: J1 accessories and tool box: what each tool and hex key is for
entries.summary: The J1 ships with doors, side panels, the PEI glass plate, two spools of filament, a calibration card (for bed levelling and Z offset in manual mode), a wiping cloth and a tool box. Hex key colours matter because guides refer to them: green is H2.5, pink is H2.0 and grey is H1.5.
facts: Tool box: USB flash drive, tweezers (remove ooze), power cable, palette knife (lift prints off the PEI plate), wire brush (clean nozzles), diagonal pliers (cut filament, remove supports), 2 filament holders and a USB-B cable for a computer.
Also included: 16 M3×6 and 4 M4×8 screws, 2 spare hot end socks, a 5.5 mm wrench for belt tension and 4 hex keys.
Green H2.5 key with M4×8 screws fits the enclosure doors; pink H2.0 key with M3×6 screws fits the side panels.
Grey H1.5 key fits the extruder drive gear set screw; the pink H2.0 or grey H1.5 key can also be pushed down through a hot end to clear a jam.
Place the printer level on a solid table with more than 30 cm free around it for filament changes.
Only connect the power cable while the power switch is off.

entries.title: J1 'Unsafe Heating - Extruder L/R' and persistent extruder temperature errors
entries.summary: When the error 'Temperature control of the left/right extruder is abnormal' or 'Unsafe Heating - Extruder L/R' persists on a J1, check in order: the silicone sock, hot end-to-PCB contact, loose PT100 or heater screws, a damaged PT100 or heater, a bent FFC cable, hot end-to-adapter-board contact, then swap FFC cables to separate print head faults from adapter board or mainboard faults.
causes: No silicone sock on the heater block.
Bad contact between the extruder and its PCB.
Loose mounting screws on the PT100 or heating tube.
Damaged or faulty PT100 or heating tube.
Bent or damaged FFC cable.
Hot end not seated firmly against its adapter board.
Faulty FFC adapter board or mainboard.
steps: Make sure the silicone sock is on the heater block; without it the temperature fluctuates.
Reseat the hot end to cure bad contact with the PCB.
Check that the mounting screws of the PT100 (white cable) and heater cartridge (black cable) are tight.
If the reading is normal when idle and errors only appear while heating, remove the PT100 and look for crushing or other damage.
Measure resistance: PT100 across pins 5-6 should be about 110 Ω; heater across pins 7-8 about 14 Ω.
Inspect the FFC ribbon cable for bends and confirm it is seated straight and tight in the PCB connector.
Check that the hot end's fixing plate is not visibly skewed and that the hot end is pushed up as far as it goes.

Carefully exchange the two FFC cables at the adapter board: a fault that follows the print head points to the head or hot end; one that stays on the same channel points to the adapter board or mainboard.

Contact fixes: on the left head, sand or file about 1 mm off the two plastic parts shown on the wiki; on either head, fit a 0.4 mm shim (or Snapmaker's printable spacer STL) at the blower fan location so it presses the hot end adapter board.

entries.title: J1 vibration compensation (input shaping) calibration
entries.summary: Vibration compensation calibration tunes the frequency used by the J1's vibration suppression to improve surface quality and reduce ringing. Tap Calibration > Vibration Compensation Calibration > Start; the printer prints a test model, then you choose the best-looking area on it to save the setting. It is the last step of the setup wizard.
steps: Tap Calibration > Vibration Compensation Calibration > Start.
Let the calibration model print.
Examine it and select the area with the cleanest surface on the touchscreen.

entries.title: J1 warping: corners lifting from the plate
entries.summary: Warping happens when upper layers cool and shrink while the heated bottom stays expanded, so edges peel up and may detach. On the J1 the causes are poor first-layer adhesion, wrong print parameters and a cold room. Fix adhesion first, use the maker's bed temperature, add a brim or raft where the material needs it, keep the part fan off where required, and close the doors and fit the top panel for materials that need a warm chamber.
causes: First layer not sticking to the plate.
Unsuitable print parameters (bed temperature, adhesion aids, fan).
Ambient temperature too low.
steps: Solve first-layer adhesion first (clean plate, calibration, clamps).
Set the bed temperature from the filament maker's data.
Use a brim or raft for models or materials that need extra adhesion.
Turn the part fan off for materials that require it.
Close the doors and fit the top panel for filaments that need a warm chamber, and keep the room within 10-35 °C.

settings.advice: Use the maker's bed temperature, e.g. ABS 90-100 °C, ASA 75-95 °C on the J1.
Add a brim for warp-prone materials and sharp corners.
Use a raft when a brim is not enough.
Off for ABS, ASA, HIPS, PETG and nylon per the J1 filament library.

entries.title: J1 cannot connect to Wi-Fi (or only to the first network)
entries.summary: If the J1 cannot join any Wi-Fi network, or only the first one it ever used, the router may use specifications the J1 does not support, be out of range, or the antenna built into the touchscreen may be damaged. Check router compatibility (the supported list is an image on the wiki), move the router close to the screen, and test a phone hotspot after a reboot. A Wi-Fi dropout during a print does not stop the job.
causes: Router specifications not supported by the J1.
Router too far away.
Damaged antenna inside the touchscreen.
steps: Confirm your router's Wi-Fi specifications match those the J1 supports.
Place the router near the touchscreen, where the antenna is.
Reboot the printer and try connecting to a phone hotspot.
If it still fails, export logs (Settings > About > System Logs to a USB drive; files FW and SC) and open a support ticket.

sources.title: Troubleshooting guide for J1 Wi-Fi connectivity problems

entries.title: Changing J1 print speed during a job with Work Speed
entries.summary: Adjust > Work Speed scales every print-related speed by a percentage while a job runs: at 50%, 100 mm/s infill becomes 50 mm/s and 120 mm/s travel becomes 60 mm/s. The result is still capped by the performance mode, so in Silent a 100 mm/s infill raised to 200% only reaches 130 mm/s.
steps: Tap Adjust while printing.
Tap Work Speed in the left menu.
Drag on the round dial to set the percentage.

sources.title: Adjusting the work speed of J1 on the Touchscreen

entries.title: J1 XY offset calibration (aligning left and right nozzles)
entries.summary: XY offset calibration measures where the right nozzle sits relative to the left in X and Y, so the two materials in a dual-colour or dual-material print line up instead of being staggered. Run Calibration > XY Offset Calibration > Start; both heads touch the heated bed in turn automatically and the offsets are saved.
symptoms: Second colour or material is shifted against the first.
Visible step or gap where regions printed by the two heads meet.
steps: Clean both nozzles so contact detection is accurate.
Tap Calibration > XY Offset Calibration > Start and let it run.
Check the result with the calibration check print.
Repeat after reseating or replacing a hot end, since that changes head alignment.

sources.title: The temperature control of the extruder is abnormal

entries.title: J1 stalling noise when homing Y: X rail out of square
entries.summary: A stalling noise while the J1 homes Y (moving toward the front) usually means a knock in transit left the X rail out of square with the Y rails, so a limit bar blocks travel before the Y photoelectric sensor triggers. Square the gantry by loosening the Y motor coupling, pushing the X rail against the front frame and retightening.
symptoms: Stalling or grinding sound when the Y axes home toward the front.
causes: X rail not perpendicular to the Y rails after an impact during shipping, so the Y photoelectric sensor is never reached.
steps: Power off. Refit the Y-axis limit bars if they were removed.
Loosen the two screws on the Y motor coupling with an H2.5 key.
Centre the print heads on the X rail, then push the X rail forward until it rests against the upper front frame.
Hold the X rail still and turn the coupling until its screws are reachable; the shaft end should not be visible in the middle of the coupling (fully engaged).
With the heads pressed against the frame, retighten the coupling screws (H2.5).
Power on and home again.

sources.title: Failing to trigger the photoelectric sensor on the Y axis

entries.title: J1 Z offset calibration (right extruder height via the thumb wheel)
entries.summary: Z offset calibration sets the right extruder to the same working height as the left, preventing weak first layers on one head, nozzle scraping and head collisions. Run Calibration > Z Offset Calibration > Start and turn the right extruder's thumb wheel as the screen instructs. For small first-layer corrections during a print, the print screen also has a live Z-offset adjustment.
steps: Clean both nozzles and complete heated bed levelling first.
Tap Calibration > Z Offset Calibration > Start.
Turn the thumb wheel on the right extruder as prompted until its height matches.
Confirm with the calibration check print.
During a print, use the Z-offset control on the print screen to nudge the nozzle closer to or further from the plate.

entries.title: Abrasive filaments and hardened steel nozzles
entries.summary: Filaments with hard fillers wear out brass and stainless nozzles quickly, widening the orifice and ruining print quality. Use a hardened steel nozzle for carbon or glass fiber filaments and for particle-filled ones such as glow-in-the-dark, marble or sparkle. Hardened steel conducts heat less well, so it may need a slightly higher temperature or lower max flow. Standard PLA, silk, matte, PETG, ABS, ASA, PC and TPU do not need it.

settings.advice: Set hardened steel when installed, so abrasive filament warnings are accurate.
Nozzle hardness used for compatibility checks.
May need lowering on hardened steel nozzles.

facts: Bambu: avoid 0.2 mm nozzles with filled filaments; 0.6 mm hardened is the first choice for low clog risk
Ellis: hardened steel may reach lower flow rates unless you raise temperature
Abrasive filaments also wear feeder tubes and extruder gears

entries.title: ABS: enclosure, warping, cooling and fumes
entries.summary: ABS is tough and heat resistant but shrinks and warps strongly, so it needs an enclosure (or at least a draft shield), a hot bed and minimal drafts. Typical ranges are about 240-260 C nozzle and 90-110 C bed, often with glue on PEI. Keep fan low on open printers; in a warm enclosure some fan is usually needed for overhangs. It emits styrene fumes, so ventilate the room without blowing air at the print.

settings.advice: Low (about 0-25%) on open printers; higher is often needed in a hot enclosure.
Use an outer brim for large or sharp-cornered parts.
Enable on open-frame printers.
Raise (e.g. 10-15 s) so small layers can cool.
A warm chamber (Orca lists 50-70 C for ABS) reduces warping and cracking if supported.
Compensate measured shrinkage for accurate parts.

facts: Prusa profile: 255 C nozzle, 100 C bed (80-110 C allowed; larger parts need hotter)
Bambu table: 240-280 C nozzle, 90-100 C bed, enclosed printer recommended
Orca table: 230-250 C nozzle, 90-100 C bed, chamber 50-70 C
Polymaker generic: fan 25% or less; brims or rafts; avoid drafts
Ellis: in an enclosure ABS often needs more fan than expected; uses at least 15 s minimum layer time
Shrinks about 1-2% after cooling; can be smoothed and glued with acetone
Poor UV resistance; outdoor parts yellow and embrittle
Dry at about 80 C for 8 h

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Filament guide material table
Ellis' Print Tuning Guide - Cooling and Layer Times
Polymaker wiki - Printing tips by material type

entries.title: ASA: UV-resistant ABS alternative for outdoor parts
entries.summary: ASA prints much like ABS but resists UV, warps a little less and smells less, which makes it a good outdoor material (heat resistance up to about 93 C per Prusa). Typical ranges are about 240-260 C nozzle and 90-110 C bed, with low fan (about 10-25%), an enclosure for larger parts and glue on PEI. It still releases styrene fumes, so ventilate. It is partly hygroscopic; dry at about 80 C.

settings.advice: Keep low (about 10-25%); reduce if layers delaminate.
Enable on open printers.
Outer brim for large flat parts.
Reverse on even can reduce warping stresses on ASA.

facts: Prusa profile: 260 C nozzle, 105 C first layer, 110 C other layers
Bambu table: 240-280 C nozzle, 90-100 C bed, enclosed printer recommended
Polymaker generic: 240-260 C, bed 90-110 C, fan 10-25%; turn fan off if layers split
Prusa: do not put acetone or ABS/ASA slurry on powder-coated sheets
Can be smoothed and glued with acetone like ABS

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Filament guide material table
Polymaker wiki - Printing tips by material type

entries.title: Build plate choice: textured PEI, smooth PEI, cool plate and glue
entries.summary: Textured PEI is the most versatile surface: good grip when hot, easy release when cool, and it protects against over-adhesion of PETG and TPU. Smooth PEI gives glossy bottoms and strong grip but PETG, TPU and PC can bond so hard they tear it; use glue stick as a release layer. Cool plates suit PLA at low bed temperatures. Engineering plates need glue. Glue stick also helps PA, PC and CF materials stick and release.

settings.advice: Select the plate actually installed so the matching bed temperature is used.
Bed temperature for textured PEI.
Bed temperature for smooth PEI / high-temperature plate.
Bed temperature for cool plate (PLA).
Bed temperature for engineering plate (use glue).

facts: Typical bed temperatures on PEI (Bambu): PLA 45-65 C, PETG 60-80 C, ABS/ASA 90-100 C, PC and PA 100-120 C, TPU 35-45 C
Cool plate: PLA 35-45 C; not recommended for PETG, ABS, ASA, PC, PA
Prusa: on textured sheets, squish the first layer a bit more so plastic fills the texture
Clean plates with dish soap and hot water; Bambu warns against acetone on its plates
Let the plate cool before removing parts; flex spring-steel plates to release
PET-CF/GF can be hard to remove from clean textured PEI; wait for room temperature or use an adhesive

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Filament guide material table
Polymaker wiki - Printing tips by material type

entries.title: Carbon and glass fiber filled filaments (PLA-CF, PETG-CF, PA-CF...)
entries.summary: Fiber-filled filaments are stiffer, more dimensionally stable and often more heat resistant than their base polymer, but more brittle with lower impact strength and layer adhesion. The fibers are abrasive: use a hardened steel nozzle, never brass or stainless, and avoid 0.2 mm nozzles. A 0.6 mm hardened nozzle clogs least; 0.4 mm works with 0.15-0.3 mm layers and moderate speed. Print about 5-10 C hotter than the base material.

settings.advice: Set to hardened steel so the slicer can warn about abrasive filament.
Set the nozzle hardness so compatibility checks work.
About 5-10 C above the base material.
0.15-0.3 mm on 0.4 mm; taller layers reduce clog risk.

facts: Prusa: lowest practical nozzle 0.4 mm and layer height 0.2 mm; cold pull before printing reduces clogs
Bambu: 0.4 mm hardened nozzle, recommended layers 0.15-0.3 mm and max about 100 mm/s
Bambu nozzle ranges: PLA-CF 210-240 C, PETG-CF 240-270 C, PA-CF and PET-CF 260-300 C
Polymaker generic: bed temperature as for the base material; 50 mm/s or less
Abrasive fillers wear extruder gears and feeder tubes; maintain more often
Brittle CF filaments can snap in long feeder paths

Bambu Lab wiki - Filament guide material table
Polymaker wiki - Printing tips by material type

entries.title: Choosing a filament by heat, UV and toughness needs
entries.summary: PLA is easiest but softens around 50-60 C and degrades in UV, so avoid it in cars, near heat or outdoors. PETG is tougher and usable to about 80 C. ASA is the outdoor choice: UV resistant and heat resistant to about 93 C. ABS is tough and heat resistant but not UV stable. PC and PA are for high heat and high strength. TPU is for flexible, impact-absorbing parts. Fiber-filled grades add stiffness but reduce toughness.
facts: Bambu rates heat resistance roughly: PLA low, PETG/ABS/ASA medium, PC and PA higher, PA-CF and PET-CF highest
Bambu rates impact resistance highest for TPU and PC, lowest for PVA and PET-CF
Prusa: PLA softens and deforms above about 60 C

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Filament guide material table

entries.title: Filament drying temperatures and times by material
entries.summary: Typical forced-air dryer settings (Bambu): PLA 50-55 C for 8 h; PETG 65-70 C for 8 h; ABS, ASA and PC 80 C for 8 h; PA, PA-CF and PET-CF 80 C for 8-12 h; TPU 70 C for 8 h; PVA 55 C for 8 h. Drying at too high a temperature can deform spools or fuse PLA and TPU loops. Store dried filament sealed with desiccant, ideally below 20% RH, and use it soon.
steps: Check the filament manufacturer's recommended drying temperature first
Dry at the material's temperature for the full time; flip or rotate the spool if heating from one side
Let the spool cool, then store immediately in a sealed box or dry box with fresh desiccant
For very hygroscopic materials (PA, PC, PVA), print directly from a dry box
facts: Drying required before use (Bambu): PVA, PC, PA, PA-CF/GF, PET-CF/GF, TPU, PETG HF/translucent; recommended for others
Heated-bed drying in an enclosed printer: e.g. PLA 60-70 C for 12 h, covered, flipping the spool every 6 h
Unload filament from the toolhead before bed drying; open-frame printers cannot dry filament this way
Prusa: nylon at least 4 h below 90 C
Snapmaker: TPU 90A 70 C for 6 h
Some third-party spools are not heat resistant enough for high-temperature drying

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Filament guide material table

entries.title: Which filaments need an enclosure (and which overheat in one)
entries.summary: ABS, ASA, PC and nylon (and their CF/GF versions) need an enclosed, warm printer to limit warping and layer splitting. PLA, PETG and TPU print fine on open printers; PETG can still benefit from an enclosure in cold rooms. In an enclosed printer, low-softening materials can overheat: open the door or lid for PLA, TPU and PVA when the bed is above about 45 C, and for PETG above about 60-70 C, to prevent heat-creep clogs.

settings.advice: Filament softening temperature used to warn about chamber heat with low-temp materials.
Enable for ABS/ASA on open printers.
Use exhaust or filtration for ABS/ASA if the printer has it.

facts: Without an enclosure, a draft shield or tall skirt helps ABS and ASA
ABS and ASA emit styrene; nylon emits odor and ultrafine particles: ventilate, but avoid drafts on the print
Enclosure heat can deform plastic printer parts over long ABS/ASA sessions (Prusa)
Higher chamber temperatures reduce filtration efficiency for ABS/ASA

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Filament guide material table

entries.title: Matte PLA: weaker layers and how to compensate
entries.summary: Matte PLA hides layer lines with a flat finish, but many users report it splits along layers more easily than plain PLA. Common fixes are printing 5-10 C hotter, slowing down, reducing extra cooling (such as auxiliary fans), and checking flow and pressure advance. Use plain PLA for load-bearing parts; plain PLA with fine fuzzy skin can imitate a matte look.
symptoms: Parts snap along layer lines
Bends less before breaking than plain PLA

settings.advice: Raise 5-10 C above plain PLA settings and confirm strength on a temperature tower.
Reduce or turn off the auxiliary fan to improve layer bonding.
Slow down if layers are weak.

facts: A forum user cited Bambu's data sheet: bending strength about 53 MPa for PLA Matte vs 76 MPa for PLA Basic
Bambu groups PLA Matte with standard PLA: no hardened nozzle needed
Bambu drying for PLA Basic/Matte: about 50 C for 8 h in a forced-air oven
Drying alone did not fix weak layers for at least one user

sources.title: Bambu Lab forum - PLA matte layer adhesion
Bambu Lab wiki - Filament guide material table

entries.title: Nylon (PA6, PA12, PA-CF): drying, warping and adhesion
entries.summary: Nylon is strong, tough and heat resistant but very hygroscopic: wet nylon bubbles, strings and prints rough, weak parts, so dry it thoroughly and keep it in a dry box while printing. Typical nozzle temperatures are about 240-290 C depending on the grade (sources range 225-300 C), with a 90-110 C bed and glue or a dedicated surface. Pure PA warps strongly and benefits from an enclosure; carbon-filled PA warps much less. Use little fan and moderate speeds.

settings.advice: Low (0-20%) for good layer bonding.
Use with glue on engineering or PEI plates.
A warm chamber reduces warping for pure PA.
Outer brim or raft for large parts.

facts: Prusa: 285 C nozzle, 110 C bed; dry at least 4 h below 90 C; can absorb up to 10% of its weight in water
Bambu: PA bed 100-120 C; dry at 80 C for 8-12 h; desiccant protection required during use
Orca table: PA6 230-260 C, PA12 225-260 C, bed 90-110 C, chamber 70-100 C
Polymaker generic: 240-280 C, fan 20% or less, 30-50 mm/s; some brands need no enclosure or high bed
Strong odor and ultrafine particles: print in a ventilated room or enclosure

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Filament guide material table
Polymaker wiki - Printing tips by material type

entries.title: Polycarbonate (PC): high temperature, enclosure and cracking
entries.summary: PC is very heat resistant and impact tough but needs high temperatures, an all-metal hotend, a hot bed and ideally a hot enclosure to avoid warping and layer cracking. Typical ranges are about 260-310 C nozzle and 100-120 C bed with glue on textured PEI; avoid smooth PEI without a release layer. Use little or no fan, slow speeds and dry the filament, since most PC is very hygroscopic. Rounded corners and fewer walls reduce warping on big parts.

settings.advice: Off or very low; cooling causes cracking and warping.
As hot as the printer safely allows if chamber heating exists.
Use a brim on small-contact or large parts.
100-120 C with glue stick.

facts: Prusa: 275 C nozzle, 110 C first layer, 115 C others; strongly recommends an enclosure
Bambu: 260-290 C nozzle, 100-120 C bed; dry at 80 C for 8 h before use
Orca table: 270-310 C nozzle, 100-120 C bed, chamber 80-100 C
Polymaker generic: no cooling, 40 mm/s or less, 50-60 C ambient; slow cooling (e.g. 2 h in a 90 C oven) helps prevent cracks
Prusa: higher infill and more perimeters increase warping on large PC parts
Cold rooms (below about 18 C) can cause bed heating problems and warping

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Filament guide material table
Polymaker wiki - Printing tips by material type

entries.title: PETG: temperatures, plates, cooling and stringing
entries.summary: PETG is tougher and more heat resistant than PLA (usable up to about 80 C) with low warping. Typical ranges are about 230-260 C nozzle and 70-85 C bed (sources range 60-90 C). It sticks extremely well to smooth PEI and can tear the surface, so use textured PEI or a glue stick as a release layer. Use moderate cooling, slower speeds than PLA and avoid excessive first-layer squish. It strings easily; drying, tuned retraction and avoid-crossing-walls help.

settings.advice: About 235-250 C; lower to cut stringing, higher for layer strength and speed.
70-85 C on textured PEI.
If printing on smooth PEI, use glue stick as a release layer.
Around 30-60%; more for bridges, less for strength.
Enable to keep strings inside the part.
Often a bit longer than PLA; tune with the retraction test after drying.

facts: Prusa profile: 230 C first layer, 240 C other layers; bed 85 C first, 90 C others
Bambu table: nozzle 240-270 C (PETG HF 230-260 C); bed 60-80 C; cool plate not recommended
Polymaker generic: 220-260 C (230-240 optimal), bed 65-90 C, fan 30-50%, print 60 mm/s or less
For maximum toughness Prusa suggests little or no fan; for detail and less stringing, more fan
Dry at about 65-70 C for 8 h; PETG HF/translucent should be dried before use
An enclosure helps interlayer strength in cold rooms; open the lid if the bed is above about 70 C
Supports can be hard to remove; for strength add walls rather than infill

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Filament guide material table
Polymaker wiki - Printing tips by material type

entries.title: PLA: typical temperatures, cooling, plates and pitfalls
entries.summary: PLA is the easiest common filament: low warping, no enclosure needed, and it likes strong part cooling. Typical ranges are about 190-230 C nozzle and 45-65 C bed on PEI (35-45 C on a cool plate). It softens around 60 C, so it is a poor choice for hot cars or outdoor parts, and UV degrades it. In an enclosed printer, open the door or lid when the bed is above about 45 C to avoid heat creep clogs.

settings.advice: Start mid-range (about 205-215 C) and refine with a temperature tower; go hotter for fast printing.
About 55-65 C on textured PEI.
High (80-100%) for PLA; it tolerates strong cooling.
1-2 layers without fan for adhesion.

facts: Prusa profile: 215 C first layer, 210 C other layers, 60 C bed; brands may need 185-235 C
Bambu table: nozzle 190-240 C; textured or smooth PEI 45-65 C; cool plate 35-45 C
Polymaker: 100% fan for overhangs and bridges, fan off for about the first 0.5 mm, at least 3 s per small layer
Retraction (Polymaker generic): 1-2 mm direct drive, 2-5 mm Bowden
Drying is recommended but optional: about 50-55 C for 8 h in an oven
Layer adhesion is weaker than many materials; parts tend to snap along layers

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Filament guide material table
Polymaker wiki - Printing tips by material type

entries.title: PLA+ (PLA Pro / tough PLA): what changes vs regular PLA
entries.summary: PLA+ is a brand term for modified PLA marketed as tougher and less brittle; formulations differ between brands, so there is no single standard. It prints like PLA but often a little hotter. eSun's published values are about 210-230 C nozzle and 45-60 C bed with full fan and no enclosure. Run a temperature tower per brand, since some PLA+ needs the upper end of the range for good layer bonding.

settings.advice: Start around 215-225 C; confirm with a temperature tower for each brand.
100% like PLA.

facts: eSun PLA+ (via a settings aggregator citing eSun): 210-230 C nozzle, 45-60 C bed, 100% fan, no enclosure needed
eSun suggests drying at 50 C for 8-12 h only if the spool is wet
Treat it like PLA for heat resistance and enclosure use

entries.title: PVA and BVOH water-soluble support filaments
entries.summary: PVA and BVOH dissolve in water and are used as support or support interface, usually with PLA because their print temperatures match. They are extremely hygroscopic: wet spools clog, tangle in gears and stick poorly, so keep them dry at all times. Use a top Z distance of 0 for soluble supports, and avoid printing them directly on the bed (a 1-2 layer PLA raft sticks better). Supports dissolve over several hours, faster in warm water.

settings.advice: Assign PVA/BVOH to the interface.
0 for soluble supports.
Mark the filament as soluble in its profile.
Keep flushing generous to avoid PLA contamination in soluble supports.

facts: Prusa: PVA+ 195 C, BVOH 215 C, bed 60 C; both adhere poorly to PEI
Bambu: PVA/BVOH nozzle 190-240 C; dry at 55 C for 8 h; desiccant required during use
BVOH dissolves at roughly 1 g per 20 ml water (Prusa)
PVA clogs more easily than BVOH; filament changes need large purge volumes
Using soluble filament only for the interface saves material and time

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Filament guide material table

entries.title: Silk PLA: getting maximum gloss
entries.summary: Silk PLA contains pearlescent additives for a glossy, metallic look. Gloss depends mainly on outer wall speed (slower is shinier), a moderately higher nozzle temperature, and constant wall speed across the part. Bambu suggests outer walls at 40-60 mm/s (try 50), about 235 C, 0.16 mm layers, and not slowing outer walls for cooling. Silk layer bonding is usually weaker than plain PLA, and it absorbs moisture fairly easily.

settings.advice: 40-60 mm/s for best gloss; keep it consistent.
Enable so cooling slowdowns do not create dull bands.
Around 230-235 C, higher if printing faster.
0.16 mm or less for smooth reflections on curves.
Archimedean chords or concentric for glossy tops.
Helps steep overhangs and warping on silk PLA.

facts: Typical silk nozzle range: about 210-240 C
Matte streaks and weak layers are signs of printing too fast or too cold
Orient key display surfaces vertically; flat curved tops show more steps and less gloss
Archimedean chords or concentric top patterns can improve top gloss
Dry at about 55 C for 8 h; store below 20% RH
Bambu does not recommend 0.6/0.8 mm nozzles for its silk PLA
Dual-color silk can have an oval cross-section that may twist and blur color transitions

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Printing with silk filaments

entries.title: Pairing support filaments with main materials
entries.summary: Dedicated support filaments separate cleanly from a matching main material, allowing a zero Z gap and smooth undersides. Breakaway supports are peeled by hand; PVA dissolves in water for internal or hard-to-reach supports. Match temperature classes: PLA-type supports for PLA and PETG, high-temperature supports (or ASA/ABS interfaces) for PA and PET-CF. Never use a low-temperature support with ABS, ASA, PC or PA, which can clog the nozzle.

settings.advice: Assign the support filament to the interface.
Keep the main filament for the support body to save time and material.
Mark support filaments in their profile.

facts: Most prints only need support filament for the interface; the support body can use the main filament
PLA and PETG can serve as interface support for each other in some cases
ABS or ASA can work as support interface for PA6-CF/GF, PAHT-CF and PET-CF
Support filament is not suitable for printing model parts: strength and quality are poor

entries.title: TPU 95A flexible filament: speed, retraction and plates
entries.summary: TPU is a flexible, impact-absorbing filament; 95A is the firmest common grade and the easiest to print. Print slowly (often 20-40 mm/s), use little or no retraction, and prefer a direct drive extruder with a constrained filament path. Typical ranges are about 210-240 C nozzle and 30-60 C bed (Prusa lists a warmer 60-75 C bed). It bonds strongly to smooth PEI, so use textured PEI or glue as a separator. It is hygroscopic: dry it before printing.

settings.advice: Keep low so the extruder does not buckle the filament; 20-30 mm/s at 0.4 x 0.2 mm lines is only about 1.6-2.4 mm3/s.
Start at 0 (Prusa) and raise slowly if strings persist after drying; Polymaker suggests 1-3 mm on direct drive.
Keep slow to avoid stretching or grinding soft filament.
Enable to hide strings inside the part.
Use about 0.3 mm for easier support removal.

facts: Bambu table: 200-250 C nozzle; textured PEI 35-45 C; engineering plate 30-35 C; dry 70 C for 8 h
Prusa: 230-245 C, about 20 mm/s typical and 30-40 mm/s max, loosen the idler, start with retraction off
Polymaker generic: 210-230 C, bed 40-60 C, 30 mm/s or less, 1-3 mm retraction on direct drive, avoid Bowden
Harder TPU (95A) can print faster than softer grades
Supports are hard to remove: Prusa suggests 0.3 mm Z gap and generous XY separation
0.2 mm nozzles are not recommended for TPU

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Filament guide material table
Polymaker wiki - Printing tips by material type

entries.title: Softer TPU (90A, 85A): extra care with feeding and speed
entries.summary: Softer TPU grades are harder to push through an extruder: they buckle, tangle in gears and jam automatic feeders. Print slower than 95A (about 30-50 mm/s or less), load manually instead of through automatic multi-spool feeders, avoid 0.2 mm nozzles and dry thoroughly. If parts deform, use full part cooling. If stringing persists after drying, raise retraction slightly and lower travel speed.

settings.advice: Lower than for 95A; soft TPU needs gentle, slow feeding.
Up to 100% if thin features deform.
Reduce if stringing persists after drying.

facts: Snapmaker TPU 90A guidance (0.4 mm nozzle): 210-240 C, bed 25-60 C, fan on, 30-50 mm/s, dry 70 C for 6 h
Bambu notes TPU 85A/90A are not compatible or not recommended with several nozzle types and its AMS feeders
If parts stick too hard, spraying alcohol at the interface helps release them (Snapmaker)
Prusa: the softer the filament, the harder it is to print; very soft flex may need glue to protect PEI

entries.title: Signs of wet filament and why it matters
entries.summary: Moisture in filament turns to steam in the hot nozzle, so the melt foams and flows unevenly. The result is stringing, oozing, bubbles and holes, rough or uneven-gloss surfaces, under-extrusion and weaker parts; some materials also become brittle on the spool. Even new, factory-sealed spools can be wet. If stringing or rough walls persist despite tuning, dry the filament before changing settings.
symptoms: Crackling or popping sounds while extruding
Heavy stringing that retraction does not fix
Bubbles, pits or holes in walls
Rough or uneven gloss surface
Brittle filament that snaps on the spool
Weaker parts than usual
causes: Spool stored open in humid air
Hygroscopic material (PA, PC, PVA, TPU, PETG)
Long prints from an open spool in a humid room
steps: Dry the spool at the material's drying temperature (see drying guide)
Reprint a small test; if stringing stops, keep the spool in a dry box
Only then retune retraction or temperature if problems remain

entries.title: Snapmaker Orca account avatar keeps spinning after login
entries.summary: After signing in, the user picture in the top-left corner may keep showing a loading animation. The login has in fact worked and the software can be used normally; the avatar download is slow because of network latency and older builds had no timeout for it. Snapmaker scheduled the fix for 2.2.0 Beta, so updating Orca resolves it.
symptoms: Avatar in the upper-left corner keeps spinning after login
causes: Slow avatar download due to network latency
Missing timeout handling in older versions
steps: Continue working; the session is logged in.
Update Snapmaker Orca to 2.2.0 or later.
