Edges can look slightly fuzzy; ironing inset keeps the pattern away from edges

entries.title: Jerk, square corner velocity and junction deviation
entries.summary: Jerk is the speed change a printer makes instantly at a corner without accelerating. Higher values corner faster but add vibration and ringing; lower values give smoother, cleaner corners. Klipper uses square corner velocity, Marlin 2 uses junction deviation by default (or classic jerk if max junction deviation is 0), RepRapFirmware uses instantaneous speed changes. Orca caps per-feature jerk to the printer's Motion ability limits.

settings.advice: 0 keeps the firmware value; set only if you have calibrated cornering.
Lower than other features for cleaner outer corners.
Can be higher to speed up infill.
Low for better first-layer adhesion.
Marlin 2 with JD: lower values give smoother corners, higher faster ones.
Set to 0 if your Marlin printer uses classic jerk so jerk settings apply.

facts: Approximate conversion: JD = 0.4 x jerk^2 / acceleration
Typical JD values are about 0.01-0.3 mm; jerk values are usually 1-20 mm/s or more
Marlin 2 only accepts junction deviation between 0.01 and 0.3 mm
Default jerk of 0 uses the printer's own default

entries.title: Layer height: choosing a value for quality vs speed
entries.summary: Layer height is the thickness of each printed layer. Thinner layers give smoother curves, finer detail and better steep overhangs but multiply print time; thicker layers print faster and bond well but show stair-stepping. Stay roughly between 20% and 80% of the nozzle diameter (about 0.08-0.32 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle); outside that range flow becomes inconsistent or layer adhesion suffers.

settings.advice: Lower (e.g. 0.12-0.16 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle) for curved or detailed display parts; raise toward 0.28 mm for fast functional parts. Keep within 20-80% of nozzle diameter.
Printer-side lower limit used by variable/adaptive layer height; leave at the profile value unless you changed the nozzle.
Printer-side upper limit (roughly 75-80% of nozzle diameter); variable layer height will not exceed it.

facts: Orca guideline ranges: 0.2 mm nozzle 0.04-0.16 mm, 0.4 mm nozzle 0.08-0.32 mm, 0.6 mm nozzle 0.12-0.48 mm, 0.8 mm nozzle 0.16-0.64 mm
Below about 20% of the nozzle diameter, flow inconsistencies and fish-scale patterns can appear, especially at high speed
Above about 80% of the nozzle diameter, layer adhesion and surface quality drop
Smaller layers reduce the unsupported step between layers, so steeper overhangs print without support
Fewer, thicker layers also mean fewer filament changes in multi-color prints, which cuts purge waste
Default in this slicer: 0.2 mm

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Reduce waste during filament change

entries.title: Line width per feature: walls, infill, top surface, support
entries.summary: Line width is how wide each extruded line is laid down. Orca lets you set it per feature, in mm or as a percentage of nozzle diameter (percentages follow nozzle changes). Around 100% of the nozzle is a safe baseline; slightly wider lines bond better and add strength, while more than about 150% risks blobs. With Arachne the values are only references because widths vary with geometry.

settings.advice: Default fallback width; ~100% of nozzle diameter is a good start.
105-120% of nozzle; go narrower for fine detail, wider for overhang quality.
120%+ of nozzle to add strength without extra walls.
Keep near 100-105% for smooth top surfaces.
About 115%; going wider increases flow demand and can hit the volumetric limit.
About 110% for good bonding.
About 100%; very thin supports are fragile.

facts: Outer wall: about 105-120% of nozzle for clean overhangs and detail
Inner wall: 120% or more for strength
Top surface: about 100-105% for a smooth finish
Sparse infill: about 115%, conservative to stay below the volumetric flow limit
Internal solid infill: about 110%
Support: about 100%; much thinner supports can break during removal
A 0 value falls back to the default line width
Wider lines raise volumetric flow at the same speed, so check max volumetric speed

entries.title: Max volumetric speed: the real speed limit for each filament
entries.summary: Max volumetric speed (mm3/s) is how much plastic the hotend can melt per second for a filament. Orca slows any feature whose flow would exceed it, so it protects against under-extrusion, weak layers and clogs regardless of the mm/s speeds set. Flow = speed x line width x layer height, so wider lines or taller layers reach the limit at lower speeds. Calibrate it per filament and keep 10-20% below the measured maximum.
symptoms: Under-extrusion or gaps only at high speeds
Matte or rough patches on fast infill
Extruder clicking during fast sections

settings.advice: Set 10-20% below the max flowrate test result; lower further for strength-critical prints.
Use the upper end of the filament range when printing near the volumetric limit.

facts: Example: 24 mm3/s at 0.4 mm width and 0.2 mm layers allows about 300 mm/s
Typical 0.4 mm brass nozzle values from Ellis: E3D V6 about 11 mm3/s, Dragon HF about 24, Rapido UHF about 30
Brand and color of the same material can change the achievable flow significantly
Higher nozzle temperature raises achievable flow; hardened steel nozzles may flow less
This value cannot be zero

sources.title: OrcaSlicer wiki - Material volumetric speed limitation
Ellis' Print Tuning Guide - Determining max volumetric flow rate

entries.title: Nozzle and bed temperatures per plate type
entries.summary: Nozzle temperature controls melt viscosity, flow and layer bonding; calibrate it with a temperature tower. A slightly hotter first layer can aid adhesion but may cause elephant foot. Orca stores bed temperatures per plate type (cool, engineering, smooth/high-temp PEI, textured PEI and others) for first and other layers. Bed temperature too low causes warping and detachment; too high softens lower layers. A rough upper limit is the material's glass transition minus 5-10 C.

settings.advice: Use the temperature tower result; go hotter for speed or strength, cooler to reduce stringing.
0-5 C hotter than other layers for adhesion; lower if elephant foot appears.
Bed temperature used on textured PEI plates.
Bed temperature used on smooth PEI / high-temperature plates.
Bed temperature for cool plates (low-temp PLA surfaces).
Bed temperature for engineering plates (usually with glue).
First-layer bed temperature on textured PEI; a few degrees higher can help adhesion.

facts: Most materials tolerate about +/-5 C bed variation
Print hotter (upper end of range) when printing fast or near the volumetric limit
Keep beds clean and free of oils for consistent adhesion

entries.title: Ooze prevention and standby temperature for multi-tool printers
entries.summary: On printers with several nozzles, idle nozzles keep oozing plastic that can smear on the print. Ooze prevention lowers the temperature of inactive extruders by the temperature variation (or to the filament's idle temperature if set). Preheat time starts heating the next tool before it is needed to cut waiting time at tool changes.

settings.advice: Enable on multi-nozzle printers when idle nozzles leave drips or strings.
More negative reduces ooze more but lengthens reheating at tool changes.
Per-filament idle temperature; set it instead of a delta for precise control.
Seconds of preheat before a tool change to reduce waiting.

facts: Default temperature variation in this slicer: -5 C
Filament idle temperature, if non-zero, overrides the temperature variation
Preheat steps are only useful on Prusa XL; set to 1 for other printers

entries.title: Overhang and bridge fan speed (force cooling)
entries.summary: Force cooling for overhangs and bridges sets a dedicated fan speed for overhang walls past a threshold and for external bridges, which reduces sagging and curling. In Orca there is no separate external bridge fan key: external bridges use the overhang fan speed. Internal bridges have their own fan value; a lower value there can reduce warping on large flat areas.

settings.advice: Enable for most materials; for ABS/ASA keep the overhang speed moderate to avoid layer splitting.
High for PLA/PETG bridges and overhangs; moderate for ABS/ASA, lowering it if layers split.
Lower threshold applies extra cooling to milder overhangs; 0% cools every outer wall.
Lower than overhang fan to reduce warping over large internal bridges; -1 uses overhang settings.

facts: Overhang threshold options: 0%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 95% of line width unsupported; 0% applies to all outer walls
Overhang fan speed is clamped below by min fan speed and can rise to max fan when layer time is short
Internal bridge fan speed -1 means use the overhang fan settings
Default overhang fan speed in this slicer: 100%

entries.title: Overhang speed slowdown and curled perimeter detection
entries.summary: Slow down for overhang prints overhanging walls at reduced speeds in four bands, defined as the fraction of line width that is unsupported (25%, 50%, 75%, 100%). Slow down for curled perimeters adds extra slowdown where edges may have curled up, such as the Benchy bow. Large speed drops at high outer wall speeds can cause bulges if pressure advance is slightly off; extrusion rate smoothing helps.

settings.advice: Keep enabled for better overhangs unless cooling is very strong.
Mild overhangs; small or no slowdown.
Moderate overhangs; slow a bit more.
Steep overhangs; slow down significantly.
Fully unsupported walls; slowest band, near bridge speed.
Enable to reduce curling on sharp overhang corners; raise min speeds if it causes wall artifacts.

facts: A speed of 0 in a band means no slowdown for that band
Percentages are based on outer wall speed for outer walls and inner wall speed for inner walls
Fully overhanging walls can be printed with bridge settings when detect overhang wall is on
For Klipper, Orca suggests a pressure advance smooth time of about 0.015-0.02 s with curled-perimeter slowdown

entries.title: Overhang tools: reverse on even, make overhang printable, extra perimeters
entries.summary: Reverse on even prints overhanging perimeters in the opposite direction on even layers, which can greatly improve steep overhangs and reduce warping in ABS/ASA, TPU and silk PLA, but may leave a texture on the outer wall (reverse internal only avoids most of it). Make overhang printable reshapes steep overhangs into cones so they print without support. Extra perimeters on overhangs add overhang walls where bridges cannot anchor.

settings.advice: Enable for steep overhangs or warp-prone materials.
Enable to keep a smooth outer wall while keeping most of the benefit.
0 to reverse all walls on even layers; higher values reverse only big overhangs.
Enable to print overhangs without support by adding conical material.
45-60 deg is typical; lower adds more material.
Enable for steep overhangs and unanchored bridges.
Keep on so overhang speeds and bridge settings apply.

facts: Reverse threshold 0 reverses all walls on even layers, which Orca recommends for best effect
Make overhang printable max angle default 55 deg; 45-60 deg suits most printers
Extra perimeters on overhangs requires detect overhang wall
Make overhang printable changes model geometry; check fit-critical areas

entries.title: Part cooling fan: min/max fan speed and layer time thresholds
entries.summary: Orca's auto cooling ties fan speed to estimated layer time. Layers shorter than the min-fan layer time turn the fan on, with speed interpolated between min and max fan speed as layers get shorter; layers shorter than the max-fan layer time get maximum fan and, if enabled, a slowdown. PLA likes lots of cooling; PETG moderate; ABS/ASA/PC little or none, though ABS in an enclosure often still needs some.

settings.advice: Raise for PLA (e.g. 80-100%); lower for PETG; keep low for ABS/ASA to limit warping and layer splits.
Cap for warp-prone materials; 100% for PLA.
Layers faster than this get fan; raise to cool more layers, lower to keep fan off on large layers.
Layers faster than this get max fan and may be slowed; raise for small parts that sag or melt.
Enable to keep the fan running at minimum instead of cycling on and off.

facts: Defaults in this slicer: min fan 20%, max fan 100%, min-fan layer time 60 s, max-fan layer time 5 s
Keep fan always on runs the fan at least at minimum speed to avoid frequent start/stop
Ellis recommends constant fan speeds where possible; varying fan can cause banding
Polymaker generic guidance: PETG 30-50% fan, ABS 25% or less, ASA 10-25%, PC none

sources.title: Ellis' Print Tuning Guide - Cooling and Layer Times
Polymaker wiki - Printing tips by material type

entries.title: Precise wall and precise Z height for dimensional accuracy
entries.summary: Slic3r-based slicers model lines as ovals that overlap, so two 0.4 mm walls make a shell about 0.71 mm thick and the outer wall can be pushed outward with Inner/Outer order. Precise wall removes the overlap between the outer wall and its neighbor, improving size accuracy and layer consistency without hurting strength. Precise Z height adjusts the last few layers so the final height matches the model even when it is not a multiple of the layer height.

settings.advice: Enable for parts that must fit; keeps strength while improving outer dimensions.
Enable when exact part height matters (stacking parts, enclosures).

facts: Example: a 20.1 mm tall cube at 0.2 mm layers normally ends at 20.2 mm; precise Z height makes it 20.1 mm by adjusting the last five layers
Precise wall is ignored for Outer/Inner and Inner/Outer/Inner wall orders

entries.title: Pressure advance (linear advance): what it does and where to set it
entries.summary: Pressure in the nozzle lags behind extruder motion: lines start thin when accelerating and bulge or ooze when decelerating. Pressure advance pushes extra filament during acceleration and pulls back during deceleration, giving sharp corners, even lines and cleaner seams. The value depends on extruder, nozzle, temperature and filament, so store it per filament and recalibrate when these change. Marlin needs Linear Advance enabled in firmware.
symptoms: Bulging corners
Gaps at the start of lines or near corners
Seam bulges or seam gaps

settings.advice: Enable to have Orca send the filament's PA value at print start.
Set from the PA calibration; raise if corners bulge, lower if corners gap or round off.

facts: Too low: bulging corners and blobs at line ends; too high: gaps or rounded, under-extruded corners
Typical Klipper values range about 0.05-1.0, the high end only for Bowden; direct drive is usually much lower
Very high PA with high acceleration can make the extruder skip
Default in this slicer: 0.02
Ellis lists recalibration triggers: different filament or brand, nozzle size, large temperature changes, input shaper changes, hotend or extruder changes

sources.title: OrcaSlicer wiki - Material flow ratio and pressure advance
Ellis' Print Tuning Guide - Pressure / Linear Advance

entries.title: Prime (wipe) tower for multi-color and multi-material prints
entries.summary: The prime tower is a sacrificial block printed beside the model where the nozzle is cleaned and flow is stabilized after each filament change, preventing blobs, under-extrusion and color contamination at the start of the next color. It must rise to the last layer with a change, so changes near the top waste more filament; reorienting a part so color changes sit low can shrink the tower a lot. Small towers can topple on tall prints; a tower brim helps.

settings.advice: Keep enabled for multi-color prints; disabling it risks blobs and color bleed after changes.
Narrower saves filament but is less stable on tall prints.
Raise if the first lines after a change are thin or blotchy; lower to save filament.
Increase for tall or narrow towers that might tip over.
Rib or Cone for taller, more stable towers.
Saves time when changes are only low in the print; check collision clearance.

facts: Default prime volume in this slicer: 45 mm3 per tool change; default tower width 60 mm
Rib wall type adds four ribs for stability; Cone adds a stabilizing base (Type 2 towers)
No sparse layers skips the tower on layers without tool changes; you must make sure the nozzle cannot collide with the print
Flushing into infill, objects or support only works when the prime tower is enabled
Variable layer height objects on one plate must share the same layer heights for a prime tower
Bambu example: flipping a part so color changes were near the bottom cut tower material by about 40%

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Reduce waste during filament change

entries.title: Print sequence: by layer vs by object
entries.summary: By layer prints every object one layer at a time and is the default. By object prints each object completely before starting the next, which reduces travel between parts and gives each part its own cooling, and means a failure only ruins one part. It needs more spacing, and only the last object may use the full height; earlier objects must stay below the extruder clearance height.

settings.advice: By object for several small parts or to limit stringing between parts; By layer for tall or large plates.
Set to your toolhead size so by-object spacing avoids collisions.
Max height of earlier objects in by-object mode before the gantry would hit them.
Use per-object skirts with by-object printing.

entries.title: Print speeds per feature: outer wall, inner wall, infill, top surface
entries.summary: Orca sets speed per feature. The outer wall is usually slowest for surface quality, inner walls and infill faster to save time, and top surfaces near outer-wall speed. Every speed is capped by max volumetric speed, machine motion limits, acceleration/jerk and the minimum layer time slowdown, so raising a speed may not change the real speed. Check the Preview speed or flow view to see what is actually printed.

settings.advice: Lower for better surface and gloss (e.g. 40-60 mm/s for silk); raise for speed if quality allows.
Can be higher than outer wall; keep flow below the volumetric limit for strong bonding.
Usually the fastest feature; capped by max volumetric speed.
Faster than top surface but slower than sparse infill for good bonding.
Close to outer wall speed for smooth tops.
Keep moderate; very fast gap fill can look rough.

facts: Defaults in this slicer: outer and inner wall 60 mm/s, travel 120 mm/s, first layer 30 mm/s (printer profiles override these)
Inner wall flow should stay well below the max volumetric speed for good layer bonding
Gap infill has irregular width and is usually printed slower
Outer wall speed is also limited by resonance avoidance settings, if enabled

entries.title: Raft layers and contact distance
entries.summary: A raft is a support-material platform printed under the object. It helps strongly warping materials (ABS, ASA, PC, nylon), parts with tiny or sharp contact areas, and worn or uneven beds. The trade-off is a rougher underside, extra time and material, and cleanup. Contact Z distance sets the gap to the object: larger is easier to remove but rougher. Try a brim first if the issue is only adhesion.

settings.advice: 2-4 for most cases; more for very uneven beds or strong warping. 0 disables.
Raise for easier removal, lower for a smoother bottom.
Wider raft spreads warping forces; costs material and plate space.
Widens the first raft/support layer for better plate adhesion.

facts: 2-4 raft layers suit most prints; half of the layers (rounded up) are interface layers
Default raft contact distance in this slicer: 0.1 mm
Rafts disable elephant foot compensation
With a prime tower, all objects must use the same number of raft layers

entries.title: Resonance avoidance speed range for the outer wall
entries.summary: Resonance avoidance keeps the outer wall speed out of a speed band where the printer resonates and leaves fine vertical artifacts (VFA). Find the bad band with the VFA speed test, then enter its min and max in the printer's Motion ability settings. Turn the option off while running ringing or input shaping tests.

settings.advice: Enable after a VFA test shows a speed band with visible artifacts.
Lower bound of the problematic outer wall speed band.
Upper bound of the problematic band.

entries.title: Retraction length and speed to control stringing
entries.summary: Retraction pulls filament back before travel to stop oozing. Too short leaves strings; too long or too fast can grind filament, cause clogs or gaps after travel. Direct drive extruders usually need about 0.5-1 mm, Bowden setups more (often 1-6 mm). Tune pressure advance first, because good PA reduces the retraction needed. If stringing persists, dry the filament before raising retraction.
causes: Wet filament
Nozzle temperature too high
Pressure advance too low
Loose nozzle or leaking hotend
Excessive Z-hop

settings.advice: Direct drive 0.4-1.0 mm, Bowden 1-6 mm; use the retraction test and pick the shortest clean value.
About 30-40 mm/s is a safe start; too fast can grind soft filament.
0 uses retraction speed; slightly slower can reduce blobs at restart.
Rarely needed; keep 0. A small positive value pushes extra filament after travel if line starts look thin.

facts: Ellis starting points: direct drive 0.5 mm at 35 mm/s (try to stay under 1 mm); Bowden 1 mm at 35 mm/s
Default in this slicer: 0.8 mm at 30 mm/s
PETG and TPU string more; PETG may never be fully string-free
Deretraction speed 0 means the same as retraction speed
Retraction can be overridden per filament in filament setting overrides

entries.title: Retraction travel threshold, retract on layer change and infill retraction
entries.summary: Retraction only triggers for travels longer than the travel distance threshold, so short hops skip retract/deretract cycles that add extruder variance. Retract on layer change makes every layer start with a depressurized nozzle for more consistent seams. Reduce infill retraction skips retraction for travels entirely inside infill, where ooze is hidden, saving time on large prints.

settings.advice: 2-4 mm is typical; lower it if short travels leave strings.
Enable for cleaner, more consistent seams.
Enable to save time; disable if strings appear inside translucent parts.

facts: Default travel threshold in this slicer: 2 mm
Orca's seam guide suggests a 2-4 mm threshold when PA, travel speed and acceleration are well tuned
Each skipped infill retraction saves tens of milliseconds, which adds up over thousands of travels

entries.title: Scarf joint seams to hide seams on curved walls
entries.summary: A scarf joint ramps the start of a loop up in height and flow so the start and end overlap like a scarf, making seams far less visible on smooth curved walls. It works less well on sharp corners and overhangs and adds a little time. Conditional scarf applies it only to smooth perimeters, keeping normal seams hidden in sharp corners. Print scarfs slowly (under about 100 mm/s).

settings.advice: Contour for most parts; Contour and hole if holes are visible.
Enable so sharp-cornered loops keep normal hidden seams.
Default 155 deg; lower to use scarfs on more corners.
Keep slow, under about 100 mm/s, or a percentage of wall speed.
Scarf length; about 20 mm blends well.
0 starts at the previous layer top; higher values shorten the ramp.
Usually off; little visible benefit.

facts: Types: None (default), Contour (outer walls only), Contour and hole
Conditional angle threshold default 155 deg; overhang threshold default 40% of wall width
Scarf length default 20 mm (0 disables); scarf steps default 10
Scarf joint flow ratio is best left at 1
Never applied on the first layer or in spiral vase mode
Enable extrusion rate smoothing if scarf speed differs a lot from wall speed

entries.title: Seam position: aligned, back, nearest or random
entries.summary: Every layer loop starts and ends somewhere, leaving a seam. Aligned stacks seams in a line, preferring concave corners; Aligned back does the same while avoiding the front; Back puts them at the rear (max Y); Nearest minimizes travel but scatters seams; Random spreads them out, leaving small zits but spreading the weak point. Aligned or Back usually look best, especially with seam painting.

settings.advice: Aligned or Aligned back for most models; Back for display parts with a front; Random for round parts needing strength.
Raise slightly (10-15%) if seams bulge; lower if a gap or notch is visible.
Enable for stronger or watertight parts.

facts: Default in this slicer: Aligned
Seam gap (default 10% of nozzle) shortens the loop end; 0-15% is typical for a tuned printer
Larger seam gap reduces bulges; smaller reduces the visible notch
Staggered inner seams offset inner-wall seams in a zigzag for strength and water-tightness
Seams on cylinders cannot be hidden in corners; consider scarf seams there

entries.title: Skirt loops, distance and draft shield
entries.summary: A skirt is a loop printed around the parts on the first layer(s) to prime the nozzle and stabilize flow before the model starts, and to check first-layer quality. Built taller as a draft shield, it surrounds the part to protect ABS/ASA from drafts on open-frame printers. Per-object skirts suit print-by-object. The skirt is placed at the skirt distance from the brim or object.

settings.advice: 1-3 loops for priming; 0 disables.
Increase to avoid touching brims or supports.
1 layer for priming; more layers for a partial draft shield.
Enable for ABS/ASA on open printers to reduce warping and cracking.
Set a few mm of filament if your start G-code has no prime line.

facts: Orca typically recommends 2 loops; default in this slicer is 1 loop at 2 mm distance
Draft shield enabled makes the skirt as tall as the tallest model
Minimum skirt extrusion length helps printers that do not print a prime line
Single loop after first layer saves filament but makes the shield weaker

entries.title: Slow down for layer cooling, min print speed and outer wall exemption
entries.summary: When a layer would finish faster than its layer time, Orca caps the fastest extrusions first so the layer takes longer to cool, never going below min print speed. Travels keep their speed. Don't slow down outer walls keeps the outer surface at constant speed (avoiding gloss changes, banding and VFA speeds) at the cost of slowing everything else more. If small parts still overheat at min speed, print several copies at once.

settings.advice: Keep enabled for small or tall thin parts; disable only when consistent speed matters more than cooling.
Raise if slowed sections show artifacts; lower so tiny layers can slow enough to cool.
Enable for glossy/silk filaments or to avoid banding from outer wall speed changes.

facts: The layer time estimate ignores acceleration, so real layers usually take a bit longer
Default min print speed in this slicer: 10 mm/s
The fan speed is derived from the layer time once the slowdown has been applied
If min print speed is 0, all extrusions are slowed by the same factor instead

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Printing with silk filaments

entries.title: Small area infill flow compensation
entries.summary: Short solid-infill lines in small areas, such as the tops of narrow letters, tend to be over-extruded. Small area flow compensation reduces flow based on extrusion length using a list of length/factor pairs, blended smoothly between points. It affects rectilinear and monotonic solid fill only: internal solid infill, top surfaces and the bottom of the first layer.

settings.advice: Enable if small top features look blobby or over-full.
Start from the default model; lower factors for short lengths if small areas still over-extrude.

facts: Model format: one 'length,factor;' pair per line, e.g. 0,0; 0.2,0.4444; ... 10,1;
Lines longer than the last listed length use full flow

entries.title: Small perimeter speed and threshold for tiny features
entries.summary: Walls whose length divided by 2*pi is at or below the small perimeter threshold (a radius in mm) print at the small perimeter speed, which can be a percentage of the outer wall speed. Slowing small loops such as pins and small holes gives each layer more time to cool and improves accuracy. A threshold of 0 disables the feature.

settings.advice: Around 50% of outer wall speed; lower if small pins or holes melt or deform.
A few mm catches small holes and pins (5 mm covers loops up to 31.4 mm long); 0 disables.

facts: A threshold of 5 mm treats any perimeter up to 31.4 mm long as small
Example at 5 mm: a 10 mm circle (31.4 mm) counts as small, a 10x10 mm square (40 mm) does not
A percentage value is calculated from the outer wall speed; Orca's documented default is 50%

entries.title: Sparse infill density: strength vs material and time
entries.summary: Infill density is the share of the interior volume filled by the sparse pattern. Higher density adds strength, weight, material and time, but strength gains flatten out: walls and top/bottom shells usually matter more. Low densities suit display parts and load-bearing parts benefit from more, but patterns interpret density differently, so actual material use varies. Very low density needs more top layers to avoid pillowing.

settings.advice: Default 20%; lower for display parts, raise for load-bearing parts, and add walls before going very dense.
Raise to make small islands solid for strength; lower to save material.
Increase slightly if infill separates from walls; too high pushes walls outward.
2-3 lines can add strength and speed without more material for supported patterns.

facts: Default in this slicer: 20%
Small sparse areas below the minimum sparse infill threshold (default 15 mm2) are printed solid
Infill/wall overlap (default 15%) improves bonding between infill and walls
Fill multiline prints several parallel lines per path while keeping density and material the same

entries.title: Choosing a sparse infill pattern (gyroid, grid, cubic, lightning...)
entries.summary: Patterns trade strength, direction, speed and material. Grid, Cubic, Quarter Cubic, Triangles and Gyroid/TPMS rate high for strength; Gyroid is isotropic and its curves spread shrinkage, reducing warping. Adaptive Cubic saves material by thinning toward the center. Lightning and Support Cubic only support top surfaces and are weak but very fast. Rectilinear has low vertical strength. Honeycomb is strong but slow and heavy.

settings.advice: Gyroid or Cubic for strong all-round parts, Grid for fast strong prints, Adaptive Cubic for big parts, Lightning for quick visual models.
If infill is visible (translucent parts), print it closer to outer wall speed.

facts: Orca ratings (strength X-Y/Z): Grid, Cubic, Quarter Cubic, Gyroid, TPMS-D rate high in both; Triangles high X-Y, normal Z
Lightning: lowest material and fastest, but low strength; for non-structural prototypes
Grid lines cross on each layer, which can cause nozzle noise or artifacts at intersections
Gyroid takes longer to slice and print than straight patterns
Adaptive Cubic is good for large prints: denser near walls, sparse in the center
Concentric suits 100% infill or flexible parts
Grid, Triangles, Cubic and Adaptive Cubic use a non-crossing path when multiline infill is enabled

sources.title: OrcaSlicer wiki - Infill patterns quick reference

entries.title: Spiral vase mode
entries.summary: Spiral vase turns a model into a single continuous outer wall that rises in a spiral, with solid bottom layers and no infill or top, so there is no seam. It suits vases, lamp shades and containers. Smooth spiral also smooths XY moves to hide seams on non-vertical walls. Starting and finishing flow ratios tune the first and last loop to avoid under-extrusion; they only apply with relative E distances.

settings.advice: Enable for single-wall, seamless vases and shades.
Enable to hide seams on sloped walls; requires relative E for best results.
Raise for smoother spirals; lower if the shape distorts.
Raise if the first spiral loop is thin.
Raise if the last loop is under-extruded.
A wider line gives stronger vase walls; stay below about 150% of nozzle diameter.

facts: Only one wall is printed, so strength and water-tightness depend on line width; wider lines help
Scarf seams and wall direction settings do not apply in vase mode
Max XY smoothing as a percentage is relative to nozzle diameter; high values may distort the model

entries.title: Support enforcers, blockers and painting supports
entries.summary: Support painting lets you mark areas that must get support (enforce) or must not (block). Blockers are best when the automatic layout is mostly right but adds unwanted support in a few spots; enforcers with a manual support type give full control and can also add a support under the middle of a very long bridge. With normal supports, Don't support bridges stops supports being generated under bridgeable areas.
steps: Select the model and open the support painting tool in the Prepare view
Paint enforcers on overhangs that need support and blockers where support is unwanted
Choose an auto support type to add painted enforcers to automatic support, or a manual type to use only painted areas
Slice and check the preview for unsupported overhangs or leftover support

settings.advice: Use normal(manual) or tree(manual) to generate support only at painted enforcers.
Normal supports: enable to avoid huge supports under bridges that print fine.

entries.title: Dedicated support or soluble interface filament
entries.summary: On multi-material printers you can print the support base and the interface with different filaments. A dedicated breakaway or soluble interface allows a top Z distance of 0, giving a smooth underside while still separating easily. To save time and material, use support filament only for the interface and the main filament for the support body. Never pair mismatched temperature classes (e.g. PLA support under ABS).

settings.advice: Choose the soluble or breakaway support filament for the interface.
Keep Default (main filament) for the support body to save expensive support filament.
Enable to avoid using the interface filament for the support body.
0 with soluble or dedicated support interface for the smoothest underside.

facts: With an interface filament and 2+ interface layers, Orca prints the last interface layer (touching the support body) in the base filament as a bonding layer
Set interface layers to 1 if you want the interface purely in its own filament
Going from 1 to 2 interface layers adds a second material and extra tool changes
Bambu notes PLA and PETG can act as support interface for each other in some cases

entries.title: Support type and style: normal vs tree, auto vs manual
entries.summary: Normal supports project straight down under overhangs and give a stable, flat base, good for large flat overhangs. Tree supports branch from trunks, use less material, touch the model at fewer points and are usually easier to remove, good for organic shapes and figures. Auto generates support wherever overhangs need it plus at enforcers; Manual only where enforcers are painted. The threshold angle decides which overhangs get support.

settings.advice: Enable when overhangs are steeper than roughly 45-60 deg from vertical (printer and material dependent) or bridges are too long.
Tree (auto) for organic models; Normal (auto) for flat overhangs; manual types for full control with enforcers.
Organic for most tree supports; Snug for material-saving normal supports; Tree Strong for heavy overhangs.
Lower to generate less support (printer must handle steeper overhangs); raise to support more.
Enable to avoid supports landing on the model; check the preview for unsupported areas.
Enable to skip tiny overhangs that print fine without support.
Tree auto only: minimal support for sharp tails and cantilevers.

facts: Styles: Grid and Snug for normal supports; Organic (default for tree), Tree Slim, Tree Strong, Tree Hybrid for tree supports
Snug saves material and reduces scarring compared with Grid
Tree Hybrid builds normal-like support under large flat overhangs
Default threshold angle in this slicer: 30 deg; smaller values support fewer, steeper overhangs
Support critical regions only (Tree auto) supports only sharp tails and cantilevers
Organic tree supports are not compatible with variable layer height in Bambu Studio

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Adaptive layer height

entries.title: Support Z distance, XY distance and interface layers
entries.summary: Top Z distance is the gap between support and the overhang above it: larger is easier to remove but leaves a rougher underside, smaller is smoother but can fuse. Interface layers form a dense flat surface under the overhang for a better finish but are harder to peel. XY distance keeps supports away from vertical walls. A Z distance of 0 is meant only for soluble or dedicated support material.

settings.advice: Default 0.2 mm; Prusa suggests 50-75% of layer height. Raise if supports fuse, lower for a smoother underside. 0 only for soluble.
Gap where supports stand on the model; raise if they scar the surface below.
2-3 for a flat, smooth underside; 0 for fastest, easiest removal but rougher overhangs.
Use where supports land on visible model surfaces.
Increase to ease removal; 0 makes the interface solid.
Raise if supports stick to vertical walls; lower to support small details closer.
Set higher than normal fan to make interfaces separate more easily; -1 disables.
Enable for custom Z gaps and faster supports when no prime tower is used.

facts: Defaults in this slicer: top and bottom Z distance 0.2 mm, XY distance 0.35 mm, 3 top interface layers, interface spacing 0.5 mm
Z distances are rounded to a multiple of layer height unless independent support layer height is on
Prusa suggests a contact Z distance of about 50-75% of layer height for same-material supports
Interface spacing 0 makes a solid interface
Independent support layer height is ignored when a prime tower is printed
A higher support interface fan speed weakens the bond and eases removal

entries.title: Top and bottom shell layers and thickness
entries.summary: Shell layers are the solid layers on top and bottom of a part, including the visible surface. More top layers bridge sparse infill better, giving flatter tops without pillowing or pinholes, and add strength. Shell thickness is a minimum: if layers x layer height is thinner, Orca adds layers, which keeps shells adequate at small layer heights. At least 3 shell layers is a common minimum.

settings.advice: Add 1-2 layers if tops show pillowing or pinholes, especially with low infill or thin layers.
Default 0.6 mm; raise it so thin layer heights still get enough top layers.
3 is typical; more for watertight or stiffer bases.
Optional minimum bottom thickness; 0 means layer count alone decides.
25-30%; raise slightly if gaps appear between top surface and walls.

facts: Defaults in this slicer: 4 top layers, 3 bottom layers, top shell thickness 0.6 mm, bottom shell thickness 0 (disabled)
Low sparse infill density usually needs more top layers to avoid pillowing
Top/bottom infill-wall overlap of 25-30% is a good start to avoid gaps where the surface meets the walls
Only the outermost shell layer uses the top surface pattern; the rest use the internal solid infill pattern

sources.title: OrcaSlicer wiki - Top and Bottom Shells

entries.title: Top surface pattern, one-wall tops and surface flow for smooth tops
entries.summary: Monotonic or Monotonic line patterns lay top lines in one direction for an even sheen and are usually recommended for top surfaces. Only one wall on top surfaces frees space for the surface pattern, which helps small tops such as raised letters. A slightly reduced top surface flow ratio can smooth a top that looks over-full, but calibrate the filament flow ratio first. Matching top surface speed and acceleration to the outer wall also helps.

settings.advice: Monotonic line or Monotonic for even, smooth tops; Concentric or Archimedean chords for decorative round tops.
Monotonic for flat, even bottoms; concentric can help on round parts.
Enable for small top features like text; set the threshold to 0 if it causes artifacts on thin features above.
Lower slightly only if tops look over-extruded after the filament flow ratio is calibrated.
Keep similar to outer wall speed for a smooth finish.
Use a value close to the outer wall acceleration.

sources.title: OrcaSlicer wiki - Top and Bottom Shells

entries.title: Travel speed and travel acceleration
entries.summary: Travel moves carry the nozzle without extruding. Faster travel and higher travel acceleration shorten the time the nozzle can ooze, which reduces stringing and blobs at seam starts. Too fast can cause missed steps, ringing or knocking parts over. Keep travel as fast as the printer reliably allows.

settings.advice: Raise within printer limits to reduce oozing and stringing; lower if you see layer shifts or parts knocked loose.
Usually higher than print acceleration to cut travel time; limited by Motion ability settings.

sources.title: OrcaSlicer wiki - Seam (troubleshooting the start of a seam)

entries.title: Tree support branch settings (angle, diameter, distance, brim)
entries.summary: Tree branch settings trade stability against reach and material. A lower branch angle makes more vertical, stable branches; a higher angle lets them reach farther. Thicker branches and a branch diameter angle add stability for tall supports. Smaller branch distance and higher branch density support overhangs better but are harder to remove; Orca suggests top interface layers instead of very dense branches. Tip diameter, density and diameter angle apply only to Organic.

settings.advice: Lower for stability on tall supports; raise to reach around the model.
Organic style equivalent of branch angle.
Raise for sturdier organic branches on tall prints.
Smaller tips leave smaller marks but hold less.
Smaller gives more contact points and better overhangs but harder removal.
Branch density; prefer interface layers over very high values.
Keep on so tall thin branches get wider brims.
Raise to leave more short bridges unsupported; 0 supports all bridges.

facts: Default tree branch angle in this slicer: 40 deg
Auto brim width (Tree Slim/Strong/Hybrid) scales each branch brim with its height, never under 2 mm
Tree support wall count 0 means auto (range 0-2)
Max bridge length: bridges anchored at both ends up to this length are left unsupported by tree supports

entries.title: Variable and adaptive layer height
entries.summary: Variable layer height uses thin layers only where the surface slope needs them (domes, gentle slopes) and thick layers elsewhere, giving smooth curves without the time cost of a uniformly fine profile. In the variable layer height tool, Adaptive sets heights automatically using a quality/speed slider, Smooth blends transitions, and manual editing lowers or raises heights at chosen points. Heights stay within the printer's min/max layer height.

settings.advice: Lower bound for adaptive heights; set by nozzle size (about 0.08 mm for 0.4 mm).
Upper bound; about 75-80% of nozzle diameter.
Base height that variable layer height modifies.

facts: Flat or gently sloped tops show stair-stepping most; thinner layers there help
A prime tower needs all objects to share the same layer heights
Bambu Studio notes variable layer height is not supported with organic tree supports
This slicer has no single adaptive layer height checkbox; use the Variable layer height tool on the object

sources.title: Bambu Lab wiki - Adaptive layer height

entries.title: Wall generator: Arachne vs Classic
entries.summary: Classic keeps every wall the same width and creates as many loops as fit, giving continuous walls and one seam per layer but losing features too thin for a full loop. Arachne varies line width to follow the shape, so small text and thin features print and gaps between walls shrink, but it can create broken or uneven-width walls that affect surface finish. Use Arachne for thin or detailed parts, Classic when you want uniform walls or predictable dimensions.

settings.advice: Arachne for thin features, text and tapered shapes; Classic for uniform, continuous walls.
Lower to keep slightly thinner features; raise for more robust thin walls.
Lower to keep very fine details that otherwise disappear.
Keep at 1 so only the innermost wall changes width and the outer surface stays even.
Lower reduces center walls in wedges but may leave gaps or over-extrude.

facts: Minimum wall width (default 85% of nozzle) is the width used to replace features thinner than a normal wall
Minimum feature size (default 25% of nozzle): features thinner than this are dropped
Wall distribution count limits width variation to the innermost walls, keeping outer walls uniform
Wall transitioning threshold angle (default 10 deg) controls when even/odd wall transitions are made
Fuzzy skin Extrusion and Combined modes require Arachne

entries.title: Wall loops (perimeters) and strength
entries.summary: Wall loops is the number of perimeters on each layer. More walls add strength, stiffness and layer adhesion, and stop infill showing through the surface, at the cost of time and material. For strong parts, adding walls usually helps more than raising infill density. Alternate extra wall adds one wall on every other layer so infill locks between walls.

settings.advice: Default 2; add walls for functional, load-bearing or screw-fastened parts. Each wall adds time and material.
Enable for extra strength by wedging infill between walls; avoid with Lightning infill.
Classic generator only: enable if thin features vanish; single-line walls are weaker.
All (default) adds solid infill under sloped surfaces; use Moderate if combining with alternate extra wall.

facts: Default in this slicer: 2 walls
Prusa notes PETG infill is relatively weak, so for solid parts add perimeters rather than infill
Alternate extra wall works poorly with Lightning infill and with Ensure vertical shell thickness set to All
Detect thin wall prints walls too thin for two lines as a single line; Arachne handles thin walls differently and disables it

entries.title: Wall printing order: Inner/Outer, Outer/Inner, Inner/Outer/Inner
entries.summary: Inner/Outer (default) prints inner walls first, so overhanging outer walls lean on them: best for overhangs but the outer wall gets pushed slightly. Outer/Inner gives the cleanest, most accurate outer wall but weaker overhangs and less consistent seams. Inner/Outer/Inner prints the third wall onward, then the outer, then the first inner wall, giving good surface and accuracy with better seams; it needs 3 or more walls.

settings.advice: Inner/Outer for overhang-heavy parts; Inner/Outer/Inner (3+ walls) for surface quality and accuracy.
Usually leave off; if used, pair with Precise wall or Inner/Outer/Inner to avoid bulging walls.
Enable with Inner/Outer to reduce outer-wall bulge and improve dimensional accuracy.

facts: Inner/Outer/Inner falls back to Outer/Inner where fewer than 3 walls exist; the first layer prints Inner/Outer
For seams, Inner/Outer/Inner is typically best, followed by Inner/Outer, because the nozzle travels only a short distance before the outer wall
Print infill first can help some overhangs but pushes walls out and may show infill through the surface
Precise wall only applies to the Inner/Outer order in this slicer

entries.title: Wipe while retracting, wipe distance and wipe on loops
entries.summary: Wipe moves the nozzle back along the last path while retracting to scrape off leaked plastic and reduce blobs after travel. Retract amount before wipe decides how much retraction happens before the wipe move. Wipe on loops tucks the end of the outer wall inward, and wipe before external loop deretracts inside the part so restart blobs are hidden. These make seams more consistent rather than invisible.

settings.advice: Enable to reduce blobs and strings at the end of extrusions.
Default 1 mm; longer wipes clean more but take time.
Lower to retract partly during the wipe; 100% retracts fully before wiping.
Enable to tuck in the outer-wall seam end.
Enable to hide restart blobs inside the part.
Enable so wipes match feature speed.
Used when role based wipe speed is off; absolute or % of travel speed.

facts: Defaults in this slicer: wipe distance 1 mm, retract amount before wipe 100%
Wipe on loops makes a short inward move of about 20% of nozzle diameter and needs more than one wall
Role based wipe speed wipes at the speed the feature was printed, recommended on
Wipe before external loop is most useful with Outer/Inner or Inner/Outer/Inner order

entries.title: XY hole/contour compensation, polyholes and shrinkage
entries.summary: Printed holes often come out small and outer dimensions slightly large. XY hole compensation grows (positive) or shrinks (negative) holes; XY contour compensation does the same for outer contours. Polyholes convert round holes into polygons that print closer to the intended diameter. Filament shrinkage (XY) scales parts to offset material shrink, e.g. for ABS. Calibrate with the tolerance test before changing these.

settings.advice: Increase in small steps (e.g. 0.05 mm) if pins or screws do not fit holes.
Use small negative values if outer dimensions measure too large.
Enable for more accurate round holes in functional parts.
Set from measured shrinkage for high-shrink materials like ABS, ASA, PA.

facts: Positive hole compensation makes holes bigger; positive contour compensation makes outer contours bigger
Shrinkage is entered as the percentage you measure, e.g. 94% if a 100 mm part measures 94 mm
Only the filament used for the perimeter is considered for shrinkage compensation
ABS parts typically shrink about 1-2% after cooling (Prusa)

entries.title: Z-hop height, type and where it applies
entries.summary: Z-hop lifts the nozzle during retracted travels so it does not scrape or knock the print, useful for tall thin parts, many objects and curling overhangs. Large hops increase stringing and time. Types: Normal lifts straight up, Slope moves diagonally, Spiral lifts in a spiral, Auto picks based on whether travel crosses overhangs. Lift can be limited to a Z range or to top/bottom surfaces.

settings.advice: 0.2-0.4 mm is typical; lower it if stringing increases, raise if the nozzle hits curled edges.
Spiral or Slope to reduce strings and marks; Normal is simplest.
Top Only limits hops to top surfaces to save time while avoiding scars.
Set a Z above which hopping starts, e.g. skip hops on the first layers.
Set a Z below which hopping happens; 0 means no limit.
Angle for Slope/Spiral hops; 90 deg equals Normal lift.

facts: Default in this slicer: 0.4 mm hop, Slope type
Ellis runs about 0.2 mm and found more than about 0.3 mm increased stringing
Traveling angle of 90 deg makes Slope/Spiral behave like Normal lift

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 3D printing specifications (A150/A250/A350, single vs dual extrusion)
entries.summary: Snapmaker 2.0 is the A series (A150, A250, A350; 3-in-1 with the Single Extrusion Module), the quieter AT series (A250T, A350T, upgraded printing, linear and power modules) and the print-only F series (F250, F350). Usable volume depends on frame size and printing module: the Dual Extrusion Module gives up some area to its second nozzle. Bed temperature limits differ by frame size, and a Quick Swap Kit shortens Y and Z travel by about 15 mm.

settings.advice: Match the work area of your frame size and module; the Dual Extrusion Module area is smaller than the single module's on every frame.
Single module: 145/235/330 mm for A150/A250/A350; dual: 110/205/290 mm. Take off about 15 mm more with a Quick Swap Kit if the profile does not already.
Never exceed 275 C on the Single Extrusion Module or 300 C on the Dual Extrusion Module.
Plan for at most 80 C on A350-size beds and 100 C on A250-size beds; temperatures near the limit take 20-30 minutes to reach.
Keep between 0.05 and 0.3 mm with the standard 0.4 mm nozzle.
Cap around 9 mm³/s for the Single Extrusion Module; the Dual Extrusion Module is rated to about 20 mm³/s.

facts: Single Extrusion Module work area: A150 160 x 160 x 145 mm; A250/F250/A250T 230 x 250 x 235 mm; A350/F350/A350T 320 x 350 x 330 mm.

Dual Extrusion Module work area: A150 135 x 140 x 110 mm with both or the right nozzle, 145 x 145 x 110 mm left nozzle only; A250/F250/A250T 220 x 235 x 205 mm; A350/F350/A350T 310 x 325 x 290 mm both nozzles, 310 x 330 x 290 mm one nozzle.
Maximum nozzle temperature: 275 C on the Single Extrusion Module, 300 C on the Dual Extrusion Module.
Rated extrusion flow: about 9 mm³/s (single) and 20 mm³/s (dual). Fans: 2 on the single module, 4 on the dual.
Both modules ship with a 0.4 mm brass nozzle; the dual module also accepts 0.2/0.6/0.8 mm brass and a 0.4 mm hardened nozzle. Dual hot ends are quick-swap, the single hot end is not.
The dual module changes nozzles by motor-lifting the right extruder; its calibration adds XY offset calibration to mesh leveling and Z offset.
Layer height range: 0.05-0.3 mm (50-300 microns).

Heated bed: the filament library caps A350/A350T/F350 at 80 C and A250/A250T at 100 C; the FAQ says 80-100 C is reachable but needs about 20-30 minutes. A third-party power supply to go hotter damages the bed.
Single module materials: PLA, ABS, PETG, TPU. Its brass nozzle is not hard enough for nylon. The dual module adds Breakaway PLA, ASA, PVA, HIPS, TPU variants, CoPA, PA6-CF, PA6-GF and PA12-CF.
Module size (W x D x H): single 90 x 51 x 91.5 mm, dual 108 x 70 x 133 mm. Power supply input 100-240 V AC.

sources.title: Quick Start Guide for Snapmaker 2.0 Quick Swap Kit

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 auto-leveling fails at the first calibration point
entries.summary: A failure at the first leveling point usually means the module cannot get close enough to the bed because the Y axis or the printing module is mounted out of position, the Quick Swap Kit install status does not match the hardware, or the proximity sensor is dead or stuck triggered. Manual leveling works as a stopgap.
symptoms: Calibration failure prompt at point 1
Module moves in the air and never descends to the bed
causes: Y-axis or printing module mounted outside the range the firmware allows
Quick Swap Kit fitted but not selected, or selected but not fitted
Proximity sensor does not trigger (no red light near steel)
Proximity sensor permanently triggered
steps: As a workaround, finish leveling with Manual calibration.
Check the Y-axis linear modules and the printing module are mounted in their correct positions.
Under Settings, set the Quick Swap install status to match whether the kit is installed.
With the machine on, bring a steel object up to the proximity sensor; if its red light stays off, replace the sensor.
If the module never approaches the bed because the sensor reads triggered all the time, replace the sensor.

sources.title: The first point failed during the automatic calibration process

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 Bracing Kit: installation overview, firmware and recalibration
entries.summary: The Bracing Kit adds five plates with spring-loaded rollers to the X, Y and Z sliders, stiffening the linear modules and preventing slider looseness. It needs Luban 4.11.0+ and firmware 1.19.0+, the install status set on the Touchscreen, and recalibration of the printing module. Leave the roller limit screws alone; their tension is preset at the factory.
steps: Jog the toolhead to mid-X and line the support platform up with the base plate holes, then power off and unplug DC power, the Touchscreen and, if fitted, the enclosure's Addon 3 cable.
Remove the toolhead and support platform (with a Quick Swap Kit, unplug the bed and slide the platform out).
Run the Z sliders to the far end, detach the X axis and fit the Z bracing plates with the original M4 x 8 screws.
Mount the X axis on the Z sliders, raise it to the top with a hand at each end keeping it level, then fit the X bracing plate.
Line the Y sliders up with the base plate holes, fit the Y bracing plates, then the platform and toolhead (M4 x 14 screws).
Reconnect enclosure, Touchscreen and DC power; set Settings > Quick Swap Kit/Bracing Kit Install Status.
Redo bed leveling (single module) or the full dual-module calibration.
facts: The kit's M4 x 22 screws are for mounting the 20W/40W laser module.
Assembly is the same on 250 and 350 models.

sources.title: Quick Start Guide for Snapmaker 2.0 Bracing Kit
Detaching the toolhead and the support platform
Attaching the Y-axis bracing plates and the support platform
What should I do when the slider of the Linear Module comes loose?

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 says 'not responding' after the Dual Extrusion Module is first fitted
entries.summary: If the screen shows not responding the first time the Dual Extrusion Module is installed, while the single module worked fine, the firmware is too old to recognize the dual module. Update it with the dual module unplugged.
steps: Power off and unplug the Dual Extrusion Module cable.
Power on and update the firmware from the Touchscreen or with the latest firmware on a USB flash drive.
Power off, reconnect the dual module, power on and check.

sources.title: The screen is not responding when the dual extruder is connected

entries.title: Calibrating the Snapmaker 2.0 Dual Extrusion Module: leveling, Z offset, XY nozzle offset
entries.summary: The Dual Extrusion Module needs three calibrations: mesh bed leveling, Z Offset, and an XY offset calibration that registers the two nozzles to each other. A Sensor Calibration (dual module only) can be run before an Auto Z Offset when first layers come out wrong. Recalibrate whenever a Quick Swap Kit or Bracing Kit is added or removed, and keep the Touchscreen install status in step with the hardware, or leveling can fail with Result 7.
steps: Update firmware first; a newly fitted Dual Extrusion Module may not be recognized on old firmware.
Check Settings > Quick Swap Install Status (Quick Swap Kit/Bracing Kit Install Status on newer firmware) matches what is installed.
Run heated bed leveling, preferably with the 25-point grid.
Run Z Offset calibration. If it is off, run Sensor Calibration and redo Z Offset in Auto mode, or do it in Manual mode.
Run the XY offset calibration so both nozzles print in the same place.
Fine-tune nozzle height during the first layer with Z Offset in the print screen's swipe-left menu.
facts: Single module calibration is mesh leveling plus Z offset; the dual module adds XY offset calibration.
Quick Swap Kit needs firmware 1.16.5 or later; Bracing Kit needs 1.19.0 or later.

sources.title: How to fix the Dual Extruder 'Result 7' error?
Quick Start Guide for Snapmaker 2.0 Bracing Kit

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 Dual Extrusion Module filament runout error (false alarm or no alarm)
entries.summary: False runout errors with filament loaded, or no pause when filament really runs out, come from a worn sensor switch on older modules without the replacement kit; on newer or kit-upgraded modules from broken wires or loose terminals, loose board screws, or a missing or reversed copper block or trigger pad. Detection may also simply be switched off.
causes: Old module without replacement kit: sensor switch worn
Broken sensor wire, damaged or loose terminal
Sensor board fixing screws loose
Copper block left out during kit install, wearing the switch
Trigger pad or copper block fitted the wrong way so the lever misses the filament
Runout detection disabled
steps: To print meanwhile, send M412 S0 from the Luban console over USB (M412 S1 re-enables, M412 reports status).
Old module without the kit: fit the replacement kit's runout sensor.
Otherwise power off, remove the module, take out the four back screws (H2.0), the hot ends and the four top screws (H1.5), then slide off the front cover and shell.
Check both sensor switch wires for breaks, loose connectors or backed-out pins; reconnect, repair or get a new wire from support.
Tighten the sensor circuit board screws if loose.
Remove the board, check the switch for wear, and check the copper blocks and trigger pads are present and facing the right way.
If detection was turned off, turn it back on from the Touchscreen.

entries.title: Fitting the filament holder and tube holder for the Dual Extrusion Module in the 2.0 enclosure
entries.summary: When the Dual Extrusion Module runs inside the Snapmaker 2.0 enclosure, replace the original filament holder with the new one and route the filament tube through the side panel so filament reaches the module smoothly.
steps: Remove the original filament holder from the enclosure.
Fit the sliding nut into the enclosure's left-side 48CA beam, positioned level with the snap bushing, and fix the new holder to it.
Squeeze both sides of the snap bushing from inside and push it out of the side panel.
Mount the filament tube holder and tube in that side panel opening.
Take the tube fixture off the module's filament entry, push the tube in and refit the fixture.

sources.title: Installing the filament holder and the filament tube holder

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 Dual Extrusion Module nozzle starts below the print sheet and hits the bed
entries.summary: On a machine without the Quick Swap Kit, a dual-module nozzle that starts lower than the print sheet and strikes the bed means the Dual Extrusion Module is mounted in the wrong position.
steps: Compare the module's mounting position with the reference in the wiki and correct it if wrong.
If the problem continues, export the logs (Settings > Export Log) and send them to support.

sources.title: The nozzle is below the print sheet at the beginning of printing

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 enclosure always reports the door open (door detection failure)
entries.summary: If the machine never sees the enclosure door as closed, a magnet has fallen off or the door sensor PCB is damaged. Check the four magnets, then the four LEDs on the sensor board.
causes: Enclosure magnet missing or detached
Door sensor PCB damaged
steps: Confirm all four magnets are on the enclosure and firmly attached.
Close the front and side doors and check that all four LEDs on the door sensor PCB light.
Alternatively bring a screwdriver close to, without touching, each of the four contacts and watch its LED.
If the LEDs do not respond correctly, replace the door sensor PCB; keep the gasket behind it when removing it.

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 enclosure not recognized (no enclosure icon)
entries.summary: No enclosure icon after plugging in the enclosure points to outdated firmware, a damaged expansion cable, or a faulty enclosure port on the Controller. Update firmware, then measure the port voltages with a multimeter to locate the fault.
causes: Outdated firmware
Enclosure expansion cable damaged
Controller enclosure port damaged
steps: Install the latest firmware.
Unplug the expansion cable at the enclosure end, leave it in the Controller, power on and measure: pin 1 to 4 about 24 V; pin 1 to 2 and pin 1 to 3 about 2.2 V. Never short pin 4 to pin 2 or 3.
All readings normal: the enclosure PCB needs replacing.
24 V normal but 2.2 V wrong: the enclosure-port CAN chip in the Controller has failed; replace the Controller.
24 V wrong: measure directly at the Controller port. Still wrong means the Controller; correct means the cable.

sources.title: Why is the Enclosure not recognized by the machine?

entries.title: Exporting Snapmaker 2.0 logs to a USB drive (FW and SC files)
entries.summary: Snapmaker 2.0 logs can only be exported to a USB flash drive, via Settings > Export Log. Wait a while after the success message before unplugging. Files starting with FW come from the main controller, SC files from the Touchscreen; higher numbers are newer.
steps: Insert a USB flash drive into the machine.
Tap Settings > Export Log and wait for the export success screen.
Wait a little longer before removing the drive so all files finish writing.
On a computer, send the newest FW and SC files to support.

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 'Fabscreen has stopped' error
entries.summary: This Touchscreen crash is caused by old firmware, a very large G-code file (common when sending over Wi-Fi), or G-code the screen cannot parse, such as output from a third-party slicer Snapmaker does not support.
causes: Outdated firmware
G-code file too large
G-code generated by incompatible third-party software
steps: Update the firmware.
Try a smaller G-code file.
Re-slice with a slicer and printer profile made for Snapmaker 2.0 (the wiki suggests the latest Luban) and try again.

sources.title: What should I do if the Touchscreen shows 'Fabscreen has stopped'?

entries.title: Updating Snapmaker 2.0 firmware over Wi-Fi or USB flash drive
entries.summary: Touchscreens on firmware V1.9.0 or later can update over Wi-Fi or from a USB flash drive; older versions must update from USB. Restart the machine afterwards. Up-to-date firmware is the first fix for many issues, such as a new Dual Extrusion Module not responding, nozzle crashes, an unrecognized enclosure and Fabscreen errors.
steps: Wi-Fi: connect to a network, swipe left on the home screen, open Settings and choose Firmware Update > Check for Updates > Update Now > Complete.
USB: download the firmware from support.snapmaker.com, copy it to the drive, plug it into the Controller, power on, then open Files > USB and select the firmware file.
When done, power off, wait 5 seconds and power on again.
facts: Quick Swap Kit requires firmware 1.16.5 or later; Bracing Kit requires 1.19.0 or later.

sources.title: Quick Start Guide for Snapmaker 2.0 Quick Swap Kit
Quick Start Guide for Snapmaker 2.0 Bracing Kit

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 first layer not sticking to the Print Sheet
entries.summary: On the Snapmaker 2.0 this usually comes from an inaccurate or unfinished calibration, a first layer printed too fast, or degraded filament. Recalibrate, nudge Z Offset live during the first layer, slow the initial layer to under 20 mm/s, and try fresh filament or glue.
symptoms: First lines curl, lift or get dragged by the nozzle
Print comes loose early and fails
causes: Leveling or Z offset inaccurate or incomplete
Initial layer printed too fast
Old, damp or degraded filament
steps: Redo bed leveling and Z Offset calibration as described in the Quick Start Guide.
Start the print, swipe left on the print screen to reveal the hidden menu, tap Z Offset and use Up or Down to move the nozzle slightly closer.
Re-slice with the initial layer speed below 20 mm/s.
Try a different spool of filament.
Spread a thin layer of glue on the Print Sheet.

settings.advice: Lower to under 20 mm/s so the first layer has time to bond to the sheet.
Lower along with initial_layer_speed, to about 20 mm/s or less.

sources.title: The first layer did not stick to the print sheet

entries.title: G-code will not transfer to the Snapmaker 2.0 over Wi-Fi
entries.summary: Wi-Fi transfers fail when the link between computer and machine drops, the signal is weak, firmware or software is out of date, or the file is too big. Restart and reconnect on the same network, update, and keep files under 100 MB.
causes: Connection between machine and software interrupted
Unstable Wi-Fi
Outdated firmware or software
G-code file too large
steps: Restart the machine and the slicer software and reconnect.
Make sure the Touchscreen and the computer are on the same network with a stable signal.
Install the latest firmware and software.
Try a G-code file smaller than 100 MB, or use a USB flash drive instead.

sources.title: What should I do if the G-code file cannot be transferred to the machine via Wi-Fi?

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 heated bed leveling modes and calibration grid (9/16/25 points)
entries.summary: The Snapmaker 2.0 printing module has a distance (proximity) sensor that probes the bed at a grid of points; the firmware then shifts Z during printing to follow an uneven Print Sheet. There are four modes: Auto, Manual, Heated Auto and Heated Manual Leveling. Auto or Manual is the normal choice; switch to a heated mode if the first layer will not stick. The grid can be 9, 16 or 25 points; 25 is recommended when adhesion is poor.
steps: Choose the mode on the Touchscreen under Settings > 3D Printing > Auto Leveling or Heated Leveling.
Choose the grid under Settings > 3D Printing > Calibration Grid (9-point, 16-point or 25-point).
For adhesion problems, preheat the bed first (for example 65 C for 15 minutes) so it is measured at working temperature.
Swipe left on the home screen, tap Calibration, then Start to run leveling; follow with Z Offset calibration.
In heated modes keep bare hands off the bed while it probes.
Repeat leveling after fitting or removing a Quick Swap Kit or Bracing Kit, or after remounting linear modules.
facts: The probed heights are stored and used to keep the nozzle-to-sheet distance constant throughout the print.

sources.title: What should I do if the 3D Printing Module pushes into the Print Sheet?

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 heated bed will not heat up
entries.summary: Usually the heated bed cable is broken (often near its solder joint from repeated flexing), the bed itself is faulty, or the Controller's bed port has failed. Inspect the cable, then measure resistance at the plug: pins 4-1 about 2.5 Ω and pins 3-2 about 110 kΩ.
causes: Heated bed cable broken
Heated bed faulty
Controller heated bed port broken
steps: Inspect the bed cable and its solder joints for visible breaks.
Break in the middle of the cable: replace the cable or the bed. Break close to the solder joint: shorten the cable and resolder it pin by pin.
If the cable looks intact, measure with a multimeter: pin 4 to pin 1 about 2.5 Ω, pin 3 to pin 2 about 110 kΩ.
Abnormal readings: inspect the bed for scratches or damage. Normal readings: the Controller's bed port is the likely fault.
Print Snapmaker's heated bed cable protector or cable clamp model to stop the cable fatiguing again.

sources.title: What should I do if the Heated Bed won't heat up?

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 linear module moves one way only, grinds at the end cap or fails homing (M119)
entries.summary: A stuck, loose or broken end-stop (limit) switch lets the linear module run into its end cap with a grinding noise, fail to home, or move in one direction only. Query switch states with M119; a switch that reads TRIGGERED at rest is the culprit.
symptoms: Homing or calibration fails with grinding noise
Module does not stop at the end cap
Axis moves in only one direction
causes: End-stop switch stuck, loose or damaged
steps: Connect by USB, open the Luban Workspace console and send M119.
Any X_min/X_max/Y_min/Y_max/Z_min/Z_max showing TRIGGERED instead of open marks the faulty axis; test paired Y or Z modules one at a time.
On that module, at the end without the cable, remove the steel strip screws (H2.0) and the end cap screws (H2.5).
Clean and inspect the switch, then press its metal lever and listen for a click.
Reseat a loose switch; replace a damaged one (replacement video, spare from the official store).
Reassemble and test; if it still misbehaves, the linear module may need replacing.

sources.title: The linear module only moves in one direction
Linear module does not stop at end cap and makes abnormal noise
Filament runout sensor and linear module limit switch replacement guide

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 loose linear module slider: bed or head wobble, Y tilt, visible layer lines
entries.summary: A loose slider lets the bed or print head wobble, tilts the Y axis and shows up as layer lines on prints. Take the slider off and turn the eccentric nut on its adjustable bearing side. The Bracing Kit largely removes the need for this adjustment.
symptoms: Bed or print head wobbles
Y axis tilts
Layer lines on prints
causes: Slider bearings have loosened on the linear module
steps: Tools: H2.0, H2.5 and H3.0 screwdrivers, tweezers. Remove the end cover on the end without the cable (H2.5/H2.0).
Pull the stainless steel strip out and slide the slider off slowly so the limit switch at the end is not damaged.
On the adjustable bearing side, loosen the bearing screw half a turn (H3.0), then the fastening screw half a turn.
Hold the eccentric nut slot with tweezers or a flat screwdriver: turn it left to loosen a tight slider, right to tighten a loose one.
Tighten the fastening screw first, then the bearing screw; repeat on the other bearing.
Refit the slider while holding the metal piece down with a screwdriver; on TMC modules also reset the anti-backlash nut.
Consider the Bracing Kit (five bracing plates on the X/Y/Z sliders) to prevent repeat loosening.

sources.title: What should I do when the slider of the Linear Module comes loose?

entries.title: Loading and unloading filament on the Snapmaker 2.0
entries.summary: Filament can be loaded or unloaded automatically or by hand, and the nozzle must be hot either way. For automatic loading, heat the nozzle and tap Load on the Touchscreen; for manual loading, heat it and push the filament through by hand. On the Single Extrusion Module, open the module latch to insert filament and close it before loading.
steps: Heat the nozzle on the Touchscreen (Control > Nozzle); 200 C is enough for PLA.
Insert the filament (open the latch on the single module), then close the latch.
Tap Load to feed automatically or push the filament by hand until it extrudes cleanly.
To remove, heat the nozzle and tap Unload.

sources.title: What should I do if the filament won't load?

entries.title: None of the Snapmaker 2.0 linear modules move
entries.summary: If no axis moves, the modules may not be fully recognized, may be mounted in the wrong positions, TMC and non-TMC modules may be mixed, or the Controller CAN interface or one module's CAN signal is faulty.
causes: Linear modules not fully recognized
Modules installed in the wrong positions
TMC and non-TMC linear modules mixed
Controller CAN interface damaged or a module sending bad CAN signals
steps: Check every linear module cable is connected and not loose.
On AT-series machines read the lead label on each module: X must be 20 mm, both Y 20 mm, both Z 8 mm.
Do not mix TMC and non-TMC linear modules.
Open About Machine; an axis value of 0 points to the module to inspect.
Export the FW and SC logs to a USB drive and send them to support.
facts: AT series leads: X 20 mm, Y 20 mm (two modules), Z 8 mm (two modules).

sources.title: None of the linear modules can move

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 detects none of its toolheads
entries.summary: When no toolhead is recognized at all, the cause is a damaged toolhead cable, a faulty Controller (toolhead port), or a malfunctioning module disrupting CAN communication. Swap the cable, strip the Controller down to essentials, and use the Addon-1 remap to test the port.
causes: Toolhead cable damaged
Controller malfunction
A faulty module disturbing CAN communication
steps: Replace the toolhead cable with one of the interchangeable cables.
Power off and unplug every Controller cable except the Power Module and Touchscreen.
Connect one toolhead, power on and check detection; repeat with each toolhead.
If none is found, the toolhead port may be faulty: send M1029 E2 and M500 over USB serial from Luban, power off, plug into Addon-1 and test again.
If toolheads are detected with the linear modules disconnected, a linear module is the likely cause.
facts: Addon-1 can substitute for the toolhead port only with 3D printing and CNC modules, not laser modules.

sources.title: What should I do if none of the toolheads can be detected by the machine?
What could happen if I plugged in the toolhead cable reversely or hot-swapped?

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 nozzle will not heat (temperature stays at room temperature)
entries.summary: If the shown nozzle temperature sits at room temperature and does not rise when loading or at print start, the heating tube in the hot end or the cable connector feeding it has failed. Check both connectors for bent or uneven contacts and measure the heater; about 17 ± 4 Ω is normal.
symptoms: Nozzle reads ambient temperature
No heat-up when loading/unloading
Print fails because the nozzle never heats
causes: Heating tube inside the hot end failed
Fault in the cable connecting the hot end
steps: Power off and remove the hot end (H2.0 screwdriver).
Inspect the module-side connector for bent or recessed contacts; straighten it or ask support for a replacement.
Inspect the hot end connector the same way; repair it or replace the hot end.
Measure the heating tube with a multimeter; if it is far from 17 ± 4 Ω, replace the hot end.
facts: Single Extrusion Module heater reference resistance: 17 ± 4 Ω.

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 Touchscreen shows -30 C or abnormally high (966 C) nozzle temperature
entries.summary: On the Single Extrusion Module, a nozzle reading of -30 C or an impossibly high value points to a broken hot end thermistor, a damaged quick-release cable, or a faulty printing module. Inspect the cable pins, then swap the hot end.
causes: Hot end thermistor broken
Quick-release cable to the hot end damaged
3D Printing Module fault
steps: Check every pin of the quick-release cable at the hot end: none should be bent, damaged or sunk back into the connector.
Replace the hot end (the wiki links a replacement video).
If a new hot end does not help, the module is suspect; contact Snapmaker support with photos or video.

sources.title: What should I do if the Touchscreen shows a -30℃ or abnormally high nozzle temp?

entries.title: One Snapmaker 2.0 linear module (or one of the paired Y/Z axes) won't move or lags
entries.summary: When a single module stops, or one of the two Y or Z modules lags behind or is noisy, the fault is in the module, its converter or the Controller port. Swap cables and converters to see whether the problem follows the part.
symptoms: One axis module does not move
Paired Y or Z modules move out of step
Noise from a Y or Z module
causes: Faulty linear module
Faulty converter
Faulty Controller port
steps: Power off and push each slider by hand; one that is much stiffer than the others marks a faulty module.
X module: swap the X and Y cables at the Controller and jog Y. If the X module now moves, the Controller's X port is bad; if not, the module is.
Y or Z module: swap the Y and Z converters. If the axis now works, the converter is bad.
Still failing on Y: remove heated bed and platform, plug the suspect module straight into the Controller's Y port and jog it.
Still failing on Z: take off the X module (leave it plugged in), plug the suspect module straight into the Z port and jog it.
Dead when connected directly means the module is damaged; working directly means the converter is.
Export FW and SC logs (Settings > Export Log) and send them to support.

sources.title: The Y-axis (or Z-axis) has one axis that does not move or two Y-axes (or Z-axis) that do not move synchronously

entries.title: Snapmaker 2.0 recommended room temperature and humidity (warping in cold rooms)
entries.summary: Run the printer between 0 and 40 C (32-104 F) and 30-70% relative humidity. Too hot can damage components; too cold slows heat-up and makes prints warp because the upper layers shrink in cool air while the heated base expands. Very damp air harms parts, very dry air brings static that can cause erratic behaviour.

settings.advice: In a cold room raise slightly to counter heat loss; prefer printing in the enclosure to reduce warping.
A wider brim helps hold corners down when a cool room causes warping.

facts: Operating temperature 0-40 C (32-104 F).
Relative humidity 30-70%.
